News.title: 'Culture shift' needed in how UK does business, PM urges
News.content:
The UK needs a "culture shift" in how it does business, Andy Burnham has said ahead of a meeting with some of the UK's biggest bosses.

The prime minister said those who take risks in business should be backed by government and local leaders should have the power to work with businesses.

The current Labour government has been criticised for increasing costs for businesses, such as with the employer national insurance and minimum wage changes under Burnham's predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.

Downing Street said Burnham will meet with the chief executives of BP, Shell, HSBC, Morrisons, Sainsbury's, BT, Vodafone, Rolls-Royce, and several others at Number 10.

Ahead of the meeting, Burnham said he would give people "the confidence that if they have a great idea, they'll get all the support they need to bring it to life".

"When local leaders have the tools to get things done and government works in partnership with business, you can pull in investment, create jobs and transform communities," he said.

He added the government would be "a partner for growth to make every part of Britain better off".

Burnham will host a reception for the business community where local leaders are invited before a private engagement with senior chief executives at Downing Street on Monday evening.

The meeting comes as higher borrowing costs in the UK and other countries present problems for governments looking to spend money on business support or investment.

Official data revealed a surprise boost in the economy in July partly driven by artificial intelligence (AI) investment, though experts expect growth to slow in the months ahead due to high energy prices.

The US-Israel war with Iran has led to a sharp jump in oil prices, which has fed through to higher energy and fuel prices, affecting households and businesses.

This rise in energy costs has led to fears that inflation will remain high, and increase the chance that central banks will hike interest rates to keep price rises under control.

The expectation of higher interest rates, as well as competition for debt from AI firms looking to spend money on development, has driven up the cost of government borrowing in many countries.

However, many argue the UK has a particular problem with high government debt. The UK yield for 10-year bonds, a key measure of government debt costs, is higher than countries such as the US, France, and Japan.

Experts say this is due to several factors affecting investor confidence in the UK, such as multiple prime ministers, chancellors and policy U-turns over a short period.

In an interview with the BBC last week, Chancellor John Healey called for a restoration of "confidence about Britain" despite acknowledging the challenge of "historic high" borrowing costs.

Others have argued that the Labour government has created its own problems by increasing costs for businesses.

Conservative shadow business secretary Julia Lopez said: "The way for the prime minister to get businesses thriving, delivering jobs and driving growth is to cut their taxes.

"Labour's jobs tax and employer red tape have been devastating for businesses. The consequence has been a drying-up of the jobs market, weaker investment and businesses facing ever greater costs."

News.title: Will record donations to Reform go down as a moment of political change?
News.content:
When news of Reform UK's two record-breaking Â£36m donations emerged this weekend, it felt as if Nigel Farage's inner circle was attempting a fightback.

The last few months have proved difficult for the party, with a dip in the polls, a spike in infighting and a series of questions about money that simply won't go away.

In contrast, the mood within the ranks of Labour and the Conservatives has been fairly chipper.

Most Labour MPs feel Andy Burnham has got off to an impressive start as prime minister, while many Conservatives are feeling confident about Kemi Badenoch's recent reshuffle of her top team.

But Reform has been quietly - and as of this weekend rather loudly - building a formidable war chest.

Even before these two mega donations, Reform had raised Â£30.5m since the start of the year, more than double their nearest rivals.

This extra Â£72m takes them into uncharted financial territory, which the party says will be used to hire the brightest policy minds, as well as up to 400 campaign managers in every target seat around the country.

In a world of fractured politics, when seats can be won on increasingly smaller percentages of the vote, having a ground campaign that is effective at getting out the core voter base could become increasingly important.

Some in Westminster have been less than convinced by Burnham's insistence that he won't call an early general election.

It might be tempting for the prime minister to go to the polls before Farage has had time to splash the cash on a shiny new party machine.

Some Labour MPs think that could factor into his thinking, but one Number 10 source insisted Reform's extra cash does not make an early election any more likely.

Burnham is now likely to come under increasing pressure to further change the rules on party donations.

Labour is already planning to introduce a cap on the amount of money a British citizen living overseas can donate.

There has been much talk about whether that could impact the donations to Reform by cryptocurrency billionaires Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo, but when interviewed by the BBC, Angela Rayner refused to say whether the two would be caught up in the rule changes.

The Liberal Democrats and Greens have also called for a cap for people based in Britain too, to prevent future mega donations.

Burnham has indicated that he's open to having that conversation, but chose not to support an effort by some Labour MPs earlier this month to tighten the rules.

Rayner confirmed this morning that it was still something being considered by ministers.

The Electoral Commission is looking at what more should be done in this area and the calls from within Labour for further change will now grow stronger.

Government sources insist this weekend's donations are not being viewed inside Downing Street as a game-changing moment in this debate.

But people across the political spectrum are now asking whether this massive injection of money will be remembered as a key moment when politics in this country changed.

News.title: Deep-fried food banned under new school dinner rules in England
News.content:
There will be a boost for fresh fruit and vegetables and deep-fried food will be banned in what the government has called the biggest shake-up to school dinners in England in over a decade.

Under new school food standards, fibre and wholegrains will also be increased, and breakfast clubs will have to follow nutrition rules for the first time, with schools also being monitored.

The Association of School and College Leaders (ASCL) welcomed the changes, but said they hoped the new rules would not become "another stick with which to beat head teachers".

The changes will come into effect from 2027 and be funded with existing money for schools, the government said.

As part of the new framework, sweet desserts, like cake, will be reduced from a regular lunch offer to twice a week in secondary schools, and once a week in primary schools. They also must now be served with a portion of fruit.

Servings of processed meats such as ham, sausages and chicken nuggets have been reduced to once a week and must come with a side of vegetables or fruit.

Education Secretary Lucy Powell said they were "once-in-a-generation changes" which would "transform school food for children across the country".

News.title: Refereeing body admits judgement error over Haaland derby winner
News.content:
The Premier League refereeing body Pro Ref has admitted an "error of judgement" in awarding Erling Haaland's Manchester City winner against Manchester United.

As City celebrated a remarkable derby victory over Manchester United, there were questions as to whether Haaland's winning goal should have stood in a match fraught with controversy.

The striker scored in the 60th minute at Old Trafford, turning home at the back post from Josko Gvardiol's cross before it was disallowed on the field for offside.

Following intervention from the video assistant referee, the goal was awarded - the Norwegian ruled to have been played onside by Patrick Dorgu's boot.

But there was debate as to whether the offside Enzo Fernandez, diving at the ball in a more central position than Haaland, was interfering with play.

In a statement, Pro Ref said: "It was established that Enzo Fernandez did not play the ball and therefore that makes any offside offence subjective.

"However, on this occasion, the VAR did not recognise the likely impact of his position and should have recommended an on-field review.

"Contact has been made with Manchester United this evening to acknowledge what we deem is an error of judgement. A review of the incident will take place."

United defender Lisandro Martinez said it was an "injustice" while boss Michael Carrick said he was "confused" by the decision.

The goal came after City had gone down to 10 men in the first half when Phil Foden was shown a straight red card for kicking out at United captain Bruno Fernandes.

Foden was dismissed by referee Michael Oliver on 23 minutes after kicking the midriff of Fernandes while he was on the turf.

News.title: Meghan shares glimpse of family life after Sussexes return to UK
News.content:
The Duchess of Sussex has shared a glimpse of family life in footage posted to Instagram following their return to the UK.

The 34-second clip, which features Wham!'s Wake Me Up Before You Go-Go, begins with Meghan, along with her husband Prince Harry, walking along a country path as she turns and says "come on, you".

UK flag and heart emojis are shown throughout the video, which also shows their son Archie running towards deer as their daughter Lilibet rides her bike.

Another clip sees Harry fishing with the children as their dog walks alongside the water.

It's the first time the Duchess has posted her family on her Instagram grid since the Sussexes returned from the US after living in California.

It is unclear when, or where, the footage posted on Sunday afternoon was taken, external, but one clip shows a pair of wellington boots walking on the spot in a puddle and the children also appear to be in waterproof boots as they head toward the deer.

The UK has had a wet start to September after experiencing its hottest summer on record.

The post offers a rare glimpse into the lives of seven-year-old Archie and five-year-old Lilibet.

Whereas Meghan does occasionally show the couple's children on social media, their faces are often obscured as they are photographed from behind or their faces are hidden by their parents.

Alongside all the outside footage, there is also a moment showing a child's feet in front of an open fire.

News.title: Andy Burnham among Great North Run finishers
News.content:
The Great North Run (GNR) returned to Tyneside this weekend, with 63,000 runners taking part in the world's biggest half marathon - including Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

England star and Newcastle captain Dan Burn rang the starter's bell, with famous faces including football personality Chris Kamara and fitness coach Joe Wicks taking on the challenge.

The 13.1-mile (21km) event saw runners and wheelchair users race from Newcastle through Gateshead and South Tyneside, before finishing in South Shields.

Britons David Weir and Melanie Woods won the men's and women's elite wheelchair races respectively. Brigid Kosgei won the elite women's contest and Zouhair Talbi won the men's race.

The half marathon is in its 45th year and raises about Â£25m for charity each time.

News.content:
The government condemned "intimidating and thuggish behaviour" at the demonstration, while stressing the right to peaceful protest.

On Friday, a 42-year-old man from Paulsgrove was charged with violent disorder and assaulting a police officer in connection with the incident. He has been remanded into custody.

A 16-year-old boy was arrested on Saturday in connection with the disorder. He has been released on bail pending further enquiries.

Rowlinson said: "The reality of public order policing is that arrests at the time are not always possible, especially where evidence may need to be reviewed to clearly identify who is responsible for offences."

The force had reviewed "hundreds of hours' worth" of footage, he said, adding: "The actions we have been taking as part of our investigation send a clear warning to anyone intent on causing disruption and disorder at any future events."

Around 500 anti-migrant protesters took to the streets of Portsmouth on Saturday and were met by hundreds of counter-protesters from Stand up to Racism.

Migrants intercepted in the Channel are typically brought to Dover for initial processing.

However, the dinghy that arrived at Eastney Marina had set off from near Cherbourg in the Bay of the Seine, about 170 miles (274km) west of Calais and significantly further west than the usual departure points.

News.title: Best friends for decades - until a DNA test revealed they were sisters
News.content:
Theirs is a story straight out of a Bollywood film.

Two Indian-born women in their 40s, adopted as babies by different families and raised near each other in the Netherlands, have now discovered they are biological sisters.

Meena Geltink and Minal Tijssen, born in the early 1980s, were adopted from two different orphanages in the western Indian city of Mumbai within months of their birth.

When they first met in their early teens at an event hosted by the adoption agency their parents had used, they were struck by the uncanny similarities in their appearance and mannerisms.

Meena, now 43, remembers the day clearly.

"All the adopted children were brought together to hang out and bond and have dinner."

Both Meena and Minal were with friends who noticed how similar they looked.

"They said, 'Look at yourselves in the mirror'.

"And I was like, 'Oh my God, she has my nose! We have the same laugh'.

"At dinner, I kept looking at her the whole time," Meena told the BBC from her home in the Netherlands.

The following day, the girls exchanged telephone numbers and addresses and promised to keep in touch.

Even though there was no indication they were related by blood, their connection was instant, and for years they wrote each other letters, often addressing each other as "Sis" because "we felt that way".

They wrote about school, friends, boys, going out and dancing. They told each other about the sports they played and discussed music, discovering they both loved Backstreet Boys.

Then 15 years ago, they lost contact. Minal had moved to France. And Meena had recently had her first child and got busy.

News.title: Reform confident it won't need to repay any of £72m under proposed new donor rules
News.content:
Reform UK believes the Â£72m in donations it has received from two cryptocurrency billionaires were "entirely in line with the law", the party's economic spokesman has said.

Robert Jenrick told the BBC he did not expect that the party will have to return any of the money from Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, who are both British and have spent time living overseas.

The government is seeking to change the law on donations to UK political parties from British expats, including a Â£100,000 cap backdated to 25 March.

"These two donations are entirely in line with the law as it is and, as far as we know, the law as it's going to be in the future," Jenrick said.

As well as limiting how much British citizens can donate to political parties from overseas, the government has proposed a minimum residency period in which the Â£100,000 cap would still apply for those who move back to the UK.

This would be in place for the remainder of the calendar year and the following calendar year after the person returns.

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that the rule changes would apply retrospectively and anyone not complying with them would have "to return that money".

Rayner added she was not commenting specifically on Delo and Harborne as she does not "understand" their "circumstances".

Answering questions about the donations following Rayner's remarks, Jenrick said: "It might be that Angela Rayner or the government keep trying to change the law to make it even harder for people to donate to Reform, nothing would surprise me.

"But, as it stands, we believe these are entirely in line with the law."

BBC News has been told that both Delo and Harborne have returned to the UK. Delo is understood to have been back in the country since last year.

Jenrick said Delo had returned to the UK "in part so that he can comply with the changes to the law".

In a statement after the programme, a Reform UK spokesman said: "We are 100% confident both [donations] are legal and won't ever have to be handed back."

One person familiar with the government's proposed changes said the issue of whether Delo and Harborne are affected would likely come down to how ministers choose to define UK residency.

They said one way would be to adopt the same definition used in tax laws, but stressed how complex the rules around residency are.

News.title: First ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland to meet in Cardiff
News.content:
The first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland will meet in Cardiff on Monday to discuss ways of "working more closely", including on constitutional issues.

It will be the first face-to-face meeting between the three nationalist leaders since Plaid Cymru's Rhun ap Iorwerth took office in May.

Ap Iorwerth will host the SNP's leader John Swinney and Sinn FÃ©in's Michelle O'Neill on Monday morning. Sinn FÃ©in president Mary Lou McDonald will also attend.

He will hold further talks with Swinney in the afternoon with both men expected to sign an agreement on "future collaboration in areas of shared interest".

For the first time since devolution began Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, all have first ministers who want to leave the United Kingdom.

A Plaid spokesperson said ap Iorwerth's meeting with Swinney, O'Neill and McDonald was "an opportunity for the leaders of Plaid Cymru, the SNP and Sinn FÃ©in to come together and talk about how we can work more closely on the issues that matter to people across our nations".

"Following the historic Senedd election in Wales and the changing political landscape across these islands, there is a strong case for practical political cooperation on areas including energy, the economy and our relationship with Europe, as well as on the wider political and constitutional questions facing our nations and on the right to self-determination," they added.

Swinney believed their was "undeniable" momentum behind constitutional change.

"Every nation across these islands is standing at a moment of incredible constitutional opportunity," he said.

"There is a growing consensus that the Westminster system simply is not fit for purpose and does not work for ordinary people.

"Prime Minister Andy Burnham has accepted that himself - and the people of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have made it clear at the ballot box."

The meetings come days after the matter of Scottish independence resurfaced in the Commons.

During Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday, Andy Burnham appeared to indicate a second referendum could be held in Scotland if there was clear public support for a vote.

He compared the situation to the conditions for a border poll in Northern Ireland explaining the Good Friday Agreement made clear a border poll would be "considered by the Northern Ireland Secretary when there is a clear consensus in the country, when public opinion has changed to the point where the call has to be considered".

"I would say that it is exactly the same situation in Scotland," he added.

The apparent softening in tone was welcomed by Swinney before Burnham clarified that another Scottish referendum remained "off limits".

A referendum on Scottish independence in September 2014 saw the country vote to remain part of the UK by a margin of 55% to 45%.

News.title: Six months without bin collections prompts council tax refund call
News.content:
A resident who has not had a bin collection for six months since moving on to a new-build estate is seeking a 100% council tax rebate as compensation.

Bins finally arrived on Hawthorn Meadows in Buckley, Flintshire, last month but Nathan Long and 60 other households can still only watch as refuse workers collect rubbish or recyclables from a nearby street.

Long said he wanted a rebate as he had been required to pay council tax since moving in and despite disposing of rubbish in skips provided by the estate developer.

The council said it was "working to resolve the situation" but a "multi-step setup process must occur" before new waste and recycling collection services are set up.

"It feels like we are not getting anywhere," said Long.

"We complain and we get responses that in part pass the buck on to others and in part pledge to do something about the problem.

"Meanwhile, we are sitting here watching bin crews collecting rubbish from across the road and wondering if they will ever come to us."

Mr Long is waiting to hear from the local authority about his request for a council tax rebate.

He added: "When we received our bins we thought that was the signal.

"But another month has passed and still nothing.

"At one point I went to lodge a formal complaint about the situation and was told I couldn't as technically we hadn't missed a collection."

Katie Wilby, council chief officer for streetscene and transportation, said: "While we normally expect developers to arrange these services before residents move in, we are currently working to resolve the situation for the occupied properties.

"A council officer will visit the site to confirm occupancy, perform safety checks, and integrate eligible homes into the collection system as quickly as possible."

Castle Green Homes said it would continue to provide skips for residents at its own cost until the matter is resolved.

News.title: Patrols to start in Essex locations visited by asylum seekers
News.content:
Speaking to BBC Look East presenter Susie Fowler-Watt, Nolan said: "Crimes and incidents associated with the Wethersfield site are very low.

"Certainly, as far as I've seen, there is absolutely no reason for anyone to be concerned about criminality associated with migrants from the Wethersfield camp in Essex."

County council leader Peter Harris said: "Six trained security guards, two each in Braintree, Chelmsford and Colchester, will provide a visible and reassuring presence on our streets, particularly for women and children.

"Our message is simple: the safety of Essex residents comes first."

David King, a senior Liberal Democrat county councillor, previously said the scheme "risks divisions and community tension".

"It could only work if the security officers integrated with already established arrangements," he said. "They won't know the place, they won't know the people, they won't be connected up."

Chelmsford City Council's Stephen Robinson, who leads the Lib Dem-run authority, said: "I think it's really important that we don't create division and that policing is carried out by the police."

Meanwhile, Conservative county councillor Lee Scott said: "We're not opposing it, but we are in the future looking at it to see if it's succeeding and making people feel safe."

The government does not record criminal offences by immigration status, but according to analysis by the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford, external, foreign nationals in England and Wales are convicted at roughly the same rate as British nationals.

The council said the trial was "a direct response to concerns raised amongst local residents - particularly women and girls - over gatherings of male migrants in town centres who were regularly transported in by bus from the former military airfield to spend their free time".

"It intends to deter anti-social behaviour, provide reassurance to residents and businesses, and gather evidence about whether additional support may be required," a spokesperson said.

The local authority said it would be funded by drawing down Â£150,000 from the "community innovation and improvement fund"., external

There would be no additional cost to taxpayers and no increase in council tax as a result of the scheme, it added.

News.title: Mass trespass staged in PM Andy Burnham's constituency
News.content:
Campaigners have taken part in a mass trespass in Prime Minister Andy Burnham's Ashton-in-Makerfield constituency over the right to roam in privately-owned green spaces.

They walked on to the Winstanley Hall estate in Wigan as part of their calls for a change in the law to bring in a Scottish-style right to responsible access to land and water that is privately owned.

Right to Roam co-director Nadia Shaikh said they hoped the protest would get Burnham's attention.

A spokesperson for developer Kingswood Homes, who are proposing to build about 400 homes on the land, said their plans included making more than 18 acres (0.07 sq km) publicly accessible.

The protest involved dozens of people walking on public footpaths and then going through a gap in the metal fencing around the site to access the private land.

Shaikh said there was right to roam access over just 1% of Burnham's constituency and "so we are here to try and get his attention, and to talk about access in this way".

She said the site should not be fenced off and the thousands of residents living nearby should be able to access it to have "a lovely one-hour walk that will just give people that sense of being in nature and calm".

News.title: Residents 'did not hear alarms' during fatal tower fire
News.content:
Some residents in an east London tower block have said they did not hear any alarms during a fire in which a man died on the 17th floor.

They told BBC London they had been alerted by neighbours banging on their doors and telling them to leave the building during the early hours of Saturday.

The man died in the flat fire at Neutron Tower in Poplar. Two adults and a child were rescued by firefighters wearing breathing apparatus, the London Fire Brigade (LFB) said.

FirstPort, the building's management company, said "it would not be appropriate for us to speculate on specific matters" while the fire was under investigation.

The LFB said: "There are a range of factors that are being investigated regarding the cause of the fire by the Brigade's Fire Investigation Team."

News.title: Veterans who died by suicide honoured at memorial
News.content:
Hundreds of people have gathered at the National Memorial Arboretum for the dedication of a permanent tribute to veterans and armed forces personnel who have died by suicide.

The Elysium Memorial, at the site in Alrewas, Staffordshire, is the first permanent memorial of its kind to be built in the UK.

More than 1,300 military veterans and personnel have taken their lives in the last 30 years, with the memorial aiming to provide a place for contemplation for those affected by the loss of a friend or loved one.

Edward Mackenzie, co-founder of the Elysium Memorial Foundation, which is behind the project, said he was "blown away" by the number of people that had turned up.

More than 300 motorcyclist rode to the arboretum from Burton-on-Trent on Sunday, with a convoy organised by community organisation Wheels for Wishes.

Mackenzie, who served in the army for more than 30 years and has lost over to 20 friends to suicide, including his best friend, said seeing those veterans' being recognised "means everything".

"This is why I did it, I did for for the friends, the families, the comrades, those that we've lost to suicide," he told the BBC.

"There's a lot of families here today that have been thanking me for achieving this memorial so I'm incredibly grateful."

News.title: 'Slim chance' government will hit 1.5m new homes target, Rayner tells BBC
News.content:
There is only a "slim chance" the government will meet its target of building 1.5 million homes in England by the next election, Housing Secretary Angela Rayner has told the BBC.

"Headwinds" including the Iran war and rising construction costs are making it harder to meet the key Labour manifesto pledge, Rayner told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg.

"But I'm definitely not giving it up," she said, and stressed that the government was "making a difference" through investing billions in social and affordable homes.

Data up to June this year suggested the government was behind on the rate of construction needed to meet the goal, which housebuilders have previously warned was too optimistic.

Labour promised to hit the target through building both private and social housing by the end of the current parliament, meaning summer 2029 at the latest.

This implied an average of 300,000 new properties would be needed each year - a rate of construction not seen in decades.

Rayner told the BBC on Sunday: "It's a slim chance, but I'm definitely not giving it up."

She said it was important to keep the goal - which she said had always been a "stretch target" - in place, but that she was "being honest with the public" that it would be difficult to achieve.

Rising mortgage rates are intensifying pressure on the UK rental market, with annual price growth projected to reach 4% to 5% by the end of the year.

Property portal giant Zoopla noted that elevated borrowing costs are keeping prospective buyers in tenancy for longer, driving up demand for rented homes.

Simultaneously, the stock of available rental properties coming onto the market has remained lower in recent months compared to 2025 levels.

Annual rent increases accelerated to 2.6% in July—up from 1.6% in February 2026—bringing average UK monthly rents to £1,340, Zoopla stated.

Protesters' placards are pictured in the window of a Foxtons estate agents' demonstrate outside in central London on December 14, 2024 ( AFP/Getty )

Richard Donnell, executive director at Zoopla, said: “The rental market is starting to tighten again after three years in which the supply of homes for rent has steadily improved and rental growth slowed, easing the pressure on renters.

“Our latest report shows how sensitive the rental market is to even modest changes in how many homes are available for rent.

“Higher mortgage rates are not just impacting the sales market, they are keeping more would-be first-time buyers in rented homes for longer, reducing available supply just as the seasonal upturn in demand gets into full swing.

“This is pushing rents higher again, mainly in regions where the availability of homes for rent has declined the most, although affordability remains an important constraint on how far rents can rise.

“The upward pressure on rents is greatest in London, where higher mortgage rates have had the biggest impact on home buyers, and in more affordable rental markets where renters have greater capacity to absorb increases.

“Low levels of new investment by landlords and renters renting for longer mean we expect UK rents to increase by four to 5% by the end of the year.

“Growing the number of homes for rent through increased investment is the most sustainable route to boosting choice for renters and ensuring stability in rent levels over the long run.”

Healthcare professionals, including dentists and GPs, are being offered targeted training to spot potential early signs of motor neurone disease (MND) under a brand new initiative.

Created by the charity foundation established by Scotland rugby star Doddie Weir, who died following his diagnosis with MND, the project is the first of its kind in the UK.

Titled RACE to Diagnose, it provides tailored guidance to clinical staff who might encounter patients displaying initial indicators of the condition.

Because MND is frequently difficult to identify in its early stages, it is hoped that enabling patients to access treatments sooner will lead to improved outcomes.

The programme also advises clinicians on how to outline urgent referrals without prompting unnecessary alarm, as well as what clinical information to provide so specialist teams can assess and prioritise each case.

Early symptoms of the life-shortening disease can include progressive or unexplained muscle wasting and weakness, or changes that impact speech, the tongue or swallowing.

Jessica Lee, who is director of research at the foundation ( PA )

Jessica Lee, director of research at the My Name’5 Doddie Foundation, said: “MND is not common, its early signs can vary considerably and there is no single test that tells you conclusively that someone has it. That means people can move between different parts of the healthcare system before they reach the right specialist.

“RACE to diagnose gives professionals practical guidance on what to look for, how to assess what they are seeing and when to make an urgent referral.”

“As treatments begin to emerge, reaching people earlier in the course of the disease may be critical to giving those treatments the best possible chance of having an effect.

“But earlier diagnosis is about much more than treatment.

“It can give people with MND and their families more time to understand what is happening, access the right support, adapt their homes and decide how they want to approach the future.”

Former NHS consultant anaesthetist Andy Vaughton experienced symptoms for several years before being diagnosed with MND in 2021.

He said delays to diagnoses can deprive people of access to care and postpone important decisions about their lives.

Mr Vaughton, from Poole in Dorset, said: “For most people, MND doesn’t progress as slowly as it has for me.

“You need time to process what is happening, access the care you are going to require and bring together all the hospital specialists who will be involved.

“You also need to deal with everything at home and with your family. I knew I had a limited window of able-bodied life left, when I could still do the things I wanted to do.

“Having time to decide how to make the most of that window was incredibly important.

“I travelled, did the sports I loved and spent precious time with my wife and boys.”

The father-of-three recently completed a continuous 100km challenge along the Jurassic Coast to raise money for MND causes

Mr Vaughton continued: “I look back on that as a period well spent and know I made the right decision.

“I have been fortunate because my MND has progressed slowly, but for some people that window can be very short.”

Earlier diagnosis of MND can enable eligible people to begin available treatments or enter clinical trials earlier in the course of the disease.

News.title: US Open final LIVE: Zverev repels Shelton fight to become a two-time grand slam champion
News.content:
Alexander Zverev with the US Open trophy after beating Ben Shelton ( Getty )

Alexander Zverev denied Ben Shelton his US Open dream to win his second grand slam title and deny the American in his bid to end his country’s long tournament drought.

It has been 23 years since an American man, Andy Roddick, last won the US Open but Shelton’s run to his first grand slam final, where he defeated defending champion Carlos Alcaraz in an epic quarter-final, suggested that he could break that spell.

However, top seed Zverev was too dominant as the German added the US Open to his French Open crown secured in June, with the 29-year-old becoming just the fourth man in the Open era to win their first two grand slams titles in the same season.

Shelton, 23, overcame a very nervy start and finally arrived in the match to break his opponent for the first time late in the third set and force the fourth, but Zverev immediately pounced to claim the opening break before serving out a 6-3, 7-6 (7-2), 5-7, 6-2 victory.

Zverev did not realise he had won the title, however, after he had lost track of the score when serving for the Championship. Zverev barely responded when Shelton put his return long and it wasn’t until he looked up to the big scoreboard for him to realise he was the champion.

Follow updates from Shelton v Zverev in the US Open final, below

News.content:

Alexander Zverev failed to realise he had just won the US Open after becoming a two-time grand slam champion in New York.

The German would have perhaps expected a muted reaction to his winning moment as he was facing the home hope Ben Shelton in the final.

But the 29-year-old must have lost track of the score because when Shelton put his return long on Championship point, Zverev barely responded.

Instead, the top seed though there was another game to come because he had already hit the balls to the other end of the court to receive.

It wasn’t until Zverev looked up to the scoreboard and the upper deck of the Arthur Ashe Stadium for him to realise he was the champion.

But there was no falling onto his back as, in one of the strangests grand slam title victories of all time, Zverev belatedly burst into a wide smile.

Zverev will pocked $5.5m by winning the US Open title while he also exorcises some of the demons from his previous US Open final appearance in 2020.

Six years ago, Zverev served for the Championship against Dominic Thiem, but lost from two sets up in a brutal collapse.

Perhaps not realising the score helped Zverev as he produced a masterclass in the fourth set to repel Shelton’s comeback after he finally arrived in the final.

The 23-year-old Shelton overcame a very nervy start and finally arrived in the match to break his opponent for the first time late in the third set and force the fourth.

But Zverev immediately pounced to claim the opening break before serving out a 6-3, 7-6 (7-2), 5-7, 6-2 victory for his sixth consecutive win against Shelton.

Zverev won his first grand slam title in June at the French Open and also reached the Wimbledon final in July in what is by far the best season of his career.

He is now just the fourth man in the Open era to win his first two grand slam titles in the same year and aiming for world No 1 is now a realistic target.

This has been Zverev’s year at the grand slams after Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner dominated the men’s game and swept the biggest titles in 2024 and 2025.

He has taken advantage of spells of injury from both Alcaraz and Sinner and has not had to beat either player in 2026 to become a two-time grand slam winner.

A newly unveiled statue of conservative podcaster and organizer Charlie Kirk was defaced outside Turning Point USA’s headquarters in Phoenix, Arizona, on Sunday.

The day after the statue was revealed, someone smeared red paint on the statue and defaced a Christian tribute posted outside Turning Point USA's headquarters. Turning Point USA was founded by Kirk.

The paint was smeared across the statue's face, on its neck — mirroring the spot where Kirk was shot and killed a year ago — and across its torso and left hand, according to Fox News.

A sign at the base of the statue with the words "Jesus defeated death so you can live" was also defaced. The word "Jesus" was crossed out and was replaced by the word "Satan."

Kirk's widow, Erika Kirk, who ascended to the head of Turning Point USA following his death, said in a statement that they would repair the statue and that the vandalism would not detract from her husband's legacy.

open image in gallery A statue of Charlie Kirk defaced with red paint outside Turning Point USA's headquarters in Phoenix, Arizona ( Turning Point USA )

"Charlie once said we should be building two statues for every statue that they tear down," she wrote. "God will not be mocked."

Phoenix police told Fox News the incident is being investigated. No arrests have been announced as of Sunday afternoon.

Turning Point USA Chief Operating Officer Tyler Bowyer said the organization planned to clean the memorial once police were done investigating the scene.

"God bless the police as they investigate the violent thugs who did this," he wrote.

There is no indication that any violence occurred at the scene.

“We will restore the statue and replace the signs, but we are also reviewing the footage of the incident and are working with law enforcement to identify who did this and hold them accountable,” Turning Point USA wrote in a statement.

The statue was unveiled a day after the first anniversary of Kirk's assassination while he was speaking at Utah Valley University on September 10, 2025. A judge recently ruled that the man accused of killing Kirk will have to stand trial for aggravated murder, which — if he is convicted — could result in a death sentence.

As the anniversary approached, Kirk's supporters began leaving flowers outside the headquarters to mark the occasion.

open image in gallery Individuals who were present at the scene of Turning Point USA founder Charlie Kirk's fatal shooting stand together on stage during a Charlie Kirk memorial service at the UCCU Center on September 10, 2026 in Orem, Utah. ( Getty )

The statue depicts Kirk in the same "Freedom" T-shirt he wore on the day he was killed.

The memorial is expected to be moved inside the organization's headquarters for security reasons.

Another Kirk statue drew attention when it was spotted in the back of a pickup truck in Utah earlier this week.

That statue, which depicts Kirk sitting cross-legged in a folding chair and holding a microphone, was briefly displayed at Utah Valley University during a memorial event marking the anniversary of the shooting, according to the Salt Lake Tribune.

A Turning Point spokesperson told the paper that they were not sure where that statue would ultimately end up, but said they were "not aware of any plans for the statue to remain on campus," noting that it was not a university-backed memorial project.

The artist reportedly told the paper they plan on taking it to Turning Point's headquarters in Arizona next week.

A Pennsylvania woman has died from complications associated with measles, the third death in the state this year involving the virus.

The 40-year-old woman died Saturday, Jefferson County Coroner Greg Furlong said in a Facebook post in which he called the death “measles-related.”

The post did not identify the woman other than as a resident of Jefferson County, a rural area about 50 miles (80 kilometers) northeast of Pittsburgh.

“This is a heartbreaking loss for the family and an unfortunate reminder that measles can be a serious and potentially life-threatening disease,” Furlong said in the post.

The post did not say whether the woman was vaccinated against measles. No more information about the case would be released, it stated.

Pennsylvania's two previous measles-related deaths involved infants. Both occurred in August and a coroner reported that the virus itself caused one of the deaths.

One infant, a boy, died shortly after birth of a ruptured spleen. The boy had measles that did not contribute to the rupture, according to Lancaster County Coroner Dr. Stephen Diamantoni.

Rather, measles was listed as a “significant condition” at the time of death.

The other infant, a 6-week-old girl with a genetic defect that left her highly vulnerable to infection, died due to measles, Diamantoni told The Associated Press.

The girl was born with a condition called Amish lethal microcephaly that causes an unusually small head and underdeveloped brain. Children with the condition typically live 6 months or less.

The first dose of measles vaccine is typically given to infants around 1 year old, meaning neither infant was old enough to be vaccinated.

As of Friday, Pennsylvania had 676 measles cases in 37 of the state's 67 counties. Of those cases, 124 involved hospitalizations and four people who were vaccinated against measles, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Health.

The three measles-related deaths reported by state and local officials as of Sunday did not square with figures of the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, which showed no such deaths this year.

"The National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) does not currently have any death records from 2026 that indicate measles is the underlying cause," read the CDC website Sunday.

Pennsylvania's Democratic governor, Josh Shapiro, and Republican President Donald Trump’s administration have clashed over details of the two previous deaths in the state.

Alexander Zverev faced jeers from the partisan US Open crowd due to the slow pace of his service play as he faced home favourite Ben Shelton in the men’s singles final.

Chair umpire Marijana Veljovic had to remind the crowd to not make noise between the first and second serves after there were groans when Zverev aborted a ball toss on 3-3, 40-40 in the second set.

Zverev was finally given a time violation warning at 2-1, 30-30 as he lead the fourth set, with the 29-year-old complaining to umpire Veljovic that he could not start his service motion because the crowd were making too much noise.

German world No 2 Zverev’s incessant bouncing of the ball before his serve was a talking point before the final after his semi-final opponent Karen Khachanov complained about the time he would take during serves.

“The way he bounces the ball, look, it annoys not only me, of course, a lot of players, because it takes so much time,” Khachanov said after Zverev was given a time violation during the match.

“At the end of the day, if it’s within the rules with the time between points, I cannot say anything against that,” Khachanov added. “If he extends the time, then he gets a time violation, so it’s as simple as that.”

Shelton, playing in his first grand slam final, appeared to be getting irritated by the pace of Zverev’s play after the French Open champion and Wimbledon runner-up took the first set on Arthur Ashe Stadium.

Zverev had spent 19 hours and 38 minutes on court during his run to a second US Open final. According to Sky Sports, if Zverev then spent 10 seconds bouncing the ball before each serve, he would have spent two hours and 30 minutes of the tournament bouncing the ball.

Speaking after his semi-final, Zverev insisted it is not a deliberate ploy. He said: “I have no idea why. I’m not doing it on purpose. I saw a stat, like, I’d bounced it 12,000 times or something like that. That’s quite funny.”

News.title: Woeful Man Utd have no excuses, Carrick is under big pressure
News.content:
Afterwards Haaland talked about City’s “personality, character” and that was exactly what United lacked. They did not adapt a tactical plan to combat 10-man City’s desire to keep their wingers high and wide, and break with intent and still try and attack.

It was telling that so little did City’s new head coach Enzo Maresca worry about United that he did not add a defensive player, and when he took off Rayan Cherki at half-time, he replaced him with the equally creative Iliman Ndiaye who impressed. Maresca knew United needed space to run in behind and denied them that. It was that simple.

City also struck the post with United goalkeeper Senne Lammens tipping an Enzo Fernández shot against the frame of the goal, and the visitors were worthy winners as they preserved their perfect start to the season to draw level on points with leaders, Arsenal.

City handled the occasion and the – admittedly toothless – opposition superbly under their new head coach and will clearly be Arsenal’s closest challengers this season.

Maresca delivered a masterclass. For Carrick? This was a disasterclass. An object lesson in how not to use a man-advantage. And now United will have to endure even more City songs after being outplayed at home like this.

Was it complacency? Was it inability? Was it a damning lack of courage, confidence, belief even? On the pitch and in the dugout United were far too passive. This was not how a big team plays and Carrick needs to wake up.

The former midfielder did so well last season to guide United into Champions League qualification but so far this campaign he has given the impression that his job is done. Rather than that the real work starts now.

News.title: Redemption Sunday for Hull and Woad as Europe reclaim Solheim Cup
News.content:
The quiet but steely 22-year-old, who everyone seemed to have forgotten was a rookie, punched her fist when she held the decisive two-footer, before the customary hug with opponent Auston Kim and then being mobbed by her team.

“This was really important,” Woad said. “I mean, I was pretty disappointed and felt like I was kind of letting everyone down. Then the captain kind of spoke to me and said that I was third on [the most] birdies [made]. So I just had to trust that and that’s golf sometimes. And it ended up I got the winning putt.”

Some will claim that Woad was only the match-winner on a technicality. Carlota Ciganda in the penultimate game had not finished off her win against Jennifer Kupcho, but when Woad tapped in, the Spaniard was three up with three to go and was guaranteed a half. So the acclaim Woad received was granted. Not that anyone in the Europe camp cared.

The previous evening they had returned to their team room feeling slightly down that they did not hold the advantage, Kupcho holing a 91-footer on the 17th and a 30-footer on the 18th to deny Ciganda and Céline Boutier. And their mood was not helped when videos appeared on social media of the Americans taking crates of beer on to the bus back to their hotel. Yet that foolish scenario only offered extra incentive. “At least we’ll be the ones taking crates of beer on to our bus this evening,” Mel Reid, the assistant captain, said quite pointedly.

News.title: Lando Norris fumes at virtual safety car rules for costing him Spanish GP win
News.content:
Welcome to our live coverage for the 2026 Spanish Grand Prix, the first time the race has been held at the all-new, purpose-built street circuit, the Madring. The track has developed a reputation in its short life for being a bit of a tricky one. Some have gone so far as to call it a “car killer”? Is it living up to that reputation? Probably, especially if you look at some of the lower formulae that have run on it.

It has also increasingly become the case for the Formula One cars, too. The first couple of practice sessions on Friday revealed little to worry about. As the drivers began to push, though, from final practice and qualifying, the mistakes and crashes happened. The biggest so far was Oliver Bearman but also a smaller one for Lewis Hamilton.

There will almost certainly be some kind of incident in the race, but whether we see red flags, safety cars and so on remains to be seen. A bigger and perhaps more significant question will be how much overtaking will take place on this track. The drivers are not optimistic. The theory goes that if tyre degradation is high then there will be, because you will have significant pace offsets between worn and fresh tyres. The problem is that the leaders tend not to differ to greatly from one another on strategy these days...

Perhaps George Russell, who qualified down in sixth and has little to lose, will be brave and put on a set of hard tyres to start with. Russell has work to do yet again. He was not miles off Antonelli in qualifying when it came to pace, but given how close it was in the top six, finds four cars between himself and the championship leader, who just missed out on pole to McLaren’s Lando Norris.

Norris said it was the best lap of his life and seemed to come from nowhere. He improved more than a second from Q2 to Q3 and continues his fine form in 2026. He will start alongside Antonelli with Max Verstappen in third, Lewis Hamilton in fourth and Charles Leclerc in fifth, before Russell.

News.title: Tora Bora’s last midwife struggles under Taliban rule as aid runs dry
News.content:
The small clinic, crowded with pregnant women, sits in the shadow of Tora Bora in eastern Afghanistan. Twenty-five years ago, those mountains commanded the attention of the world’s most powerful military. Roughly 15 miles from the clinic, in the Tora Bora cave complex, Osama bin Laden was believed to be hiding as American bombs rained down in the hunt for the architect of 9/11.

Today, another consequence of the West’s long entanglement with Afghanistan is playing out beneath those same mountains – in the struggle to keep mothers and babies alive.

In the baking courtyard of Gandab Kharoti health centre, dozens of women enveloped in sapphire blue burqas sit shoulder to shoulder beneath trees waiting to see Shila Ibrahimi, a 27-year-old midwife.

The women rest against walls, dusty, barefoot children play, and mothers cradle sick babies beneath folds of cloth. Some have walked for hours through the mountains to reach her.

Among them is Fawzia, 30, seven-and-a-half months pregnant with her seventh child. Suffering from headaches, she has walked for miles through the heat.

Her husband works far from the village, so she makes the journey with her children and mother-in-law, hoping the Taliban do not stop her for the “crime” of travelling without a male escort.

Under the Taliban’s morality rules, women face restrictions on travelling alone, while UN monitors have documented the regime’s morality inspectors ordering some health facilities not to treat unaccompanied women.

But enforcement varies and Fawzia says nobody challenged her on her journey here. Asked where she would give birth if the clinic closed she says: “We have nowhere else to go. We cannot afford that. We are poor.”

News.title: Springboks look like World Cup champions elect… again
News.content:
“South Africa are very good at creating opportunities and taking their chances, and so they scored it under the posts. That was a big moment in the game, and so we know if we can do a couple of things a bit better, limit their opportunities, and be a little bit more clinical, the result could go another way. But they are a very good side, and they scramble really well, and yeah I think the better side probably won in the end.

“We could talk about scrums, but we will have to be better. They have got a great scrum, they have got a great maul, so our ability to stay in front of that maul is important. And when we did that, we limited their ability to hurt us, and likewise at scrum time. The easiest way is to limit those occurrences. So, if we are more accurate, there are fewer scrums and greater continuity for us, and we do not kick the ball out.

“There are fewer lineouts for them, and discipline comes into it. You cannot just make their strengths disappear. But our job is to limit the amount of opportunities they get. I think on our ball, the scrum was reasonably solid. We got it badly wrong on one, then got punished with one of their feeds, and so look, it is a weapon for them, and that is the challenge. We want high continuity. If you make an error, they get to go to a set-piece. They get a penalty off that. They march up the field, and so it is still an area we are going to have to be better at.”

News.title: Sabalenka smashes racket and swears at cameraman after Rybakina clinches US Open
News.content:
Sabalenka and Rybankina have now played four slam finals, with the spoils evenly shared after this 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 grapple in the Apple – as a boxing promoter might have referred to it.

There is certainly something pugilistic about the way these two go toe-to-toe. The emphasis is on landing the first blow, so the rallies tend not to be particularly long: only four points out of 193 went beyond nine shots. But the precision of the ball-striking was breathtaking. At one point in the first set, Rybakina had hit eight winners to just a single unforced error – the sort of ratio to send coaches starry-eyed.

Sabalanka arrived on court in her showy jewellery – which is worth more than £300,000 for the full set, according to the manufacturers – and an orange Nike dress that put one in mind of the Dutch national football team. “Total tennis” may have been the goal, but sometimes your opponent doesn’t allow you to play. This was the case in the early stages as Rybakina – whose own yellow-and-black outfit evoked the natural warning signs of a wasp or hornet – seemed to flush every ball right out of the centre of her racket.

Sabalenka actually did a sterling job of digging herself out of trouble in her service games, saving four of five break points in the first set. But this still wasn’t enough, given that Rybakina was defending her own serve with the same serenity that characterises everything she does.

News.title: Former Geordie Guimaraes taunts Sunderland fans as Arsenal show mark of champions
News.content:
Hello and welcome to live, minute-by-minute coverage of Sunderland v Arsenal at the Stadium of Light. Sunderland are the latest team tasked with stopping Arsenal, who have begun their title defence in formidable style: they’ve won out of three, including a dominant comeback victory against Chelsea last weekend, and look well equipped to become the first Arsenal team to retain the title since the mid-1930s.

There’s a long way to go, and Arsenal fans will remember how blisteringly they started their last two title defences in 2002-03 and 2004-05, only to ultimately fall short. But right now, they could barely be in better shape. Their fine start to the season came with a Champions League win in Naples, achieved despite a delay to their flight from London.

“I love those challenges,” said Mikel Arteta. “I try to create them in pre-seasons so when they happen, we already experience them and we already know. So get to the stadium very late, change the routine and suddenly the players have to do something else.

“Because when it happens, and it can happen, you can miss the flight, the train can be delayed, there’s so much traffic and I don’t want the players, but not only the players, the staff as well, panicking. So when that happens, adapt to it.”

Arteta has tested his squad in a variety of ways. “[We have] delayed the meals, delayed the transport, taken a different route. We’ve done many things – made the dressing room hotter, more difficult, more challenging, less beds... because we’re going to have to adapt to different contexts.”

So far, they’re adapting very well to the context of being the reigning champions.

Kick off 8pm.

News.title: £329m spent and still no goals for sorry Tottenham
News.content:
Tottenham Hotspur have never before in the club’s history begun a league season without scoring a single goal in the first four games, although having done so after spending £329m on new players really does take some doing.

“Please score a goal!” was the homemade sign from two Spurs fans upon which the television cameras lingered at the end of the game, although the jaunty felt-tip design and glued-on team crest were rather upbeat compared to the gloom of the stadium. Spurs have tried to outrun their past but it just keeps catching up with them.

A team reimagined, a manager freshly launched and yet they are back in the same grip of anxiety that accompanied them on two consecutive 17th-place finishes in the last two seasons. By the end of this they might have been glad to escape with a single point against Everton, the one team in the Premier League who closed the window with a net transfer profit.

For Roberto De Zerbi, there was another passionate defence of his team afterwards. “The people, the fans already understand if I make excuses or not,” he said. “I came last season when the s--- was like this”, he gestured to a level somewhere around the midpoint of his forehead. “I have always been… not positive but realistic. I am sorry for the result that it’s not immediately the improvement. We played as a team. We didn’t score. We didn’t win [but] we played as a team.”

Sports.title: Man Utd vs Man City officials were ordered to get Haaland decision WRONG – something’s seriously off with VAR
Sports.content:
A MONTH into the season, and it’s all about the referees and VAR again.

And, surely, that cannot be good for anyone.



Lisandro Martinez, left furious by the latest controversy, explained how confidently officials run through the rules at the start of each season.

But when absolutely nobody inside a stadium can understand why a decision was made, something has to be wrong.



And, surely, only the inhabitants of the VAR booth at Stockley Park could see any reason why Erling Haaland’s Manchester derby winner was allowed to stand yesterday.

The Norwegian juggernaut slid in at the back post to direct Josko Gvardiol’s diverted cross into the roof of the United net.



But the flag went up instantly, with both the Norwegian and Enzo Fernandez seemingly offside – and nobody in City even celebrating.

Yet after an age, two and a half minutes, with Old Trafford wondering why there was ANY delay, VAR Matt Donohue told ref Michael Oliver that Haaland was fractionally onside.

More bizarrely and crucially, that Fernandez’s failure to make any contact with his diving header meant he had NOT interfered with play, even though he was NEXT to Lisandro Martinez.

BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Martinez did pull out of making a play for the ball after it passed his fellow countryman but that, surely, was not relevant, given Enzo’s dive for the ball so close to goal.



The United defender was beyond perplexed. And justifiably so.

Martinez said: “He was offside. He was there. I went to him because he was there in front of me. That’s why Haaland was free at the back.

“I want to be calm now and control myself. It is so hard because you lose. You lose a derby and three points at home.

“Every season they come to our club and explain for one hour, one hour and a half the rules and they look so confident with that.

“Then after, to have five or six people making this kind of mistake in the Premier League is unacceptable



“Because you have the best teams in the world in this league, you have the best players in the world.

“And now we have to go home with this injustice. I can’t understand it.

“Let’s see what they want to say now, let’s see. I want to hear – their decision was based on what? I want to hear now.”



Pro Ref’s public concession late last night that it was a howler was the minimum acceptable response although it will not make Michael Carrick or United feel any better.

But such mistakes simply cannot be made at this level. It just gives the conspiracy theorists more ammunition.

Viewers at home were shaking their heads, United supporters in particular seething.

The studio pundits, irrespective of their club allegiances, were equally left wondering if the universe had been inverted.

Gary Neville, who will never hide his United colours, said: “I need the offside law explaining to me, that has lost me I have to say.



“It will need an official to explain to us why he’s not offside.

Wayne Rooney agreed: “Surely it’s offside? Martinez is impacted by Enzo’s movement, and he is offside.”

Not according to Mr Donohue. Despite all the evidence.



Maybe, looking at Enzo’s leap and Martinez’ decision, you might find an arcane rationale for the call – even if that seems ridiculous.

But in the round, taking every other aspect of the play into account – and the fact that the City players seemed to have accepted the flag without any real arguments – it makes absolutely no sense whatsoever.

And if players, managers and fans alike do not see HOW a call has been made, even by the most pedantic of readings of the Laws, something is more than a little awry.

Even without the Haaland winner, there would have been a sense of disbelief.

Not so much that Phil Foden was sent off for kicking out at Bruno Fernandes in the first half – Enzo Maresca accepted that one WAS right.



But that the United skipper was entirely unpunished for booting the England man in the backside AFTER kicking him to the ground.

Rooney felt Foden was unfortunate, arguing “That can’t be a red card. It was more of a flick or a gesture, than a kick out.”

Then again, he has previous of his own.

But Roy Keane pointed out: “Bruno catches him, gives the foul away and gives him a little kick.

“For me Bruno is the one who is violent here, Foden is a bit daft but so is Bruno. He has got to do better there.”



Micah Richards argued: “When he got kicked, the second action from Fernandes, if Foden starts screaming the decision is reversed.

“Fernandes kicks him. I don’t agree with the reaction from Foden but it was Fernandes who started it.

“As soon as Foden touches him Fernandes starts screaming and rolling about so if you are the referee of course it looks worse than it is.”

That was an arguable one. But the Haaland winner was clear-cut.

The officials at Old Trafford got it right. But they were ordered to get it wrong. How can that make any sense?

Sports.title: Mikel Arteta’s ‘incredible’ new Arsenal model reaping rewards already as David Raya hails Gunners’ strength in depth
Sports.content:
DAVID RAYA used the word “incredible” to describe it.

But the Arsenal goalkeeper was not talking about his stunning penalty save to deny Sunderland midfielder Enzo Le Fee.



Nor was the Spaniard paying tribute to Bruno Guimaraes’ bullet of a strike just 121 seconds later.

Raya was instead hailing the Gunners’ frightening firepower off the bench, which ultimately secured them this 2-0 win to maintain their perfect start to the season.



Guimaraes opened the scoring 13 minutes after coming on at half time, before he combined with Mikel Merino late on to create the penalty that Bukayo Saka won and scored.

Merino and Guimaraes were two of the five substitutes Mikel Arteta used – and their combined transfer fees total around £250million.

Raya said: “It is incredible. All the players coming off the bench were really important.

“That is the model that we have. It is not only the starters, but the people coming from the bench who are really important.

“We had Bruno scoring, and then he and Merino made the pass for Bukayo to win the pen. The whole squad is going to be very important throughout the season.”

BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

Arsenal’s strength in depth is what makes it hard to see who can stop them defending their Premier League crown.



No other side can compete with what Arteta has at his disposal, and last week underlined that.

This trip to Sunderland came off the back of a tough Champions League opener at Napoli in midweek.

The Gunners came through those tests with victories and clean sheets, and Arteta was able to make four changes for both games.

The Spaniard will no doubt make even more changes for tomorrow night’s Carabao Cup third round clash at Ipswich – but don’t expect the quality to drop.

Martin Zubimendi, who was signed for £51million from Real Sociedad a year ago, is one of those hoping to make his first start of the season.



Arteta will argue it is no surprise he has players shining off the bench given the importance he places on that.

One of the many changes the Arsenal boss has made since being hired seven years ago was renaming the substitutes.

They are referred to as ‘finishers’ and that is a product of Arteta being in a coaching WhatsApp group with former England rugby boss Eddie Jones.

It is drilled into the squad how, even if they do not start, they have a crucial role to play off the bench.



That message is clearly getting through and in the Prem last season Arsenal had 23 combined goals and assists from their substitutes, more than any other side.

Raya said: “You have to follow and trust what the boss wants you to do.

“Sometimes you are going to start, and sometimes you are going to be on the bench.

“Having that mentality to be important no matter when and how many minutes you play, is very important – especially when these seasons are so, so long.



“You are going to have your opportunity and you have to take it like everybody does.

“Last season we scored a lot of goals with people from the bench, who changed games. So, hopefully, this season it is the same.”

Guimaraes was a ‘finisher’ on Saturday night, but it surely won’t be long before he is a starter.

Injuries have led to him having a disrupted start since his £75m move from Newcastle this summer.

He looks fully fit now, though, and a cracker of a goal against Sunderland could be the perfect springboard.



Myles Lewis-Skelly has been partnering Declan Rice in midfield this season, however it will surely now be Guimaraes starting at Brighton on Saturday.

Raya said: “Obviously, Bruno has been very unlucky with his start. He had two little injuries that kept him out of the team.

“He brings a lot of things. He brings maturity, competitiveness and leadership. He is a warrior, but he is so technically gifted.

“He reads the game very, very well and he will put his life [on the line] to defend and attack.

“He is a fantastic player to have with us – and hopefully he stays free of injury so we can enjoy him a lot.”

Sports.title: Ref bosses admit Erling Haaland winner in Manchester derby was MISTAKE as Man Utd told investigation to follow
Sports.content:
MANCHESTER UNITED have been told Erling Haaland’s winner in the Manchester derby should NOT have stood.

The Norwegian star handed Man City a 1-0 win at Old Trafford after slotting home at the back post.



But Enzo Fernandez, who was in an offside position, dived for the ball on its way to Haaland, drawing the attention of Lisandro Martinez and Senne Lemmens.

Now, a Pro Ref statement has indicated that Fernandez’s involvement DID influence Man United’s defence and the goal should not have stood.



A Pro Ref spokesperson said: “Following the incident in the 60th minute of Sunday’s Premier League fixture between Manchester United and Manchester City at Old Trafford, we can provide clarification regarding Erling Haaland’s awarded goal.

“The on-field decision was offside against Erling Haaland – that was checked by VAR and he was found to be in an onside position.

“In the same attack, it was established that Enzo Fernandez did not play the ball and therefore that makes any offside offence subjective, however, on this occasion, the VAR did not recognise the likely impact of his position and should have recommended an on-field review.

“Contact has been made with Manchester United this evening to acknowledge what we deem is an error of judgement. A review of the incident will take place.”

Just earlier in the day, the Premier League had backed the decision to award the goal.

BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

The Prem statement read: “VAR checked the referee’s call of no goal for offside – and determined that Haaland was in an onside position and recommended that the goal was awarded.



“The VAR also deemed that while in an offside position, Fernandez didn’t play the ball.”

But Gary Neville knew it was an error from the start and forsore this apology from the Pro Ref.

He told Sky Sports: “They have given the goal… I’m lost. I’m going to need the offside rule explained to me.

“The officials will be nervous about this goal.

“When they look back on this, they will recognise they got this wrong. The question is does Fernandez, who is offside, stop Martinez getting the ball? He does.”



Former referee Mark Halsey also told The Sun that they had got the major decision wrong. It seemed Pro Ref admitting the mistake themselves was all there was to wait for.

But of course, that does not help Manchester United and it does help Manchester City continue their perfect start to the season.

Martinez, the defender who was drawn to the offside Fernandez instead of Haaland, insisted straight after the game that the goal had to be offside.

He said: “It’s the best league in the world, you have the best teams in the world, the best players in the world, and now we have to go home with this injustice.



“I think it was offside. What I can’t understand is the rules. He [Fernandez] was there, in front of me, and I went to him. So that’s why Haaland was free at the back.

‘It’s so hard because you lose a derby and you lose three points at home. Every season they’re coming to our club and explaining the rules for an hour-and-a-half.

“They look so confident, and then after that five or six people are making these kind of mistakes. It’s unacceptable.”

Boss Michael Carrick, who has started the season with four points from four games, also rejected the Premier League’s analysis of the goal.

Speaking to Sky Sports in his post-match interview, Carrick blasted: “I’m confused.



“We put things in place in the game now. We have people in offices with all the screens for this decision.

“It’s more worrying about if that’s the interpretation of football now.

“If that’s the interpretation of not interfering in the game now, that’s really worrying for me. It’s a STAGGERING explanation.”

Sports.title: Should Erling Haaland’s controversial winner vs Man Utd have been disallowed? VOTE NOW
Sports.content:
ERLING HAALAND scored a controversial winner for Manchester City as they edged past Manchester United.

The Norwegian ace crashed home the winner on the hour mark of the Manchester derby, seeing City leave Old Trafford with three points despite Phil Foden‘s first-half sending off leaving the visitors with 10-en for most of the game.



However, Haaland’s goal only stood after a lengthy VAR check.

Referee Michael Oliver had initially called the 26-year-old as offside.



But the City ace was actually being played on by Patrick Dorgu‘s outstretched toe.

Although the controversy came down to Enzo Fernandez’s involvement in the sequence of play.



City’s record buy had been seen standing in an offside position when he lunged towards the ball and impacting Lisandro Martinez’s attempt to clear it.

He did not touch the ball as he attempted to dive towards it before it fell to Haaland who crashed it home into the roof of the net in front of the visiting fans.

And the goal was then given by VAR, with a statement from the Premier League Match Centre explaining: “VAR checked the referee’s call of no goal for offside – and determined that Haaland was in an onside position and recommended that the goal was awarded.

“The VAR also deemed that while in an offside position, Fernandez didn’t play the ball.”



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

However, this seemingly contradicts Ifab’s definition of the offside law.

Law 11 states a player should be penalised for offside if they prevent an opponent from playing or being able to play the ball by clearly obstructing their line of vision.

ProRef – fronted by Howard Webb – have now confirmed it WAS a mistake and that a review of the incident will take place.

Former Prem ref Mark Halsey told SunSport: “We saw more controversy in the Manchester derby. Haaland has put Manchester City 1-0 up only for the assistant referee to rule the goal out as offside.

“Now when we look at it, Haaland is not offside but Fernandez is offside. When the ball comes across, he’s in an offside position.



“Being in an offside position is not an offence in itself. It only becomes an offside offence if the player involved becomes involved in active play by interfering with an opponent or making a deliberate play to play the ball.

“In my opinion, Fernandez does that. And I believe that the assistant referee was correct in flagging Fernandez as offside.

“Obviously all goals are checked. VAR have looked at it, and they have decided that the goal is onside.

“In my opinion, it’s subjective to whether you feel Fernandez is making a deliberate play for the ball, or becoming involved in an active play and interfering with defenders.

“If that’s the case, the subjectivity – VAR – should not have got involved. They should have stuck with the on-field decision of offside, which I believe was the correct call.”
