World.title: U.S. Embassy Marks 25 Years Since 9/11 With Memorial Walk in Monrovia
World.content:
At 9:03 a.m., marking the moment United Airlines Flight 175 struck the South Tower of the World Trade Center, participants began a symbolic 2,977-step memorial walk./ Credit: U.S. Embassy, Monrovia.

Monrovia — The United States Embassy in Monrovia on Friday commemorated the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks on the United States, honoring the 2,977 people who lost their lives in one of the deadliest attacks in U.S. history.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

The commemoration began with the lowering of the U.S. flag at the embassy, followed by a moment of silence led by U.S. Chargé d’Affaires Joe Zadrozny at 8:46 a.m.—the exact time American Airlines Flight 11 crashed into the North Tower of the World Trade Center in New York.

A member of the United States Marine Corps then did a beautiful rendition of the U.S. national anthem, before Zadrozny delivered remarks reflecting on the lives lost, the bravery of first responders and the international solidarity that followed the attacks.

Chargé d’Affaires Zadrozny said the anniversary was an opportunity to remember the 2,977 innocent civilians, first responders and service members killed at the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and in a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania.

“At 8:46 AM, the world shifted in an instant,” Zadrozny said. “What began as a bright September morning transformed into a day of unprecedented tragedy.”

He said the anniversary was an opportunity to remember the 2,977 innocent civilians, first responders and service members killed at the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and in a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania.

The Chargé d’Affaires also paid tribute to firefighters, police officers and paramedics who rushed toward danger, as well as passengers aboard United Airlines Flight 93 who resisted the hijackers before the aircraft crashed in Pennsylvania.

“We remember the courage of the firefighters, police officers, and paramedics who ran toward danger so that others might live,” Zadrozny said. “We remember the ordinary citizens on Flight 93, who performed extraordinary acts of bravery.”

Liberia’s Solidarity Remembered

Zadrozny also recalled Liberia’s response to the tragedy, noting that the Liberian government organized an intercessory service and declared three days of national mourning for the victims, including at least one Liberian.

The commemoration began with the lowering of the U.S. flag at the embassy, followed by a moment of silence at 8:46 a.m.—the exact time American Airlines Flight 11 crashed into the North Tower of the World Trade Center in New York./ Credit: U.S. Embassy, Monrovia. “As our flag flies at half-staff, we carry a duty not only to remember the past, but to live out the values of resilience, public service, and unity that defined the days after 9/11,” he said. 2,977 Steps in Memory of 2,977 Lives At 9:03 a.m., marking the moment United Airlines Flight 175 struck the South Tower of the World Trade Center, participants began a symbolic 2,977-step memorial walk. The walk started at the embassy flagpole, proceeded through the main gate and around the embassy compound along UN Drive and Benson Street. Each step represented one of the 2,977 people who died in the September 11 attacks. Despite a heavy downpour, Zadrozny joined the walk alongside Liberian government officials, U.S. Embassy staff and members of the press. The memorial concluded with participants returning to the embassy grounds, where they gathered for coffee and refreshments. The 9/11 attacks killed 2,977 people after four hijacked commercial aircraft were used in coordinated attacks against the World Trade Center in New York, the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia, and a target that was not reached after Flight 93 crashed in Shanksville, Pennsylvania. Zadrozny said the anniversary should serve not only as a moment to remember the past but also as a reminder of the values of resilience, public service and unity. He described Liberia’s solidarity with the United States following the attacks as an enduring element of the two countries’ relationship. “Our Liberian hosts and international partners stood together with the United States in our grief, reminding us that we do not stand alone,” he said. “That solidarity remains a cornerstone of our work together today.”

World.title: Liberia: Boakai Shuffles Cabinet: New Acting Defense, Commerce Ministers; Gender Deputy Suspended
World.content:
Monrovia – President Joseph Nyuma Boakai Sr. has shaken up several government ministries and agencies, announcing a wave of new appointments this week.

Cllr. Oswald Natu Tweh takes over as Acting Minister of National Defense, stepping in for Geraldine J. George. Over at Commerce and Industry, Stephen Marka Yekeson Jr. steps into the acting minister role, replacing Magdalene E. Dagoseh. Both George and Dagoseh will be reassigned to other government positions.

The president also tapped Christopher Ben Bailey to serve as Acting Superintendent of Grand Gedeh County. At the National Food Assistance Agency, Mike Khailelu B. Jabateh moves into the role of Acting Deputy Director General for Publicity.

In another appointment, Daniel Frank Gould II has been named to the Board of Commissioners of the Public Procurement and Concessions Commission, though his nomination still needs Senate confirmation.

On the disciplinary side, Frederick S. Cooper, Deputy Minister for Administration at the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection, has been suspended for 60 days without pay. The Executive Mansion says the move stems from conduct it considers incompatible with Cooper’s role as a public official.

Boakai used the moment to send a broader message to his administration, warning officials that public office comes with real accountability — and that conduct undermining government integrity or public trust won’t be tolerated.

World.title: Liberia: A Mystery Vessel, a Prison, and a Warning Nobody Answered
World.content:
MONROVIA — There is a version of this story in which the boat behind the Monrovia Central Prison is nothing more than a stray vessel, pushed toward shore by the tide and forgotten within days.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected] and Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

But Thursday’s discovery is difficult to view in isolation.

Five weeks ago, the prison’s Deputy Superintendent for Operations, Jackson K. Kolako, publicly warned that he believed a plan was being developed to facilitate a mass jailbreak—potentially freeing foreign nationals detained in connection with Liberia’s largest cocaine investigation.

Now, before dawn on Thursday, a vessel of disputed ownership and unexplained movements was found at the beach behind the same prison.

Coincidence is possible. But the timing has raised questions that authorities have yet to fully answer.

What Kolako Actually Said

Kolako’s account dates to August 1, when, according to him, two men arrived at the prison claiming to be National Security Agency officers. He said the men were dressed in a manner inconsistent with prison security rules and sought access to one of the foreign nationals detained in connection with the drug case.

Kolako said he questioned whether the prison’s chief superintendent and the Assistant Minister of Justice for Corrections had authorized the visit.

He says he was arrested later that day, in front of his officers, on the orders of a senior Justice Ministry official.

According to Kolako, he spent six days in custody without giving a statement and was pressured to surrender his phones and passwords. Following his release, he publicly raised his concerns and appealed to President Joseph Boakai to consider moving detainees connected to the drug investigation to a more secure facility outside Liberia, suggesting Morocco as one possible destination.

Kolako’s account, however, remains contested.

He has not publicly produced evidence establishing that an actual jailbreak plot was underway, while officials he implicated have not publicly addressed all of his allegations. Ministry of Justice records have reportedly presented a different explanation for his suspension, saying he was sanctioned over alleged obstruction of a lawful operation rather than for raising security concerns.

The competing accounts have yet to be reconciled.

On Thursday, Kolako again took to social media, emphasizing the need for heightened coordination among the Liberia National Police, Armed Forces of Liberia and corrections authorities.

Kolako, using the name Gertrude’s Pap on Facebook, said the detention of people connected to sensitive and high-profile cases requires preparedness, coordination and vigilance.

“Security is stronger when institutions work together,” Kolako wrote.

Mystery Vessel Sparks Calls for Independent Probe

The vessel’s appearance has now triggered calls for an independent investigation.

Liberian activist Martin K. N. Kollie, whose network first reported the boat, is calling for an independent inquiry into how the unidentified vessel came to be at the beach behind the Monrovia Central Prison, commonly known as South Beach.

Kollie has described the vessel as a “ghost boat” and questioned conflicting accounts surrounding its ownership, origin and movements.

He has specifically called for an investigation outside the Liberia National Police, including Inspector General Gregory Coleman, arguing that the circumstances require investigators viewed as independent by the public.

The vessel was later moved toward the Miami Beach area, according to accounts surrounding the incident, further raising questions about who controlled it and why it had initially been positioned near the prison.

The Question of the Boat

Kollie has also challenged claims that the vessel found at South Beach belongs to a person identified publicly only as “Charlie,” who reportedly described himself during a radio interview as a Canadian miner.

Kollie maintains that images circulated by people claiming ownership show a different vessel from the one found behind the prison.

That claim has not been independently verified by FrontPage Africa.

The unresolved questions are nevertheless straightforward: Who owns the vessel? Where did it come from? Who was operating it? When did it leave the St. Paul River? How did it reach South Beach? And was anyone aboard at any point during the journey?

Those questions become more consequential because of the vessel’s location.

The beach behind the prison sits within a highly sensitive security environment, particularly as the facility houses detainees linked to Liberia’s ongoing drug-trafficking investigation.

A Country That Has Seen This Boat Before

The episode comes against a backdrop of growing scrutiny over Liberia’s maritime security.

In June, a vessel identified as the IB Atlantic IV remained off the coast of Grand Cape Mount County for several days as Liberian authorities considered how to respond before the vessel eventually moved away and was later intercepted and seized in Ivorian waters.

No drugs were officially reported recovered from the vessel.

The episode nevertheless became another example of the challenges facing Liberia in monitoring and securing its coastline.

The latest vessel presents a different but related set of questions.

Despite competing ownership claims, authorities have not publicly established who owns the boat, how it reached South Beach or whether it was carrying anything when it arrived.

Nor has any official investigation publicly established a connection between the vessel and the ongoing drug-trafficking cases.

What Remains Unanswered

For now, the boat remains less an answer than a question.

There is no publicly established evidence that the vessel was part of a jailbreak attempt. There is also no publicly established evidence that it was connected to the drug investigation.

But the combination of its location, the conflicting accounts surrounding its ownership and movement, and the prison security warnings raised weeks earlier has created a legitimate public-interest question.

An independent investigation could establish the facts without relying on competing narratives—determining the vessel’s ownership, registration, route, occupants, cargo, movements and circumstances surrounding its arrival at South Beach.

Until those questions are answered, the vessel behind the prison wall will remain what it became Thursday morning: a mystery sitting in plain sight.

World.title: Liberia: Expert Warns of Security Risks if Legislature Fails to Approve War Crimes Court Before U.N. Security Council Presidency
World.content:
Summary

Transitional justice expert Aaron Weah warns that failure to approve legislation establishing Liberia’s long-delayed War and Economic Crimes Court could create new security risks, particularly among a young generation raised on memories of the civil wars.

Liberia is preparing to assume the rotating presidency of the U.N. Security Council in December, putting a renewed international spotlight on the country’s unfinished transitional justice process.

Weah says Liberia must address how the wars are remembered and taught, warning that the absence of an agreed historical narrative, public memorials and museums has left younger Liberians exposed to disinformation about the conflict.

By Anthony Stephens, senior justice correspondent with New Narratives

Aaron Weah, the leading historian and transitional justice expert, has warned of security risks if the country fails to approve legislation establishing a War and Economic Crimes Court before it assumes the rotating presidency of the United Nations Security Council in December.

Despite years of advocacy, the push for a long-delayed court to prosecute those accused of “bearing the greatest responsibility” for atrocities committed during Liberia’s two civil wars, which the United Nations estimates left about 250,000 people dead, remains unfinished as the Legislature has so far failed to overcome opposition to the courts among lawmakers.

A recent poll by FrontPage Africa/New Narratives found 89 percent of survey respondents in 11 counties wanted to see the worst perpetrators tried in a war crimes court for atrocities committed during the war.

“You don’t want to raise expectations of people and let them down. I think it has a lot of security risk because we have a youthful population,” Weah, director of the Ducor Institute for Social and Economic Research, said in a FrontPage Africa/New Narratives interview.

Weah’s warning comes at a pivotal moment for Liberia’s unfinished transitional justice process. The country is preparing to preside over the Security Council for the first time while lawmakers consider competing proposals for the long-promised court. At the same time, a population dominated by young people who did not directly experience the wars is confronting unresolved questions about justice, reparations and how the conflict should be remembered and taught.

Weah said establishing the court is about more than prosecuting alleged perpetrators. He argued that it could help clarify Liberia’s wartime history and said abandoning the process after years of promises could create new resentment and security concerns.

His warning echoes concerns raised by the Liberian government and the United Nations. In an October 2025, statement to the U.N. General Assembly’s Sixth Committee, which deals with international legal issues, the government warned that “the absence of justice perpetuates the cycle of conflict.”

Liberia’s civil wars claimed an estimated 250,000 lives. Credit: Chris Hondros / Getty Images.

The United Nations has also linked the proposed court to preventing recurrence. Christian Mukosa, its top human rights official in Liberia, said that operationalizing a victim-centered court could “contribute to reconciliation and prevent recurrence.”

According to Liberia’s 2022 Population and Housing Census , three in every four of the country’s 5.25 million people were 35 or younger. Forty four percent of the population was born after the civil wars ended in 2003. Weah said many young Liberians have instead grown up with memories of the wars passed down by their parents. After taking the court process this far, he warned, abandoning it could have consequences beyond the justice debate.

Liberia’s official campaign graphic for its successful bid for a non-permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council for 2026–2027. Credit: Government of Liberia

Liberia previously served on the Security Council in 1961, but the December presidency will be its first time chairing the body. The 81st United Nations General Assembly began September 8, with President Joseph Boakai expected to deliver his third address during the General Debate, which begins September 22.

Jallah Barbu, executive director of the Office for the Establishment of the War and Economic Crimes Court, recently urged Boakai to recall lawmakers from their annual constituency break to act on the legislation.

Six proposals involving a War and Economic Crimes Court and a National Anti-Corruption Court are before the Legislature. They include proposals from the Liberian National Bar Association and a civil society coalition led by the Independent National Commission on Human Rights ; separate proposals from Senate President Pro Tempore Nyonblee Karnga-Lawrence and Senator Joseph Jallah; and two bills from the government’s court office.

Boakai reenergized the process when he renewed the Office’s mandate in May and later submitted its bills to the Legislature. But lawmakers went on their annual constituency break in July without approving legislation.

Before the recess, the Senate Judiciary Committee began consultations aimed at harmonizing the proposals, while more than 40 House members participated in a two-day technical session in Buchanan in June.

Some proposals have raised concerns among justice advocates over issues including the role of international experts and the appeals process. Senator Jallah has suggested international lawyers could serve as “consultants to Liberians” , rather than take direct roles.

“The final bill should include all benchmarks of fair, independent, meaningful and credible trials: crimes and modes of liability in line with international standards,” Michelle Reyes Milk, senior international justice counsel at Human Rights Watch, wrote in Just Security, a nonpartisan law and policy journal based at New York University School of Law. She also called for “full guarantees of due process for defendants” and “genuine participation and protection for victims and witnesses.”

Weah said Liberia’s Security Council role could showcase the country’s progress since the wars. He pointed to the success of international peacekeeping and the peaceful resolution of the closely fought 2023 presidential election as signs of the country’s resilience.

But he warned that sustaining that progress requires Liberia to confront how its wars are remembered and taught to younger generations.

“We have no public memorials. We have not agreed on a historical text on the war to teach kids in school,” Weah said. “And so much of what the children learn that’s passed for history is mostly the opinions of history teachers, is the opinions of civic teachers in school, and that’s dangerous.”

Weah said museums, memorials and other forms of public education could give younger Liberians a more structured understanding of the country’s past and help address violent memories transmitted from one generation to another.

Liberia has made some steps up efforts to address memorialization. A high-level government delegation has returned from a United Nations Development Program-supported study mission to Rwanda and South Africa in late August and early September, where it examined approaches to reconciliation, memorialization, peacebuilding and preserving national history. The lessons are expected to inform President Boakai’s proposed Liberia Peace, Reconciliation and Memorial Museum, envisioned as a national institution to preserve the country’s history, promote reconciliation and strengthen civic education.

TRC’s Controversial Decision to Sanction President Johnson Sirleaf Remains a Point of Debate

But Liberia’s efforts to establish an authoritative account of the wars have themselves generated controversy. More than 15 years after the Truth and Reconciliation Commission issued its final report, parts of its findings remain contested.

The commission recommended a 30-year public-office ban for a number of people, including then-President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, because it said they had been associated with former warring factions. In 2011, Liberia’s Supreme Court struck down the sanction as unconstitutional , finding that it had been imposed without due process.

Liberian civilians flee Paynesville amid fighting between rebel forces and the Armed Forces of Liberia on Aug. 10, 1990, during the country’s first civil war. Credit: Pascal Guyot/AFP via Getty Images.

In testimony to the U.S. Congress in June 1990 , as Taylor’s rebellion was terrorizing people across the country, Sirleaf portrayed Taylor’s uprising as a broad-based struggle, saying people, “many of them children,” had joined what she called a “struggle for freedom,” and describing the rebellion as an opportunity to transform Liberia’s political system. (Taylor’s alleged use of child soldiers was seen as a particularly egregious act that was copied by other warring factions in years to come.)

Weah argued that the commission’s treatment of Sirleaf contributed to her reluctance to champion implementation of its recommendations and questioned whether the report sufficiently established the extent of her involvement in the conflict.

“I think she felt embarrassed. She felt stigmatized,” Weah said. “Before you mention the names of people in report, there has to be a duty of care to make sure that your work is thorough, is rigorous. It can stand up to basic scrutiny.”

John Stewart, a commissioner who chaired the committee that wrote the TRC report, rejected Weah’s criticism. He said Sirleaf was sanctioned because commissioners concluded that her testimony about when she distanced herself from Charles Taylor conflicted with evidence they had obtained.

“We did not do so because we wanted to embarrass Sirleaf,” Stewart said. “We did so because we wanted to be fair to all others. And her being president was no exception to the rule.”

The disagreement underscores the difficulty Liberia still faces in establishing a broadly accepted account of its violent past — the problem Weah says younger generations should not be left to navigate alone.

Against that backdrop, Weah recently co-launched Liberia: Remembering the Future with British journalist Gerry Naughton. The podcast, airing on 10 radio stations across Liberia, examines the country’s history, its transition from war to peace and its election to the Security Council.

Weah said the project aims to provide historical context and clarification for Liberians, particularly younger people, as well as international audiences seeking to understand the country as its global profile rises.

This story was a collaboration with New Narratives as part of the Investigating Liberia project. Funding was provided by the U.N. Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights and the European Union. The funders had no say in the story’s content.

World.title: SpoonTV CEO Details Cooperation With U.S. Investigators That Led to Reduced Sentence and Early Release
World.content:
Monrovia — SpoonTV CEO Stanton Witherspoon has offered a detailed account of how his decision to cooperate with U.S. federal investigators ultimately helped secure his release from prison after he was convicted in a multimillion-dollar scheme involving fraudulent nursing diplomas and transcripts.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

Witherspoon, who pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud, was sentenced in November 2023 to 41 months in prison and three years of supervised release.

But on September 9, 2026, U.S. District Judge Rodney Smith granted a motion by federal prosecutors to reduce the sentence to time served, eliminating the supervised-release requirement and dismissing the remaining counts against him.

The reduction was granted under Rule 35(b) of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure, which allows prosecutors to seek a reduced sentence for a defendant who provides substantial assistance to the government after sentencing.

Witherspoon said Thursday that his cooperation was not simply a strategy to obtain a shorter sentence, but a decision he made after his lawyer and one of his Spoon Talk colleagues advised him that cooperating early could benefit his case and help investigators pursue others involved in the alleged fraud.

‘Cooperate’

Recounting the events on Spoon Talk, Witherspoon said panelist Abdullah Kiatamba advised him in 2023 to consider cooperating with investigators.

According to Witherspoon, Kiatamba told him that he was not making a judgment about his guilt or innocence but was speaking from his understanding of the U.S. legal system.

“He said, no matter what you do, I’m going to talk to you from experience. Cooperate,” Witherspoon recalled.

Witherspoon said he initially questioned the advice.

“I said, what are you talking about? He said, Stanton, I’m not saying you are guilty. I’m not saying you are not guilty. But I know the system. Talk to your lawyer.”

He said he followed the advice and consulted his attorney, who also recommended that he cooperate with investigators at an early stage.

According to Witherspoon, his lawyer warned that delaying cooperation could diminish its value if other defendants cooperated first.

“Every other day, the lawyer would say, Stanton, if you’re the last to cooperate, you are not needed. If you must cooperate, cooperate now,” he recalled.

Witherspoon said his lawyer subsequently explained the cooperation process and its potential implications to him step by step.

What Prosecutors Say He Provided

The government’s court filings indicate that Witherspoon’s cooperation went beyond simply providing information about his own conduct.

According to prosecutors, he was interviewed by agents from the FBI and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General about individuals involved in nursing-school fraud schemes.

Prosecutors said his cooperation contributed to cases against several defendants, including Carleen Noreus, Cimoyne Alves, Lemuel Pierre and Cleophat Tanis.

Witherspoon testified against Noreus, who operated a separate fraudulent nursing program known as Carleen Health Institute. Following his testimony, prosecutors said Noreus pleaded guilty to wire fraud and money-laundering conspiracy charges and is awaiting sentencing.

Witherspoon also signed an affidavit identifying nursing students who received fraudulent degrees and transcripts. That information was provided to the National Council of State Boards of Nursing so state licensing authorities could take remedial action.

‘I Was a Star Witness’

Witherspoon described himself as a key witness for the government, saying investigators needed information and supporting documents that he possessed because of his involvement in the nursing-school business.

He said he had recruited students for multiple schools and therefore had knowledge of people involved in the operation.

“Now they have so many big, big people that were involved in this thing. And a lot of them came to me to recruit students for them,” Witherspoon said.

He said investigators already knew some of the individuals but needed additional evidence.

“The government knew them, but the government needed supporting documents from me.”

According to Witherspoon, one of the principal defendants initially refused to cooperate, leading prosecutors to call him to testify.

“I had to take the stand for the government. For four months, the woman couldn’t break. And the government called a star witness. And I was a star witness.”

Witherspoon said that after he testified, the defendant subsequently agreed to plead guilty.

“After I testified, the next day, the woman begged for the plea. She’s scheduled to be sentenced. It’s a public record.”

The account corresponds with prosecutors’ description of Witherspoon’s cooperation in the case involving Noreus.

A $5.17 Million Fraud

Federal prosecutors said Witherspoon was a 50% owner of Siena Education Center LLC and Siena College of Health II LLC and was also the founder and president of Nursing Education Resource Center LLC.

Prosecutors alleged that Witherspoon, working with Rene Bernadel, Alfred Sellu and Cimoyne Alves, used NERC to recruit and fraudulently train aspiring nurses.

He later worked with Eunide Sanon and Siena to provide fake nursing diplomas and transcripts, which students allegedly used to obtain fraudulent certification as registered nurses or licensed practical nurses.

Witherspoon was held responsible for approximately $5.17 million in losses.

His total offense level was calculated at 26, with a criminal history category of I, producing a federal sentencing guideline range of 63 to 78 months. He ultimately received a 41-month sentence.

‘I Wanted This to Stop’

Witherspoon said his decision to cooperate was motivated by more than his own legal circumstances.

He said he wanted to expose the broader operation and help prevent others from being harmed by fraudulent nursing credentials.

“I had to do it not because I was fighting for myself. I had to do it because I wanted this to stop,” he said.

“I had to do it because I want the system to be right.”

Witherspoon said the information he possessed was extensive and involved conversations with professionals and others connected to the business.

He also thanked his attorney for guiding him through the cooperation process.

Prosecutors Backed Sentence Reduction

The government’s motion to reduce Witherspoon’s sentence was supported by prosecutors and investigators from the FBI and HHS-OIG, who cited the scope of his cooperation.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Christopher J. Clark filed the motion on behalf of the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Florida.

Judge Rodney Smith subsequently ordered Witherspoon released on time served and removed the three-year supervised-release component of his original sentence.

The remaining counts against him—Counts 2 through 6 and Count 8—were dismissed.

For Witherspoon, the sequence of events—from advice to cooperate, through interviews and testimony, to the government’s Rule 35(b) motion—ultimately culminated in his release.

“Yes, indeed, I cooperated with the government. And that’s why I took a plea. And today, the result of the plea is that Stanton is a free man,” he said.

He ended his account by thanking his lawyer and those who supported him during his legal battle.

World.title: Borrowed Majesties: Why Paramount Chiefs Are Afraid of Chief Mukuni
World.content:
By Kapya Kaoma

Judge Pixie Yangailo’s refusal to grant Chitimukulu, the Litunga, and Undi joinder in Chief Mukuni’s petition seeking paramount-chief status is a major blow to the “traditional” establishment. The chiefs have reasons to be nervous: this case could be revolutionary. It has the potential to transform the very definition of paramount chieftainship.

It is telling that the trio’s anxiety hinges upon how “junior chiefs” might interpret Mukuni’s victory—it would “destabilize traditional governance.” What they omit, however, is that the creation of paramount chiefs by colonial rulers was itself an act of social destabilization.

Until the colonial era, the concept of a “junior chief” did not exist among the Tonga. The same is true for the Chishinga and other tribes. Every paramount chief in postcolonial Zambia is a product of colonial policy of divide et impera (divide-and-rule) often associated with Frederick Lugard. The trio is deeply afraid because someone is finally questioning an injustice passed off as ancient tradition. Yet nothing socially constructed remains scrutinized. What was constructed can be deconstructed and reconstructed.

Reading Chief Mukuni’s petition, it seems his claim rests primarily on “tradition” rather than ethno-history. It is unclear whether this legal strategy is deliberate, given that tradition is manufactured over time. Yet the claims of the Litunga, Chitimukulu, and Undi over vast territories similarly lack ethno-historical foundation. Instead, their status rests on an assumed history of conquest and the subjugation of neighboring groups. Paramount chieftainship historically had less to do with organic tribal conquest than with fulfilling the colonial administrative agenda.

As a Tonga, for example, Chief Mukuni cannot claim his ancestors defeated other Tonga groups in battle to establish political hegemony. Traditionally, the Tonga were acephalous societies–they never had kings or chiefs. Instead, authority was decentralized around sikatongos (or bami ba mfula)—“owners of rain”—whose responsibility was rainmaking.

Because Tonga life depended on balanced rainfall for their two season harvest, sikatongos whose lands received better rains attracted larger communities, as was the case with Monze and Mweemba. Yet, because a sikatongo’s authority was derived from local ancestors (basangu), his influence didn’t extend beyond his immediate neighborhood. In Tonga cosmology, ancestral reach is strictly bound to ancestral land—a principle still celebrated during the Lwiindi ceremony. Moreover, historically, the Tonga were known for their resistance to any centralized monarch.

Two historical forces disrupted this sociopolitical organization: slave raiding and colonialism. Because the Tonga lacked centralized military structures, they were vulnerable to slave raiders. In response, charismatic sikatongos began organizing defensive alliances. Then came European colonialism. David Livingstone was among the first to label Mweemba and Monze as Tonga “chiefs,” even though the title and its political implications were alien to Tonga society. The term sikatongo does not translate to “king” or “chief.”

Colonial authorities later codified select sikatongos into official chiefs, granting them arbitrary authority over neighboring communities. Today, that administrative convenience is celebrated as authentic Tonga culture. Mukuni’s claim rests in this frame. Yet, like the office of paramount chief itself, Mukuni’s current area of authority was codified by the state as opposed to unbroken lineage.

No doubt Mukuni is making a clever calculation. With Hakainde Hichilema in power, he sees a window for elevation. This is what Chitimukulu, the Litunga, and Undi fear most–the very state system that elevated their offices could now elevate others or dismantle their exclusive status.

They have enjoyed unchecked top-tier authority for over a century, but Mukuni is stubborn enough to challenge the setup. If he succeeds, other leaders may seek to undo these social imbalances. Hence they are losing sleep–”official” history could be rewritten in a courtroom—ending in the creation of “Paramount Chief Mukuni.”

I believe Chief Mukuni would likely strengthen his claim by grounding his case in the political history of Zambian chieftainship rather than relying solely on “tradition.” As I have noted, cultural experts can easily contest traditional claims due to a lack of ethno-historical evidence. However, the political argument can hardly be refuted: no Zambian paramount chief historically exercised total control over all the territories and sub-chiefs currently assigned to them. Those regional monopolies were constructed by colonial and postcolonial bureaucracies.

So just as provinces, districts, and constituencies are regularly redrawn to reflect modern realities, there is no logical reason to treat colonial-era paramount titles as immutable. There is nothing ancient about the office of paramount chief—a reality symbolized even by the Litunga’s colonial-British-inspired ceremonial uniform.

Because tradition is fluid, paramount chieftaincy was meant to support narratives of domination. Over time, these constructs were ritualized to marginalize and subordinate other traditional leaders.

Who doesn’t know that history is written by the powerful, while truths remain buried with the powerless? If paramount chieftainships were created by colonialists, shouldn’t contemporary realities invite modernized structures? This question extends beyond Chief Mukuni. It is an issue all “junior” traditional leaders could bring before the Constitutional Court.

Even if Chief Mukuni loses, he is forcing us to question whether colonial structures should be treated as sacred texts. Is it time to re-evaluate the institution of paramount chieftainship today?

It takes stubborn people to expose the blind spots of cultural assumptions. This is what Chief Mukuni is doing.

World.title: Farmers cautioned against selling their entire harvest
World.content:
BuyZed Campaign Founder and Chief Executive Officer Evans Ng’oma says Zambians could face higher food prices if the impending El Niño disrupts local food production.

Mr Ng’oma has implored the government to put in place measures aimed at safeguarding the country’s abundant food stocks, following a bumper maize harvest of close to five million metric tonnes.

He told the media in an interview today, that farmers should resist the temptation to sell off their entire harvest and instead retain sufficient maize stocks for household and national food security.

Mr Ng’oma noted that Zambia is currently enjoying a bumper harvest of close to five million metric tonnes, giving the country an opportunity to build reserves before possible El Niño-induced production challenges emerge.

He has urged small-scale and commercial farmers to keep adequate stocks, while calling on the government to increase the Food Reserve Agency’s (FRA) maize purchases from the current 500,000 metric tonnes, to about three times the said quantity.

Mr Ng’oma explained that stronger reserves would help stabilise food supplies and cushion consumers from possible price shocks if local production declines.

He has also called for improved storage facilities by the FRA, saying reduced post-harvest losses is critical to ensuring that the country has sufficient food reserves to withstand possible disruptions, as well as ensuring that more of the country’s maize remains available for both local consumption and export.

Meanwhile, Mr Ngoma has urged farmers to prepare for the anticipated erratic rainfall by planting drought-tolerant and early-maturing crop varieties and adopting water-conserving practices such as potholing.

He encouraged farmers to also seek guidance from agricultural camp officers on measures to mitigate the effects of the El Niño.

BuyZed Founder has further called for greater diversification away from maize, particularly through increased production of sorghum, which he says is better suited to extreme weather conditions.

Mr N’goma has since urged the government to consider providing small-scale farmers with sorghum seed through the Farmer Input Support Programme (FISP), to help strengthen food security and reduce dependence on maize.

World.title: Public warned, seek guidance before engaging in any exercises
World.content:
Health authorities in North‑Western Province have urged members of the public to access physiotherapy services to improve quality of life and help prevent non‑communicable diseases.

Speaking during the World Physiotherapy Day commemoration held in Solwezi District, Provincial Public Health Specialist Kizito Sampa said engaging in exercises promotes fitness and supports a healthy life for all age groups.

Dr Sampa explained that lack of exercise has a significant impact on health adding that it leads to cardiovascular diseases.

He said the country has been recording an increase in non-communicable diseases such as diabetes and hypertension stressing the need for members of the public to engage in physical exercises to help prevent them.

Dr Sampa has encouraged members of the public who may suffer from diseases such as stroke to urgently seek attention at health facilities in their localities.

He stated that the physiotherapy department is working closely with the psychiatric department, noting that physical health has a bearing on mental health.

“Today we are raising awareness for physiotherapy and suicide prevention because these two are negatively affecting people and the impact is negatively affecting lives,” he noted.

Solwezi General Hospital Senior Physiotherapist Emmanuel Mikiloni has cautioned members of the public against engaging in physical exercises without guidance from health practitioners.

He added that members of the public are encouraged to get a prescription for exercises they can engage in which are in line with their age and health condition.

“People should not just start exercising without guidance because exercises can affect their bodies,” Mr Mikiloni emphasised.

Solwezi General Hospital Clinical Psychiatrist Chongo Chanda has called for concerted effort in raising awareness on suicide.

He has expressed sadness that lives have continued to be lost to suicide because people fear opening up.

Mr Chanda has encouraged people to seek mental health attention when faced with mental health issues, further calling on members of the public to desist from discriminating against people suffering from mental health conditions but to offer them support to help them heal.

World.title: FAZ appointments Kunsanama as head coach Zambia U15 Coach
World.content:
The Football Association of Zambia (FAZ) has appointed Brian Kunsanama as Head Coach of the Zambia Under‑15 Boys National Team ahead of the first‑ever FIFA U‑15 World Cup and Festival.

Kunsanama will lead a newly constituted technical bench that will begin preparations immediately for the tournament scheduled for Baku, Azerbaijan, from October 22 to 31, 2026.

FAZ General Secretary Charles Chakatazya said Kunsanama will be assisted by Lawrence Lubinda, Josephat Nkhoma, Brian Lubaba and Joyford Mambe.

Former Chipolopolo and Zanaco goalkeeper Racha Kola has been named Goalkeeper Coach, while Mike Mudenda will serve as Physical Trainer.

The full bench also includes Erick Mwanampwaya as Team Manager, Dr Michael Mbelenge as Team Doctor, Stanley Malasa as Team Security, Owen Munsaka as Physiotherapist, and Obbey Mweetwa as Equipment Manager.

Chakatazya said Kunsanama comes with experience in youth development, having previously coached Atletico Lusaka before moving to National Division League side Aguila Stars.

He noted that this U-15 bench is different from the one set up for school-going players, as this team will be open to all eligible players.

“However, in essence, players in this age group are largely school-going,” Chakatazya said.

Zambia will be among 211 teams from all FIFA member associations expected to participate in the inaugural FIFA U-15 World Cup and Festival.

“The newly appointed U-15 technical bench has been tasked with preparing a competitive team for Zambia’s participation,” Chakatazya said.

He added that FAZ expects the coaches to use the platform to build a strong foundation for future national teams.

“As you may be aware, FIFA has created the U-15 World Cup and Festival as an international youth football competition for national teams of players up to the age of 15 in order to promote youth football,” Chakatazya said.

“The first edition will be for boys, while the girls’ competition will follow next year, this will be an annual tournament, and our coaches must use this platform to build strong youth teams for the future, ” he added.

Full U15 Technical Bench include Head Coach: Brian Kunsanama, First Assistant Coach Lawrence Lubinda, Assistant Coach Josephat Nkhoma, Assistant Coach Brian Lubaba, Assistant Coach Joyford Mambe, Goalkeeper Coach Racha Kola, Physical Trainer Mike Mudenda, Team Manager Erick Mwanampwaya, Team Doctor Dr Michael Mbelenge, Team Security Stanley Malasa, Physiotherapist Owen Munsaka, Equipment Manager Obbey Mweetwa.

This is according to a statement released to the media by FAZ Head of Media and Communications Nkweto Tembwe.

World.title: Man robbed of motorbike in Chipata
World.content:
A 26‑year‑old man has been attacked and robbed of his motorbike by two unknown men in the Chizongwe School area of Chipata District.

Eastern Province Police Commanding Officer Robertson Mweemba said the incident occurred on Saturday, September 12, 2026, around 18:00 hours.

Mr Mweemba said the victim, identified as George Zulu of Mchini Compound in Chipata, reported the matter at Chipata Central Police Station at about 20:12 hours the same day.

He said Zulu was attacked by the two men, who robbed him of his Gatoma motorbike, registration number ARD 1925, black in colour, valued at 26,500 Kwacha.

Mr Mweemba said the victim sustained multiple cuts to his face after being assaulted with an unknown object.

He said a police medical report form was issued to the victim.

Mr Mweemba said no arrests had been made and the motorbike had not been recovered.

He said police had since instituted investigations into the matter.

World.title: Anthrax outbreak in Mpika
World.content:
Government has intensified measures to contain an anthrax outbreak in the Nabwalya area of Mpika District in Muchinga Province.

This follows the confirmation of cases among both animals and humans.

Muchinga Province Permanent Secretary Tuesday Bwalya says the government has since heightened disease surveillance and community sensitisation in the affected area to prevent further transmission of anthrax.

Dr Bwalya said the Ministry of Health, in collaboration with the Disaster Risk Management Division (DRMD), is intensifying surveillance of infected animals to ensure that affected carcasses are safely disposed of.

Speaking to the media in Nabwalya, Dr Bwalya stated that the Ministry of Health has stepped up its efforts to supply medicines to surrounding health centres to treat people infected with the disease.

“We have also commenced community engagements with the local people here by sensitising them on the dangers of consuming meat which is infected,” he said.

Dr Bwalya further stressed that government will continue strengthening interventions aimed at containing the outbreak as well as preventing the disease from spreading to other communities.

And Muchinga Provincial Health Director David Silweya, confirmed that about 14 patients infected with anthrax are currently receiving treatment in various health facilities in the district.

Dr Silweya noted that the condition of the patients is stable, adding that the treatment being administered is proving to be effective.

He has since urged members of the public to avoid accessing or handling carcasses of animals suspected to have died from anthrax, saying this could increase the risk of further infections.

“As the Ministry of Health, we have also started providing Information, Education and Communication materials to the surrounding communities on anthrax,” he said.

Meanwhile, the Department of National Parks and Wildlife Senior Warden Peter Sichivula, disclosed that more than 26 wild animals have so far died from anthrax in the affected area.

Mr Sichivula said the number of infected animals could increase as surveillance and monitoring activities continue.

He pointed out that the Department of National Parks and Wildlife working with other security wings, has also intensified measures to restrict the movement and consumption of wild meat in an effort to curb the spread of the disease.

Anthrax is a serious infectious disease caused by a bacterium called Bacillus anthracis and mainly affects animals such as cattle, goats, sheep and some wild animals, but humans can also become infected.

World.title: Arrows soar into CAF Cup 2nd Round
World.content:
‎Zambian representatives Red Arrows have advanced to the second preliminary round of the CAF Confederation Cup after a dominant 4-0 aggregate win over FC Rouge of Madagascar.

‎

‎The Airmen completed the job on Sunday afternoon with a 2-0 victory in the return leg played in Port Louis, Mauritius.

‎

‎Rouge are hosting home games in Mauritius because Madagascar has no CAF-certified stadium.

‎

‎Forward Ackim Mumba was the hero, scoring in both halves to seal progress.

‎

‎He opened the scoring in the 23rd minute and added his second in the 55th minute.

‎

‎Arrows had already beaten Rouge 2-0 in the first leg a week ago at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium, Ndola.

‎

‎That makes it a commanding double for Chisi Mbewe’s side.

‎

‎Red Arrows now face a massive test in the Second Preliminary Round.

‎

‎They will take on South African giants Kaizer Chiefs.

‎

‎The first leg is scheduled for 16-18 October and the return leg for 23-25 October.

‎

‎The winners advance to the Confederation Cup group stage.

‎

‎Arrows’ progress comes as welcome news for Zambia after Power Dynamos were eliminated from the CAF Champions League on Saturday.

‎

‎Power lost 1-0 at home to Al Merrikh in Ndola, and went out 2-0 on aggregate after losing the first leg 1-0 in Kigali.

World.title: Kabwe Residents Give Police Notice Of Protest Over Poll Results
World.content:
Residents of Kabwe have notified police of a planned peaceful demonstration against the general election results, setting up the first organised street challenge to the outcome in a town where three separate races are in dispute.

The Kabwe election protest concerns results in Kabwe Central, Bwacha North and Bwacha South, together with the mayoral election. The residents describe the outcome as the product of a fraudulent poll and say they want answers from the Electoral Commission of Zambia.

Their complaints include allegations of irregularities across those races and of interference by armed personnel. Those allegations are untested and have not been the subject of any published finding.

What The Law Requires

Zambian law does not require permission to hold a public gathering. It requires notification.

Under the Public Order Act, organisers give police advance notice of the time, place and purpose of an assembly, and the police role is to regulate for order and safety rather than to grant or withhold approval. A notified demonstration that proceeds peacefully is a lawful exercise of the right to assemble.

That places a duty on the police in Kabwe. They are required to engage the organisers on arrangements, and if they hold concerns about the venue or timing, to propose alternatives rather than simply prohibit.

Police in Central Province have not publicly stated their position on the notification, and no date has been confirmed for the demonstration.

The Electoral Commission has not responded to the specific complaints raised by the Kabwe residents. Petitions challenging results in several constituencies are already before the High Court, and an aggrieved party in any parliamentary race retains the right to petition within the period the law allows.

Title Deeds In Makululu

The notification arrives in the same week that the area member of parliament turned to delivery.

Bwacha South member of parliament Sydney Mushanga handed 135 title deeds to residents of Makululu, a township long associated with insecure tenure, and framed the exercise as the fulfilment of a campaign commitment.

“During the campaigns, we promised our people the provision of title deeds, and today, 135 residents of Makululu have received their title deeds,” Mr Mushanga said.

He described the handover as more than ceremonial.

“This is more than a ceremonial occasion. It marks a profound shift from uncertainty to security, from vulnerability to empowerment, and from marginalisation to recognition and dignity. We promised, and we are delivering. Now, we get back to work,” he said.

Mr Mushanga thanked Habitat for Humanity Zambia, the Ministry of Lands and the provincial administration for facilitating the exercise, and said the period after the elections called for peace accompanied by hard work.

He has held the Bwacha South seat across four terms, and has previously served as a provincial minister. He has described his own approach to the seat in terms of remaining resident among constituents and treating accessibility as the basis of the mandate.

“The greatest hallmark of being a member of Parliament is listening to the people. You will never go wrong. Listen to what they want; do not impose things on them,” Mr Mushanga said in comments on his record in the constituency.

The Two Things Happening At Once

Kabwe is doing two things in the same week, and both are ordinary in a constitutional democracy.

A lawmaker is delivering on a campaign promise, which is what a mandate is for. Residents who believe the count that produced part of that mandate was wrong are organising to say so publicly, which is what the right to assemble is for.

Neither cancels the other. A demonstration does not invalidate a title deed, and a title deed does not answer a question about a tally.

The measure of how this period is handled will be whether the notified demonstration proceeds without incident, whether police treat the notification as the law frames it, and whether the Electoral Commission addresses the specific complaints rather than the general ones.

Residents have made their notification. The next move belongs to the police.

World.title: Africa: New World Map Makes Africa Look Bigger - What's the Fuss About? Cartographers Explain
World.content:
The Equal Earth map projection shows continents and countries at their true sizes relative to each other.

analysis

The UN has passed a non-binding resolution to endorse the Equal Earth Projection, a map which more fairly represents the true size of the Earth's landmasses. The current commonly used projection, called the Mercator Projection, greatly exaggerates land towards the north and south poles, which makes Africa look much smaller. In the Mercator projection, countries near the north and south pole can be anywhere from two to 14 times their true size. In the Equal Earth projection these distortions are minimised, making Africa look larger in comparison.

We asked Jack Swab and Derek Alderman, cartographers and geographers who study the social and communicative power of maps, to explain what's going on.

What is a map projection?

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

A map projection is a technique that cartographers (map-makers) use to transform the round, three-dimensional Earth into a flat, two-dimensional map that we see on the wall or on our computer screen. As cartographers flatten the globe, the map becomes distorted, changing shapes and areas. There is no map projection that does not distort the Earth, but some projections are better suited for some uses than others.

A cartographer's job is to choose from the hundreds of different map projections, and consider where the map is focused and how it is going to be used. No single projection is best for every use. This new Equal Earth projection is better suited than Mercator for producing global scale world maps for educational, public communication and policy purposes.

The Equal Earth supports a more accurate geographic understanding of the relative sizes of countries and continents. It provides a fairer perspective for the public to compare regions in terms of population, environment, development, politics and other global patterns.

Is the Mercator projection still useful?

While the Mercator projection isn't good for showing the size of the Earth's landmasses, we won't see it totally disappear. For example, it's very useful for navigational purposes as it maintains the accuracy of a compass bearing between two points without having to recalculate it.

This is why most online mapping platforms like Google Maps or Apple Maps rely on a variation of the Mercator projection to provide directions. Using the Equal Earth projection for navigation would not be as effective as the Mercator projection.

How will the Equal Earth projection be used?

Map-making is decentralised and there is no single authority regulating which map projection is used. What the UN did was endorse the broader message that Equal Earth is a fairer projection that more equitably displays the true size of the Earth's land. And although this action is happening at a global level, there are movements underway in cartographic communities to make the Equal Earth projection the default world map projection.

The UN resolution by itself will not make Equal Earth a globally adopted projection. That requires intentional revision of maps used in textbooks, databases, media productions and diplomatic discussions, which requires labour and financial investment.

The Equal Earth projection was developed by cartographers and is a popular choice among map-makers since it was unveiled in 2018. It's now possible to buy wall maps with the Equal Earth projection on them, and the projection has already been used in a wide variety of media. That said, individuals will need to opt in to using the Equal Earth projection over other types.

Why has the Equal Earth projection sparked resistance?

Resistance to the Equal Earth projection has been quite limited. There were several abstentions from the United Nations General Assembly vote, but most of this was for other reasons. Ukraine, for example, raised concerns over the depiction of the contested Crimean Peninsula on the map, which the Equal Earth Projection website depicts as contested territory.

This spurred a Russian response, along with points from other nations about contested territory. Given the UN resolution was a vote on how the world is portrayed and not about any specific political boundaries (a point that both Russia and Ukraine agreed on), these discussions amounted to geopolitical posturing about non-map issues.

The lone outlier, and only "no" vote against the Equal Earth projection, came from the United States. It claimed that the proposal was part of a "radical and ideological project" that was not appropriate for the United Nations to be debating. American delegates took issue with language linking Mercator's distortions to colonial legacies and the marginalisation of Africa. This is not surprising since the current administration denies the existence of structural systems of inequality.

It is hard to miss the hypocrisy at play. The US wants other countries not to discuss the political implications of cartography even as President Trump engages in his own nationalist branding of the map. He has unilaterally renamed the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America and Lake Ontario to Lake America for clear ideological reasons and without international consultation.

Close 

How does the new map matter when it comes to changing global views of the world?

The argument that African nations put forward was that the Equal Earth projection is a form of "cognitive justice". Cognitive justice recognises that people often equate power and value of places with their apparent size on maps. Traditional views of Africa as a smaller continent compared to Europe or North America typically reflect the perceived importance of these parts of the world.

Equal Earth may make it easier to teach, broadcast and discuss a different view of Africa and its prominence in the world. Today, African countries are among the world's fastest growing economies and fastest growing populations. Map projections alone cannot change people's attitudes. Yet, as African nations seek to have more influence in international affairs, correcting the mental map of global leaders is an important step in amplifying the continent's relevance and rights.

Jack Swab, Assistant Professor Department of Geography & Sustainability, University of Tennessee

Derek H. Alderman, Chancellor's Professor of Geography, University of Tennessee

World.title: West Africa: BYRM Hits 555 Points As Rally Extends Into September
World.content:
West Africa's BRVM extended its 2026 rally in the week ended September 11, with the Composite Index gaining 1.25% to a record 555.48 points. The BRVM 30 rose 1.42% to 269.06, the Prestige Index added 1% to 201.81 and the Principal Index gained 0.43% to 407.43. The market table puts equity market capitalization at XOF 21.42 trillion, up 1.25% from the prior week.

Trading volume increased 2.99% to 7.35 million shares, but the value of transactions fell 4.38% to XOF 13.56 billion. Sonatel Senegal remained the most traded stock for a third week, accounting for XOF 2.83 billion, or 20.87% of turnover. Société Générale Côte d'Ivoire and BIIC Benin followed with 8.19% and 5.90%, respectively.

The market was less broad than the headline index gain suggests, with 20 stocks rising, 25 falling and 2 unchanged. BOA Mali led gains, rising 11.72% to XOF 7,150. Orange Côte d'Ivoire gained 6.85% to XOF 22,450, while Vivo Energy Côte d'Ivoire added 6.25% to XOF 2,550.

SAPH Côte d'Ivoire was the biggest loser, falling 17.12% to XOF 8,300 after first-half net profit dropped 88% from a year earlier. SAFCA lost 11.04% and NEI-CEDA declined 8.33%, with the latter affected by its ex-dividend adjustment.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Bond market capitalization fell 0.34% to XOF 12.72 trillion. Trading reached XOF 3.4 billion, with Senegal's 6.75% 2025-2032 bond accounting for 84.89% of turnover after 300,000 securities worth XOF 2.8 billion changed hands.

Key Takeaways

The BRVM's move above 555 points extends a rally that has pushed the Composite Index up about 60.7% in 2026, while the BRVM 30 has gained about 61.9%. The Principal Index has risen about 87.2%, showing that the advance is not limited to the exchange's largest companies.

But this week also offers a warning against reading the index alone: 25 stocks fell compared with 20 gainers even as the Composite reached another record. That means gains in larger or higher-weighted companies were enough to offset weakness elsewhere.

Orange Côte d'Ivoire is one example, with the stock up about 57.5% this year after another 6.85% weekly gain. Sonatel's share of trading also shows that liquidity remains concentrated, with 1 company accounting for more than 20% of weekly turnover. SAPH's 17.12% decline provides another reminder that earnings are starting to matter more as valuations rise.

Close 

After a market gain of more than 60% in less than 9 months, investors will increasingly need profit and dividend growth to support higher prices. The next stage of the BRVM rally may therefore depend less on broad market momentum and more on which companies can deliver results that match the gains already reflected in their shares.

World.title: Sudan: Fuel Prices Rise As Shortages Deepen Across Sudan
World.content:
Fuel prices have risen in several Sudanese states as shortages and long queues return to Khartoum, piling pressure on households already struggling with soaring food prices and a weaker pound.

The White Nile State Council for the Organisation and Development of Public Transport approved a new fuel price composition, setting a gallon of petrol at SDG38,805 Sudanese pounds in Kosti, Rabak, El Guteina and Ed Duweim localities.

The council recommended adding SDG20 per gallon in transport costs across a number of towns and localities.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

For families in White Nile State, the struggle is increasingly about getting through each day.

Wa'ad Idris, a housewife and mother of four, told Radio Dabanga that she starts each morning calculating what the family can afford and what it must go without.

"We start our day and we worry about how to get through it. Life has become very difficult," she said. "During the war we used to say that life is difficult, but with the recent circumstances and the rise of the dollar, the prices of everything have risen significantly, and the citizen has become unable to meet his simple daily needs."

Idris said cooking oil had risen from about SDG10,000 to SDG19,000, while a bottle of onions increased from SDG2,000 to SDG7,000. A pound of milk for children costs about SDG3,000.

She said the family had cut its meals from two a day to one basic meal, with the second depending on whether food was available or affordable.

"Sometimes it is just a snack or tea at night, only to help complete the day," she said.

Even tea has become uncertain, she added, saying the family may settle for red tea without milk, or go without it altogether.

Idris said a simple tomato salad made with dakwa (peanut butter) or oil can now cost about SDG7,000 or more, while a kilogramme of sugar has reached about SDG7,000.

"A solution must be found to this situation, because it has become unbearable," she said.

"The family is no longer able to manage its needs."

Fuel shortages return

Khartoum and several other states have also entered a fresh fuel crisis, with stations closing and petrol and diesel becoming scarce amid expectations of further price rises.

A Khartoum resident told Radio Dabanga that the crisis began after reports of an expected increase in the customs dollar and fuel prices. Several stations, he said, had stopped selling fuel.

Close 

He alleged that some station owners were keeping fuel in their tanks until new prices were announced.

"The fuel is inside the station, but once it is known that there is an expected increase, some stations close, and after the release of the new pricing, the same fuel stored is sold at the new price," he said.

He said shortages had affected petrol and diesel across Khartoum, with the expected increase potentially reaching SDG5,000 to SDG6,000 per gallon.

Fuel shortages and long queues, he added, have become almost monthly occurrences, with some crises lasting more than a week.

"The least crisis until it is resolved can take about nine days, and the citizen spends a large part of the month looking for fuel and moving between stations," he said.

Residents are increasingly forced to choose between waiting for hours at stations and paying inflated black-market prices.

"The citizen may stand 12 hours in line, or buy from the black market at a higher price," he said.

World.title: Josh Allen torches one of NFL's best defenses to make case it's time to move on from 2025 playoff loss
World.content:
Josh Allen finished last season in tears and the sight of one of the NFL's great players sobbing in the Buffalo Bills locker room after a playoff loss to the Denver Broncos led ownership to fire head coach Sean McDermott. That memory of that scene and the burden it put on Allen was buried on Sunday.

Josh Allen played sensationally against the Houston Texans in a stirring 36-31 game this day. And this means stuff:

It means new Bills coach Joe Brady won his head coaching debut.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

It means the Bills have just sent the NFL the message that they remain a Super Bowl contender for 2026 because, well, the Texans team they just beat are a Super Bowl contender.

And it means Josh Allen has already joined the MVP race in earnest after he exorcised the ghosts of his horrible postseason performance and that loss which haunted all offseason.

Allen also made the statement that he can indeed play up to his standard even against the Texans.

"We do like Reliant Stadium, woo-hoo!" Allen exclaimed after the game. "It feels good. It feels good to start the season off right. Obviously coach Joe getting his first win as an NFL head coach ... really happy for him. [He] called a heck of a game."

JOSH ALLEN DELIVERS FULL-THROATED UNSOLICITED DEFENSE OF BUFFALO BILLS' HIDEOUS NEW UNIFORMS

The Texans had dominated Allen in five previous games. The Texans won four of those and limited Allen to 196 passing yards per game.

Not this game.

Allen played up to his billing this time. He played like he's one of the league's best players.

He passed for 334 yards and two touchdowns. And he rushed for two touchdowns. Allen was in some way responsible for all four of his team's touchdowns, by either running or passing for them.

Amid all those numbers, Allen tried to put the focus on others.

"It's the players that we got, man," Allen said in his postgame interview with CBS.

"Looking down at these stats, man, our guys made some great plays."

Don't believe Allen. He delivered superstar stuff against the defense that was the NFL's best against the pass last year and was second-best in points allowed behind only the Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks.

Translation: Houston dominates on defense.

And Allen dominated Houston as the Bills scored the most points that defense has allowed since 2023.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

"We scored 36 points against a fantastic defense," Allen said. "However you get to 36 points in the NFL, you'll take that any other week. As long as it's more than the other guys."

Allen smiling and joking after this game is quite a different snapshot than the one we got from him in his previous game – that playoff loss to the Broncos. Allen turned the ball four times in that fateful game.

He fumbled twice, and threw two interceptions, including interception that set up the Broncos' game-winning drive.

Allen hasn't said he lost that game for the Bills, but he has taken responsibility for it. And whether he did lose it or not, the NFL narrative that Allen couldn't get his team into the Super Bowl grew.

It's impossible to make the case this was a big game on par with the playoffs. But in recording his 26th game-winning drive in the fourth quarter or overtime – the most in the league since 2018 – Allen reminded everyone that he's over that past disappointment.

And in this new season he gets another shot at the Super Bowl.

World.title: Trump unloads on AOC, Mamdani for laughing during sacred 9/11 ceremony at Ground Zero
World.content:

President Donald Trump slammed Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani for appearing to laugh during the solemn reading of victims’ names at the 9/11 Memorial, calling their behavior "terrible" and "inappropriate."

"I think it’s terrible," Trump said when asked about the video of the two Democrats. "It’s not a place to be laughing, especially in that case."

"I thought it was terrible," he continued. "The fact that they were laughing together at a very important part of the ceremony was inappropriate."

The president’s condemnation came after video of Ocasio-Cortez and Mamdani sharing what appeared to be a lighthearted exchange at Ground Zero sparked widespread criticism online.

AOC, MAMDANI INTERACTION CAUGHT ON CAM AT 9/11 MEMORIAL SPARKS ONLINE FURY

A television feed from Friday’s ceremony showed a young man overcome with emotion near the memorial before cutting to Mamdani and Ocasio-Cortez smiling and appearing to laugh as they spoke. Their conversation could not be heard.

9/11 WIDOW TERRY STRADA ACCUSES US OF PROTECTING SAUDI ARABIA 25 YEARS AFTER TERROR ATTACKS, ADDRESSES VANCE

The moment unfolded as mourners read aloud the names of those killed in the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks and the 1993 World Trade Center bombing during ceremonies marking the 25th anniversary of 9/11. Nearly 3,000 people were killed in the 2001 attacks.

The video quickly spread across social media, where critics accused the pair of showing disrespect on one of the nation’s most solemn days.

MAMDANI DRAWS FURY FROM 9/11 MOURNERS OVER GROUND ZERO APPEARANCE: ‘DISRESPECTFUL’

"As the names of Americans murdered on September 11th are read aloud at Ground Zero, AOC and Mamdani are laughing and smiling together," Rep. Wesley Hunt, R-Texas, wrote on X.

"There is a time and a place for politics. This isn’t it. Ground Zero is sacred ground," Hunt added. "September 11 is not a photo op, it is not a networking event."

MAMDANI HEADS TO 9/11 MEMORIAL DESPITE 110,000-SIGNATURE PUSH FROM VICTIMS’ FAMILIES TO STAY AWAY

Meghan McCain also reacted to the video, asking on X, "Why the f--- are these two laughing?"

New York City Councilwoman Inna Vernikov, a Republican, similarly ripped the moment.

ZOHRAN MAMDANI URGED TO SKIP NEW YORK CITY'S 9/11 MEMORIAL: 'VILE ANTISEMITE'

"After thousands of families of victims of terror beg Mamdani not to show up, he stands there and laughs while families weep," Vernikov wrote. "This is NYC’s Mayor."

Mamdani had already faced opposition from some victims’ families ahead of the ceremony. A petition urging him to stay away from Ground Zero gathered more than 110,000 signatures, though Mamdani attended and remained for the ceremony.

DE NIRO CALLS CONTROVERSIAL MAMDANI POLICE COMMENTS 'RIDICULOUS' AS HE DEFENDS MAYOR GOING TO 9/11 SERVICE

However, Michael Ragusa, who has served as a member of former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani’s entourage, disputed claims that Mamdani and Ocasio-Cortez were joking about the ceremony.

"The videos of [them] laughing are not true. I was standing next to them the whole time," Ragusa wrote on X.

MS RACHEL DEFENDS 'AWESOME' MAMDANI AMID 9/11 MEMORIAL CONTROVERSY, SAYS HE'S VICTIM OF ISLAMOPHOBIC ATTACKS

"The camera just caught her greeting him hello," he added. "Multiple other politicians were laughing and joking behind me. Republicans and Democrats."

Mamdani was seen standing somberly at other points during the ceremony. It remains unclear what he and Ocasio-Cortez discussed during the brief exchange.

World.title: Kyler Murray knocked out of Vikings debut after forearm to the helmet and blow to neck by two Packers
World.content:
That start of Kyler Murray's career with the Minnesota Vikings has been a disaster.

That might be understating the matter.

The team's new starting quarterback threw an interception on the second play of the regular-season opener. It was his first pass in a Vikings uniform.

At home, no less.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

MINNESOTA VIKINGS SURPRISINGLY DEMOTE FORMER FIRST-ROUND PICK JJ MCCARTHY TO THIRD STRING

Then Murray got knocked out of the game on his team's third possession.

Murray, signed by the Vikings in the offseason as their next major quarterback project, did not make it out of the first quarter on Sunday.

Murray left the game and underwent a concussion evaluation. He was listed officially as questionable to return, though the severity of the hit made clear to those watching that his day was over.

The Vikings eventually ruled Murray out.

Murray was scrambling when he took a forearm to the helmet from Packers defensive end Lukas Van Ness, but that wasn't all.

As Murray collapsed in a heap, he took another blow from safety Javon Bullard around the neck and head area, causing Murray's helmet to fly off.

And he seemed to go into a fencing response position, which is an involuntary body posture where an injured person extends one arm rigidly and flexes the other into the air for several seconds after a blow to the head.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Bullard drew a personal foul for unnecessary roughness. Murray was ultimately able to walk off the field and make his way to the locker room without assistance.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Carson Wentz took over for Murray after the play, and here's the rough part:

Murray will enter the NFL concussion protocol. That means he will be tested, and independent physicians will determine when he can eventually return to play.

For a player experiencing his first concussion, the standard return-to-play timeline is roughly two weeks, though absences of one week or three weeks are not uncommon.

So, yes. It's been a terrible start to the season, and his Vikings career, for Murray.

World.title: Lions avoid franchise-worst collapse as defense stops Saints two-point conversion in OT
World.content:
The Detroit Lions needed overtime and a moment of stellar defense to avoid a franchise-worst collapse against the New Orleans Saints to begin their 2026 NFL season.

What appeared to be a comfortable path to a Week 1 win became a contested, back-and-forth affair, with the Saints pushing the game to overtime after Juwan Johnson hauled in a touchdown with 1:07 remaining in the fourth quarter.

The Saints almost completed the 21-point comeback when kicker Daniel Carlson tried to knock through a 62-yard field goal at the buzzer, but he was wide right to force the first overtime game of the new campaign.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

But just like it was in the second half, the Lions and Saints both traded touchdowns, as Amon-Ra St. Brown scored to open up the extra period, while tight end Noah Fant caught one on the other side of the field on the ensuing drive.

The difference? New Orleans head coach Kellen Moore didn’t feel like tying the score anymore. He was going for the win with a two-point conversion.

After an 80-yard drive, the Saints wanted to walk it off with the victory, but the Lions’ defense came through when they needed it most. A three-man stack of receivers broke off for the Saints when the ball was snapped and quarterback Tyler Shough threw it up for rookie Bryce Lance, but the pass was broken up to the delight of everyone inside Ford Field in Detroit.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

The Lions celebrated their hard-fought victory, but it shouldn’t have been that close if you ask them.

If Detroit lost, their 21-point lead would’ve been the biggest in franchise history that they gave up in a defeat. So, this group, which has high hopes out of the NFC North this season, is happy not to be on the wrong side of history.

Things were going well for the Lions until Shough and company, who struggled throughout most of the game, finally got on the scoreboard in the third quarter with a touchdown by running back Kendre Miller. From there, the Saints put together three more scoring drives, including a touchdown grab by Devaughn Vele and a field goal from Carlson.

The Lions will hope to clean up things defensively, but offensively, it’s clear as day what Jahmyr Gibbs can do, especially with an extra workload, now that David Montgomery is no longer in Detroit.

The star running back finished the game with 156 yards rushing with two scores on the ground, while hauling in five of Jared Goff’s passes for 30 yards. Gibbs turned 34 touches into 186 scrimmage yards, and that’s what many are expecting each week from one of the most explosive and dynamic offensive weapons in the sport each week.

Meanwhile, Shough threw for 410 yards on 35-of-56 through the air, though he was intercepted twice by the Lions’ defense. Chris Olave, his top target, finished the game with 10 catches for 182 yards.

World.title: Hayden Panettiere's boyfriend Brian Hickerson involved in bloody bar altercation weeks after star's death
