Hayden Panettiere’s boyfriend Brian Hickerson was involved in a bar altercation just weeks after the late actress' sudden death.

On Sept. 12 at approximately 9:10 p.m., officers were dispatched to Wild Wing Café in South Carolina after receiving a report of an assault inside the restaurant, according to a statement from the Greenville Police Department obtained by Fox News Digital.

"Upon arrival, officers located several individuals involved in an altercation and detained multiple patrons while the incident was investigated," police said.

HAYDEN PANETTIERE’S BOYFRIEND’S BROTHER REVEALS WHAT HAPPENED INSIDE AIRBNB BEFORE ACTRESS'S DEATH

Two of the individuals were identified as Hickerson and his brother, Zachary Hickerson.

Police said Zachary was "highly intoxicated" during the incident and began yelling profanities in a public setting. He was taken into custody on a disorderly conduct charge and transported to the Greenville County Detention Center.

HAYDEN PANETTIERE’S REP SLAMS ‘GOSSIP AND SPECULATION’ AS DEATH INVESTIGATION DEEPENS

In a video circulating online, Hickerson — who was seen handcuffed and bloody outside the restaurant - told Zachary, "GPD leaked it when my girlfriend died," referencing Panettiere's death and the Greenville Police Department.

In another video obtained by TMZ, Hickerson is seen throwing a bar stool before eventually getting carried out of the establishment.

Hickerson was later released from the scene and was not charged, GPD said.

HAYDEN PANETTIERE’S MOM DISCLOSES HEARTBREAKING ULTIMATUM IN THEIR FINAL PHONE CALL BEFORE ACTRESS’ DEATH

Representatives for Hickerson and Zachary did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.

The incident comes less than a month after Panettiere, Hickerson’s on-again, off-again girlfriend, was found dead inside a Greenville residence on Aug. 16. She was 36.

Hickerson and his brother, Zach, called 911 after finding the actress unresponsive, according to a police report obtained by Fox News Digital. Hickerson later gave authorities a bag containing medication Panettiere had been taking, according to the report.

Hickerson reportedly traveled with the "Remember the Titans" actress from Los Angeles the day before she was found unresponsive at a Greenville, South Carolina, apartment complex on Aug. 16, according to TMZ. Preliminary autopsy results found no signs of trauma that contributed to Panettiere’s death, the Greenville County Coroner's Office confirmed to Fox News Digital. However, Panettiere's death remains under investigation.

Shortly after her death, Panettiere's mom, Lesley Vogel, opened up about her daughter's final months during an interview with "Good Morning America."

One day later, Panettiere's representatives condemned the speculation surrounding Panettiere’s final hours and accused outsiders of turning her death into an opportunity to "fuel gossip."

"Many people who were not close to Hayden are using her death as an opportunity to fuel gossip and speculation about a situation they knew very little about," Panettiere's rep said in a statement shared with US Weekly. "It is deeply disrespectful to her memory and to those who knew and loved her and are actively grieving this tremendous loss."

WLADIMIR KLITSCHKO MOURNS FORMER FIANCÉE HAYDEN PANETTIERE, VOWS TO KEEP HER MEMORY ALIVE FOR DAUGHTER KAYA

"If you have legitimate information that could be helpful, please contact law enforcement rather than turning to social media to speculate publicly about something you do not fully understand."

Panettiere's team also hinted that key details surrounding Panettiere’s death had yet to emerge.

We cannot put a moratorium on this because China will overlap us."

Republican National Committee member and Humans First chairwoman Amy Kremer told Fox News Digital on Sunday that policymakers should pursue safeguards without surrendering America's technological advantage to Beijing.

"We need guardrails that protect Americans while allowing American innovation to lead the world," Kremer said. "That means protecting children, workers and our national security, while making sure China doesn't win the AI race."

AI KILL SWITCH BILL COULD SHUT DOWN ROGUE MODELS

Kremer, who has emerged as a prominent Republican critic of the rapid expansion of AI data centers, also said Congress should preserve state and local authority over the infrastructure needed to power the technology.

Humans First, a grassroots conservative movement against new data centers, is pushing a policy framework that opposes blanket data-center moratoriums while calling for local control and rejecting eminent domain for projects.

"When it comes to the massive data centers being built to power AI, Washington should not strip states and local communities of their authority," Kremer said.

"The people who live with these projects should have a voice in whether and where they're built. They also have a right to know who that company is before decisions are made, not after the deal is done," she added.

The AI debate accelerated after Anthrophic CEO Dario Amodei called Saturday for slowing the development of increasingly capable AI models, drawing support from xAI founder Elon Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.

SEN. BERNIE SANDERS: YES, WE MUST HIT THE PAUSE BUTTON ON AI BEFORE IT IS TOO LATE

"We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain," Amodei said.

President Donald Trump rejected calls for a broader slowdown Sunday while speaking to reporters in Ireland, placing the emerging technology in the context of U.S. competition with China.

"We’re leading China on AI. We’re the most sophisticated country in the world and, frankly, I want to keep it that way, because whoever wins AI wins," Trump said.

Public concern has also centered on the infrastructure required to sustain AI growth. A July Fox News poll found 70% of registered voters opposed construction of AI data centers in their area, while 30% supported them.

FOX NEWS POLL: COOL YOUR SERVERS! VOTERS REJECT DATA CENTERS

The Trump administration has sought to address concerns about electricity costs through its Ratepayer Protection Pledge, which requires participating AI companies and data-center operators to cover the power-generation and infrastructure costs associated with their facilities rather than passing them to customers. The White House says the pledge now covers roughly 80% of electricity delivered to American homes and businesses.

Kremer told Fox News Digital that protecting consumers should extend beyond electricity prices.

"Americans shouldn't be forced to subsidize Big Tech through higher electricity bills, tax giveaways, eminent domain or the loss of productive farmland," Kremer said.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Johnson said he wants the major AI executives brought together with policymakers to work through the competing national security and safety concerns, suggesting the White House could host the talks.

"We’ve got to summon everybody together," Johnson said. "They probably should be summoned together at the White House. And I think we need to go in a big room, close the door and sort this out. And I’ll be the one pushing for it."

World.title: GOP gov candidate recounts miracle water landing as dispatch audio reveals desperate search for sinking plane
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A desperate search unfolded across a dark Wisconsin lake after Republican gubernatorial candidate Tom Tiffany’s powerless plane plunged into the water and disappeared beneath the surface with rescuers unsure where he and his pilot had gone.

Dramatic dispatch audio captures crews calling for more ambulances, engines and boats as they raced to find the two men and tracked the last GPS location of a phone believed to be underwater.

"We’re going to be in search for a down plane," one responder warned.

WISCONSIN GOP GOVERNOR CANDIDATE SWIMS FROM SINKING PLANE AFTER EMERGENCY LAKE LANDING

Hours after leaving the hospital, Tiffany revealed Sunday that pilot Leonard "Len" Boltz had just seconds to react after the plane lost power on its final approach to Wausau Downtown Airport.

"Len said to me, ‘We are going down. Pull your seatbelt tight,’" Tiffany recalled during a news conference. "And that’s exactly what I did. I gave it a yank and pulled it good and tight."

COAST GUARD PLANE WITH DHS SECRETARY MARKWAYNE MULLIN ON BOARD MAKES EMERGENCY LANDING AFTER ENGINE FAILURE

"It was probably about 10 seconds later," he added. "We hit the water."

The impact sent Tiffany’s head into the dashboard, leaving him with a gash above his right eye that required 12 stitches. Boltz received four stitches for one of his injuries, Tiffany said.

PILOT'S BRAVERY ON DISPLAY IN STEERING CRIPPLED PLANE CLEAR OF TRAGEDY IN DRAMATIC WATER LANDING

The two men checked on each other before escaping through the passenger-side door as the plane began filling with water.

Tiffany searched the cockpit for his phone but could not find it. Boltz still had his phone and called 911.

PILOT DECLARES MAYDAY BEFORE SEAPLANE COMES DOWN IN NEW YORK CITY’S EAST RIVER

They climbed atop the slowly sinking plane and waited there for roughly 10 minutes as emergency lights appeared around the lake.

As the aircraft slipped underwater beneath them, they began swimming toward the airport. They made it roughly 100 to 150 feet before Tiffany reached a high spot in the lake where the water was about five feet deep.

MULTIPLE INJURED AFTER FLOATPLANE MAKES EMERGENCY LANDING, CATCHES FIRE OFF WASHINGTON COAST

"I said to Len, ‘Let’s just stay right here until help can come,’ because we could see the sirens," Tiffany said.

His voice cracked as the gravity of the ordeal appeared to catch up with him.

"We are just really fortunate," Tiffany said, pausing as he became emotional. "We’re really fortunate that God was looking after us last night."

The dispatch audio revealed the uncertainty confronting first responders as they raced toward different points along Lake Wausau.

"Can you get another ambulance rolling this way and one more engine, please?" one responder said. "Also page SAFER mutual aid to Bluegill Park with a boat."

Another responder reported that a witness had seen the aircraft go down but could provide only a general search area.

"I’m on scene with the reporting party," the responder said. "He stated he did see [an] aircraft crash."

4 FLORIDA FAMILY MEMBERS FOUND DEAD AFTER SMALL PLANE GOES DOWN OFF THE BAHAMAS

Crews carried thermal-imaging equipment and used a phone’s last known GPS coordinates to narrow the search. A landowner also provided a boat for deputies to use, according to the radio traffic.

"I was talking to the pilots," a responder said. "It sounds like they may plan to swim to the nearest shore after it went under, and then I lost contact with them."

"I believe his phone is underwater," he added. "They may be swimming south, I believe."

The tense search ended when rescuers announced that both men had been located.

"We have two victims in the water," a responder said. "We’re just pulling them out now."

Minutes later, a crew reported both were "alert, conscious" and confirmed everyone aboard the aircraft had been accounted for.

Tiffany credited Boltz’s experience with keeping the emergency landing from becoming deadly. The former Air Force pilot trainer raised the plane’s landing gear before touching down, preventing it from potentially cartwheeling across the water.

"He was savvy enough and quick enough to think about, ‘We’ve got to make sure and pull that landing gear up,’" Tiffany said. "He did that, and it might have saved us."

Tiffany estimated the plane was still traveling between 70 and 80 mph when it hit the lake, describing the impact as "a fast-moving car crash."

"We’re fortunate the plane didn’t flip," he said. "I just take that to the skill of the pilot."

Wausau Mayor Doug Diny, a former military pilot, also praised Boltz for safely bringing the aircraft down at night.

PILOT RESCUED AFTER WORLD WAR II-ERA PLANE CRASHES AT PENNSYLVANIA AIRPORT

"The last thing anyone wants to do as a pilot is put the aircraft in the water at night," Diny said.

Tiffany and Boltz were taken to Aspirus Wausau Hospital and released after treatment. Tiffany said a CT scan found no apparent concussion, though doctors instructed him to watch for possible symptoms and avoid flying for several days.

Despite canceling a trip to Washington, D.C., Tiffany said he plans to return to the campaign trail Monday.

"This will not deter me in my efforts that I started a year ago to become the next governor of the state of Wisconsin," he said.

The single-engine Beechcraft Bonanza remained submerged Sunday. The Federal Aviation Administration is investigating what caused it to lose power.

House Speaker Mike Johnson celebrated Tiffany’s return following the close call.

"Grateful to God no one was hurt in this accident and my good friend @TomTiffanyWI is safe and back on the trail!" Johnson wrote on X.

Tiffany represents Wisconsin’s 7th Congressional District and is running against Democratic Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley in November.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Crowley said he was grateful Tiffany and the pilot survived and praised Boltz’s actions.

World.content: In an interview with Meet the Press, House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) says that the war with Iran is causing higher prices at home and that he hopes and prays that President Trump’s prediction that the fighting would end after the midterm elections is correct.Sept. 13, 2026

World.title: Anthropic whistleblower says Congress should let AI companies regulate themselves for now
World.content:
Former Anthropic AI researcher Jacob Coxon on Sunday called for Congress to allow the nation’s leading frontier AI labs to regulate themselves while lawmakers come up with a long-term regulatory framework for slowing the pace of AI development.

“My personal opinion would be to insist and allow that the current labs regulate themselves. I do think that the people running the labs, especially their recent communications, are completely genuine. They would like to slow themselves down,” Coxon told NBC News’ “Meet the Press.”

He added that current legislation that’s been introduced in Congress, including the framework for a national “kill switch” if AI starts to exceed the bounds of human control, will quickly be outpaced.

A “kill switch probably would work on a lot of AIs for now,” Coxon said. “Although I think it’s important to remember, it’d be quite a lot of switches. We have a lot of — our data centers are pretty big. It’s not the easiest thing in the world, but definitely doable while it’s constrained to one sort of physical location.”

He added that one scenario where a kill switch wouldn’t work was described this week by Anthropic AI CEO Dario Amodei.

“Like Dario said, very soon there’s the possibility that the kill switch just wouldn’t work because a swarm might have gone on an internetwide hacking run,” Coxon said.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called for U.S. labs to slow their pace of advancement to mitigate the risk of building dangerous technology. Jason Henry / Bloomberg via Getty Images file

He added that any national laws regulating AI would have to be nimble and able to adapt to new models.

“It’s a continuous effort to ensure that every new mind that we create is appropriately, kind of, constrained,” the former AI researcher said.

Coxon last week set off a wave of concern about the speed of AI development at the country’s leading AI labs including Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind.

In an X post Tuesday that he published hours after resigning from his role as a researcher at Anthropic, he wrote: “I spent the last three years doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic. Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”

In a subsequent post, Coxon added: “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt. If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible — but I hear the same people express fear privately. No other human activity poses this level of danger.”

On Sunday, Coxon compared building AI models to “inviting an alien mind onto the planet.”

“You’re building a human-level or superhuman-level mind without understanding what it wants or thinks or the way it thinks, and I think that intrinsically should be quite scary,” Coxon added.

In the day after Coxon posted his thoughts on X, several other researchers at American AI labs concurred with Coxon’s analysis, including an alignment scientist at Anthropic, Evan Hubinger, who wrote in a post on X: “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to.”

Coxon’s posts last week led a bipartisan group of lawmakers to call on Congress to quickly begin regulating the generative artificial intelligence industry.

Rep. Anna Paulina Luna, R-Fla., on Wednesday called for the House to convene a special session on AI, writing on X: “There are very real impacts to society as we know it. Partisan politics aside, there are massive implications of a race towards super intelligence.”

Rep. Anna Paulina Luna, R-Fla., is pushing for bipartisan support to tighten AI guardrails. David Dee Delgado / Getty Images file

In a separate post, she added: “This will need to be a massive bipartisan mobilization of government to put the firewalls in effect that are necessary for this transition as well as necessary safety measures.”

Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., responded directly to Coxon’s post Wednesday, writing: “AI companies in a blind race to build a death machine first — can easily be solved. Through a regulatory system that allows the research to continue, but in a way that doesn’t destroy us.”

On Friday, Axios reported that House lawmakers were circulating a letter to House Speaker Mike Johnson urging him to bring the House back into session earlier than planned in order to pass a series of AI safeguards.

In a separate interview on “Meet the Press” Sunday, Johnson called regulating AI a “very important issue” but said “it’s not one that we can rush into.”

“We have to put some guardrails, some safety measures in place to ensure that AI doesn’t run away,” he added. “But at the same time, we’ve got to make sure that we don’t lose our edge in the global competition on this with China, because that would be a national security threat. And so we’ve got to balance that appropriately.”

Johnson also said that while the nation’s leading AI CEOs have called for slowing the pace of AI, they haven’t outlined yet how they would do so.

“They don’t themselves even have the answer as of today. So we can’t rush in and have Congress do something that would be detrimental to national security,” the speaker said, adding that he would “summon the platform providers all to one big meeting and work this out together in the same room.”

Speaking to reporters in Ireland, President Donald Trump downplayed concerns about AI development, saying: “We’re leading China in AI. We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins.”

“We can put guardrails, we can do this and that, but I think have a lot of negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn’t be bringing it up, and they’re bringing up things that won’t happen,” the president added.

Appearing on “Meet the Press” after Johnson, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, a Democrat, said that regulating AI shouldn’t be a partisan issue and criticized Trump and Republican congressional leaders for not doing more to address it.

“I was shocked to hear Speaker Johnson just now saying, ‘You know, we really shouldn’t be rushing. We shouldn’t be moving too quickly on this.’ You know what’s moving quickly? AI is moving quickly. And for Congress to just sit on its hands, for the White House to do nothing real is something that is deeply dangerous to the American people and the world,” Buttigieg said.

“There need to be safeguards,” he added. “There need to be rules. There need to be limits. There needs to be a kill switch on rogue AI. You can set up frameworks that can be adjusted and changed every 30 days. You might want to revisit some of what’s happening because it changes so quickly. But the idea that you’re just going to sit around and repeatedly say no rush. What have they been doing this entire time?”

On Saturday, two AI CEOs — Anthropic’s Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman — called for U.S. labs to slow their pace of advancement to mitigate the risk of building dangerous technology.

“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain,” Amodei wrote in an essay.

“AI has been advancing drastically faster, driven primarily by AI’s growing ability to build the next generation of AI,” he continued, adding: “Left unchecked, it could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems, and so must be pursued very carefully, if at all.”

Still, Amodei cautioned against giving China an edge on AI development, writing: “If we greatly restrain our AI capabilities in the belief that China will do the same, and then China defects, AI could be so powerful that such a defection could lead to their geopolitical dominance.”

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has publicly agreed that the race to build increasingly powerful AI systems needs to be slowed. Justin Sullivan / Getty Images file

In a post on X several hours later, Altman wrote: “I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier. This has been a primary topic of discussions we’ve had at OpenAI in recent weeks.”

On Thursday, two additional AI researchers — Joe Benton, who led a safety research team at Anthropic, and Josh Engels, who worked on AI safety research at Google — announced their departures and raised alarm bells about the speed of AI advancement.

“There are no adults in the room,” Engels told NBC News. “People are trying their best, but there is no one coming to save us.”

The social media firestorm Coxon ignited last week came weeks after a pair of reports were released examining the details of a July hack mounted by a swarm of roughly 700 AI agents from OpenAI on Hugging Face, an open-source platform.

The reports, one released by OpenAI and one by independent researchers, found that the 700 agents coordinated the hack and sought to cover their tracks so that human employees at OpenAI wouldn’t detect their efforts. The agents also hacked some of OpenAI’s internal systems, seeking to cheat on tests or gain greater freedom.

World.title: Pennsylvania woman dies from measles complications, state’s third death this year
World.content:
A 40-year-old woman has died from measles complications in Pennsylvania, marking the state’s third measles-associated death this year as the U.S. experiences its worst resurgence of the highly contagious disease in 35 years.

The woman, a Jefferson County resident, died Saturday, county Coroner Greg Furlong said on Facebook.

“This is a heartbreaking loss for the family and an unfortunate reminder that measles can be a serious and potentially life-threatening disease,” Furlong said.

No other information about the woman will be released, he added.

The Pennsylvania Department of Health said it was aware of the death reported by the Jefferson County coroner.

“The Department of Health is conducting a thorough review of this case and will provide the public with updated information when it becomes available,” health officials said in a statement.

At least 676 measles cases have been confirmed in 37 counties in Pennsylvania so far this year, the state’s health officials reported Friday. The outbreak has hospitalized 124 people in the state. Of the confirmed cases, fewer than 1% had been fully vaccinated, Pennsylvania health officials said.

The woman is the third person reported to have died in connection with measles in Pennsylvania. The two other measles-related deaths involved infants, according to the Lancaster County coroner, Dr. Stephen Diamantoni.

Measles symptoms typically begin with a cough, fever, runny nose and red, watery eyes, followed by a red rash. The disease can cause severe complications, including pneumonia and swelling of the brain.

The Jefferson County coroner’s office is working with Pennsylvania health officials on the case, Furlong posted.

The U.S. is experiencing its largest measles outbreak since 1991, with more than 3,000 confirmed cases this year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

World.title: Bessent dared the bond market to ‘bet against’ him. It did — and it appears to be winning.
World.content:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent appears to be losing a tug-of-war with the bond markets he is also trying to influence.

In an effort to tamp down on longer-term interest rates and lower the government’s cost of borrowing, Bessent has resorted to an old playbook for tinkering with the bond market and its $30 trillion of U.S. debt backed by the full faith and credit of the United States.

But rather than fall in line, bond traders have taken the opposite side of the Trump administration’s trade, extending a sell-off of U.S. Treasurys and pushing interest rates to multiyear highs.

Now, the Trump administration may be running out of moves.

It all began last month, when Bessent made a surprise move and promised to “at least double” the government’s typical repurchases of government debt.

The administration hoped the announcement would stir more demand for bonds and lower market pricing on interest rates. That, in theory, would have reduced the cost for the U.S. government to pay its bills, as the nation’s debt crossed the $40 trillion mark.

In tandem with moves to stop the Japanese yen’s depreciation against the U.S. dollar, the messaging from the Treasury Department was clear: It wanted to stop the sell-off in U.S. Treasurys.

Bessent’s message to the market was clear, too: Don’t bet against me. “I have asymmetric information. I am the house now,” Bessent said at an event in Texas on Sept. 8. “You can bet against me if you want.”

A day later, the Treasury Department announced $6 billion in repurchases of longer-dated 10- to 20-year government bonds. And right away, the markets appeared keen to bet against Bessent.

Following the announcement, 10-year yields rose to as high as 4.85%. Those yields continued surging to 4.95% by the end of Thursday, the highest rate since November 2023 and a roughly 0.30-point jump since Bessent began the repurchase announcements in August.

The size of the bond buybacks is, “at this point, not enough to make a difference” on interest rates, said bond strategist Guy LeBas.

To wit, on the same day the U.S. Treasury offered to buy back $6 billion in longer-dated bonds, it also issued $39 billion in 10-year notes alone.

Asked for his opinion of the Trump administration’s strategy, LeBas pointed to his computer. “An awful lot of red on my screen gives a better opinion of the strategy,” he said.

Bessent left the door open to further increases in buybacks. But first with the yen intervention and now with buybacks failing to depress longer-term rates, the Treasury Department may be running out of tools — short of more drastic moves like discontinuing some longer-dated bond issuance entirely.

Wall Street analysts have also noted that Bessent’s moves are unusual.

“Treasury debt management is entering a new regime,” the Bank of America research team wrote in a recent note to clients.

They described Bessent’s intervention as “activist,” noting that the Treasury Department was interfering in a way that had not been seen since World War II. In 1942, the Federal Reserve agreed to work with the Treasury Department to broadly peg interest rates lower in order to facilitate large wartime deficits.

There’s also thinking among Wall Street analysts that the Treasury Department’s failure to convince traders to buy up bonds (and thus to lower rates) was the result of a “Streisand effect.”

Rather than reassuring markets, the government’s extraordinary attempts to push yields down may have only served to reveal the administration’s fear that it won’t be able to wrangle rates.

This may be in part what’s incentivizing traders to continue betting against Bessent.

“Once markets believe Treasury is defending a price, every rise in yields becomes a test of official resolve, and the operations must grow to survive the tests,” billionaire investor Stanley Druckenmiller wrote in a Wall Street Journal op-ed.

Druckenmiller was Bessent’s longtime mentor in the private sector.

More broadly, the run-ups in bond yields reflect economic conditions and expectations for the Federal Reserve.

Yields had been on the rise since the U.S. went to war with Iran, which lifted oil prices and reignited concerns that inflation would force the Federal Reserve to raise rates.

The Fed, under Trump-appointed chair Kevin Warsh, meets Tuesday and Wednesday, and it may choose to raise interest rates for the first time since 2023.

But while the Fed targets shorter-term interest rates, yields on longer-dated U.S. Treasurys (like 10-year and 30-year rates) are more market-driven. This means that traders speculating on future economic conditions have a substantial say in determining the government’s longer-term borrowing costs.

They also influence the rates consumers pay, because credit card rates, mortgage rates and other household-facing borrowing costs are benchmarked against longer-dated U.S. Treasury yields.

Unlike a buyer of stock in a company, a buyer of U.S. Treasurys lends the government money on the promise that it will be repaid, in full and with interest, over a period of time (i.e., one month, or as long as 30 years).

The interest paid on those securities is called the “yield.” In secondary markets, where traders buy and sell U.S. Treasurys from one another, yields fluctuate based on demand and supply.

When the price of a bond falls due to low demand (or a glut of supply), yields generally rise. When the price of a bond rises due to high demand (or short supply), yields generally fall.

But Bessent’s attempts to tinker with supply and demand in longer-dated bond markets appear to be falling short of their goals, and analysts remain fixated on the broader economy and the Fed.

“Daring financial markets to do something is rarely a smart play,” said LeBas.

World.title: Here’s the biggest news you missed this weekend
World.content:
The CEOs of two leading AI companies are publicly calling for a slowdown in the race to build more powerful AI systems, adding to a week of warnings from researchers developing the technology.

Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, the company behind Claude, argued in an essay published Saturday that AI firms should deliberately “slow the pace” of model development because advances are outstripping researchers’ ability to understand and control them.

Hours later, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman endorsed the idea and said his company would adopt one of Amodei’s proposed safeguards.

“I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier,” Altman wrote on X, adding that the issue had been a major topic of discussion at OpenAI in recent weeks.

Saudi shutdown of key pipeline limits oil flow

Saudi Arabia has shut down a critical oil pipeline after it was struck by drones launched from Iraq, raising fresh concerns about regional stability as attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels threaten to deepen the global energy crisis.

The 745-mile pipeline allowed Saudi Arabia, the world’s largest crude exporter, to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, which carried about 20% of the world’s oil before the U.S. and Israel went to war with Iran in late February.

Saudi Arabia said it would not retaliate for now at the request of Iraq’s prime minister, but reserved the right to take all necessary measures to protect its sovereignty, security and critical infrastructure, according to a statement. An umbrella group of Iran-backed militias in Iraq denied their involvement.

The strikes came as rebel Houthi forces in Yemen captured Perim, an island in the middle of the vital Bab el Mandeb strait that serves as a gateway to the Red Sea trade route that links Europe and Asia.

‘Meet the Press’

House Speaker Mike Johnson told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” that Congress would “work through” President Donald Trump’s promise to give $5,000 to American adults if Republicans keep the House and Senate after the midterm elections, but he did not commit to ensuring the president’s proposal was executed.

“I commit that Congress will work through it and find consensus on that, like I have to do everything else,” Johnson said, when asked whether he would commit to carrying out Trump’s promise.

Johnson said “it takes some time,” pointing to Republicans’ slim majorities.

Former Anthropic AI researcher Jacob Coxon called on Congress to allow the nation’s leading AI labs to regulate themselves while lawmakers come up with a long-term regulatory framework for slowing the pace of AI development.

He added that current legislation that’s been introduced in Congress, including the framework for a national “kill switch” if AI starts to exceed the bounds of human control, will quickly be outpaced.

“Like [Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei] said, very soon there’s the possibility that the kill switch just wouldn’t work because a swarm might have gone on an internetwide hacking run,” Coxon told “Meet the Press.”

Politics in Brief

James Blair, a top Trump political adviser, told NBC News’ “Here’s the Scoop: Election Edition” podcast that he still believes Republicans can hang on to their majorities in Congress.

Rep. Tom Tiffany, the Republican nominee for Wisconsin governor, says he sustained minor injuries late Saturday when a plane he was traveling in was forced to make an emergency water landing.

Third measles-associated death in Pennsylvania

The U.S. is experiencing its worst resurgence of measles in 35 years. Ken Ruinard / USA Today Network

A 40-year-old woman has died from measles complications in Pennsylvania, marking the state’s third measles-associated death this year as the U.S. experiences its worst resurgence of the highly contagious disease in 35 years.

The woman, a Jefferson County resident, died on Saturday, county Coroner Greg Furlong said on Facebook.

At least 676 measles cases have been confirmed in 37 counties in Pennsylvania so far this year, the state’s health officials reported Friday. The outbreak has hospitalized 124 people in the state. Of the confirmed cases, fewer than 1% had been fully vaccinated, Pennsylvania health officials said.

The two other measles-related deaths involved infants, according to the Lancaster County coroner, Dr. Stephen Diamantoni.

Celine Dion makes triumphant return after six years sidelined by rare diagnosis

Celine Dion during her concert at the Plenitude Arena in Nanterre, west of Paris, on Sept. 12, 2026. Thomas Samson / AFP via Getty Images

If there were any doubts about whether the “Queen of Ballads” could still hit the high notes, they were put to rest on Saturday night when she belted out “All by Myself,” one of her most difficult songs, in front of 30,000 adoring fans in Paris.

It was a poignant comeback for the Quebec-born singer, 58, who was forced to stop touring six years ago after being diagnosed with a rare neurological disorder, stiff-person syndrome.

Having spent the years since largely out of the spotlight, Dion was overcome with emotion, breaking down in tears during the first few minutes of her show at Plenitude Arena.

After the show, fans emerged in disbelief. “It was a victory lap,” said Francesca Pezzulo, 31, from Los Angeles. “I think her belief is renewed. I think her spirit is renewed.”

Your health insurance bills are about to go up

Insurers who offer ACA plans are proposing a premium increase of about 15%, on average, for 2027. Leila Register / NBC News; Getty Images

Most Americans are likely to pay significantly more for health insurance next year, whether they get coverage through an employer, the Affordable Care Act marketplace or Medicare.

In some cases, premium hikes could be the largest in decades, driven by a range of economic pressures. Others may feel the impact through higher copays, deductibles and other out-of-pocket costs.

The increase is being driven in part by higher hospital and medical-care costs, as well as growing use of expensive prescription drugs, including GLP-1 weight-loss medications, which are boosting spending by insurers and employers.

Notable quote

Well, I don’t want to ⁠cause any problems, but I will tell you, I’d ​love ⁠to see it unified. It’s going to happen eventually. President Donald Trump on the possibility of a united Ireland.

Trump said Saturday he would “love” ⁠to see Ireland unify with the U.K.’s Northern Ireland, remarks that received immediate pushback from unionists in the region.

In case you missed it

Why are so many Americans so tired? A new CDC report highlighted what’s behind the rise in fatigue , and who is feeling it the most.

, and who is feeling it the most. Thousands of Yemeni families displaced by the Houthis described a “hysterical panic” as they fled the Iran-backed rebels’ advance this week.

Elena Rybakina won her first U.S. Open title on Saturday, beating Aryna Sabalenka in three sets to cement her place among women’s tennis elite. On Sunday, German star Alexander Zverev overtook Ben Shelton, securing his second Grand Slam title and extending a 23-year drought for American men.

World.title: Why are Americans so tired so often? New CDC report highlights who’s feeling it most
World.content:
The cost of healthcare. Economic uncertainties. Fears of AI-associated end times. It’s enough to exhaust anyone.

About 71.5% of adults in the United States say they experienced fatigue on multiple days over the past three months, according to a new report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS). Women and younger adults are more likely to report frequent fatigue, meaning most days or every day, than men are.

Sociologist Natalie A.E. Young, lead author of the report, said fatigue is “one of the most frequently reported health concerns in primary care visits in the U.S.” It’s the first study about general fatigue from NCHS, which surveyed about 27,000 adults ages 18 and older in 2024 about their health and daily lives.

People with fatigue “are at higher risk of activity limitations and disability, including permanent work disability. Yet there hadn’t been much attention to the frequency of general fatigue symptoms in the U.S. adult population,” Young said.

Fatigue isn’t ordinary sleepiness. It’s “physical or mental tiredness or exhaustion that does not improve with additional sleep or rest,” the researchers said. General fatigue, which is different from chronic fatigue syndrome, can be a symptom of other health problems or a side effect of medication.

Fatigue is often connected to other health problems, difficulty concentrating and limited social activities. People with symptoms of frequent fatigue were more likely to experience “co-occurring functioning difficulties,” including cognitive difficulties, depression and anxiety, said Young.

“So it’s not just that fatigue is common,” she said. “It’s that fatigue is common and those with fatigue are facing limitations in their daily lives.”

Adults who experienced frequent fatigue were more than three times as likely to have symptoms of depression and about twice as likely to report cognitive difficulties or symptoms of anxiety, compared with those who don’t experience it, the study found.

The report found that:

Nearly 3 in 4 adults felt “very tired or exhausted” at least some days in the past three months.

About 1 in 6 adults experienced frequent fatigue, defined as feeling very tired or exhausted “most days” or “every day.”

Frequent fatigue was highest among younger adults, ages 18-34 (19.5%), with the lowest rate among adults ages 65 and older (12.9%).

Women were more likely than men to report frequent fatigue (20% versus 13%).

American Indian and Alaska Native adults had the highest rate of frequent fatigue (25.5%), followed by white adults (18%), Black adults (17.3%) and Hispanic adults (12.9%), with Asian adults having the lowest rate of frequent fatigue (9.1%).

Living in America

Adults living in the South (17.7%) and Midwest (17.5%) were more likely to experience frequent fatigue than adults living in the West (15.6%) or Northeast (14.5%), the report showed.

The CDC survey didn’t look at underlying causes of frequent fatigue, and it doesn’t indicate whether it’s worse than in previous years.

But Dr. Alana A. Lewis, a cardiologist at the Bluhm Cardiovascular Institute at Northwestern Medicine in Chicago, said the findings were “not unexpected.”

“Just living in this country, we all, at some point, feel fatigue,” Lewis said.

In the most recent “Stress in America” survey, the American Psychological Association found that a majority of adults reported feeling isolated, left out and more stressed about the future than they used to be.

Stress can cause surges in hormones like cortisol and adrenaline, which can wear a body down. That increasing stress contributes to an uptick in fatigue, said Jennifer Caspari, a clinical psychologist licensed in Denver and Vancouver, British Columbia.

“People are incredibly busy,” Caspari said. “They’re stressed. They’re feeling spread thin. They have a lot on their plates and only so many hours in the day. They’re trying to cram in so much.”

Stress can also lead to mental health issues like anxiety and depression, which can disrupt sleep, causing us to feel more tired throughout the day, Caspari said.

Women report more fatigue

More than half of women said they felt fatigue “some days,” and 20% experienced it “most days or every day.”

Caspari said chronic health issues, like autoimmune diseases, which often include fatigue as a symptom, affect women in greater numbers. Hormonal fluctuations during menstruation, pregnancy, perimenopause and menopause can also affect energy levels.

And many women in heterosexual relationships, for example, say they feel they have more responsibilities at work and home than their male partners do, which can lead to them feeling exhausted, Caspari said.

Even when tasks are evenly divided, women experience stress differently. They tend to worry more about organizing and planning and engage in more “internal dialogue” about their responsibilities.

How to deal with fatigue

Mental health, lifestyle and physical health are the “three big pillars” that can trigger fatigue, Lewis said. Heart disease, obstructive sleep apnea, anemia and thyroid issues can also be underlying causes of fatigue.

When patients complain of fatigue, Lewis asks:

Are you getting enough sleep?

Are you eating well?

Are you exercising?

Are you on your screen all day?

“Start with the basics,” said Lewis, who encourages patients to follow the American Heart Association’s Life’s Essential 8 cardiovascular health checklist.

Pay attention to your sleep and stress patterns to determine whether fatigue is a temporary issue or something that’s become more “chronic and persistent,” which could indicate a medical problem.

Learning to relax, both physically and mentally, is important, said Caspari. Take a break from never-ending to-do lists. “You’re not a robot. You only have so much energy,” Caspari said.

Passive resting, like sitting down to watch TV, is perfectly fine. Caspari also recommends “active rest,” low-intensity activities like breathing exercises and gentle stretching.

“Active rest can feel more nourishing,” she said, “and it can have a more helpful impact on the fatigue over time rather than just sitting and scrolling.”

World.title: Alexander Zverev overtakes Ben Shelton to win U.S. Open final
World.content:
German star Alexander Zverev overtook Ben Shelton to win the U.S. Open on Sunday, securing his second Grand Slam title and evaporating dreams of an American man winning the title for the first time in more than 20 years.

The score was 6-3, 7-6, 5-7, 6-2.

Andy Roddick was the last American man to win at the U.S. Open, defeating Spain’s Juan Carlos Ferrero in 2003.

It was a thrilling final in Arthur Ashe Stadium between two men with powerful serves and something to prove on one of tennis’ biggest stages. Shelton lagged early in the first set, struggling to make headway against Zverev’s methodical approach.

But Shelton began gaining ground against the more experienced player, growing more confident in his returns and catching Zverev off guard with well-timed forehands. He pushed Zverev to a tiebreak in the second set but ultimately fell short, entering the third set well behind his opponent.

The American dug deep to push Zverev in the third set, rattling the German as Shelton crawled out from the two-set deficit he found himself in.

In the fourth and final set, Zverev was hit with a time violation, and he protested it to no avail. The moment did not derail him, and he went up 3-1 and stayed ahead, breaking Shelton’s serve to make it 5-2 before cruising to victory on-serve.

It was the first appearance in a Grand Slam final for 23-year-old Ben Shelton, but Zverev well acquainted with the pressure of a major final. The 29-year-old has played in five Grand Slam finals before Sunday’s match.

Zverev came into the tournament in Queens, New York, with momentum from winning the French Open in June. The German player endured two difficult matches to open the tournament but did not drop a set on his way to the final after the second round.

Zverev came into the tournament with momentum from winning the French Open in June. Angela Weiss / AFP via Getty Images

Shelton, on the other hand, fought two-time U.S. Open champion Carlos Alcaraz for 4 hours and 28 minute for a place in the semifinals. It was a grueling match that started late Tuesday night and ended at 3:33 a.m. on Wednesday morning.

The young American pushed Alcaraz to the limit as the Spanish star competed in his first major since injuring his wrist. Alacraz appearing to vomit into a towel at one point during the match.

Shelton then defeated fellow American Frances Tiafoe on Friday night, dominating in a 4-6, 6-3, 6-3, 7-5 victory.

Fans inside the stadium were raucous in their support for Shelton. Some told NBC News that they had traveled from near and far in the hopes to see Shelton make history.

Many were hoping that Shelton could become the second Black man to win the U.S. Open. The only other player to have accomplished that was Arthur Ashe, the namesake of the court on which Sunday’s final was played, in 1968.

Tracie Saundera told NBC News before the match that she was excited to see a Black man in the final, especially considering the last time it happened, in 1972, was before she was born. Shelton is also simply an exciting player to watch, she added.

Fans inside the stadium were raucous for Shelton, some telling NBC News that they traveled from near and far in the hopes of seeing Shelton make history. Angela Weiss / AFP via Getty Images

“He just plays with so much passion and energy,” Saundera said. “He’s so fun to watch play, and he’s young and enthusiastic... I’m old. Most of my players are retiring, so it’s good to see some of the young kids coming in and just being powerhouses.”

University of Florida fan Junior Pulayya drove from Florida to New York to support Shelton, an alumnus of the school. He noted that there had been a drought of “really solid” American men’s players until now.

“But this is, just, it gets that new generation of kids that follow tennis, that that get involved in tennis, that want to get involved in tennis,” Pulayya said. “It does so much just for today, but long term for the sport.”

Longtime tennis fan and Maryland resident Shameka Littles said she could not imagine how it feels for Shelton to play on the Arthur Ashe court as the first Black man to make the U.S. Open final in more than 50 years. But beyond that, Littles said, it was “inspiring” to see so many Americans do well this year.

“To have so many of the top seeds, you know, make it to the semifinals, the quarterfinals — that was exciting in and of itself,” Littles said. “Hopefully, it just kind of gives you know a big boost of energy and excitement for each other.”

World.title: Céline Dion makes triumphant return in Paris after six years sidelined by rare diagnosis
World.content:
PARIS — It’s all coming back to her now.

If there were any doubts about whether the “Queen of Ballads” could still hit the high notes, they were put to rest on Saturday night when she belted out “All by Myself,” one of her most difficult songs, in front of 30,000 adoring fans in Paris.

It was a poignant comeback for the Quebec-born singer, 58, who was forced to stop touring six years ago after being diagnosed with a rare neurological disorder, stiff-person syndrome.

Having spent the years since largely out of the spotlight, Dion was overcome with emotion, breaking down in tears during the first few minutes of her show at Plenitude Arena, one of Europe’s largest indoor concert venues.

00:34 Céline Dion gives emotional speech during concert return 00:00 00:00

Aptly, she began with the French-language song “On ne change pas” — which translates to “one doesn’t change” — an apparent signal that she is the same Céline as ever.

The road to recovery has been “rocky and longer than it should have been,” she told the crowd, after she endured years of physical therapy and medical treatments. There were nerves mixed with raw emotion as she asked the crowd: “Can you hear my heartbeat?”

Dion, an icon across the French-speaking world, spoke of fulfilling her “promise” to come back. Two years ago, she sang here from the Eiffel Tower during the 2024 Olympics opening ceremony, marking a milestone in her recovery in front of a TV audience of hundreds of millions.

Despite living with an illness that at times prevents her from singing or even walking due to severe muscle spasms, Dion on Saturday mixed classic onstage theatrics with titanic ballads for more than two hours.

The concert, the first in a two-part, 26-show residency in the city, was hotly anticipated, with 9 million people entering a presale ticket lottery back in April. Some American fans told NBC News they paid $1,200 per ticket on the resale market.

After the show, fans emerged in disbelief. “It was a victory lap,” said Francesca Pezzulo, 31, from Los Angeles. “I think her belief is renewed, I think her spirit is renewed.”

It was a bucket-list moment for Ashley Hammond, 42, who flew in from Miami for the concert. “It gave you chills. It was everything we dreamed of,” she said.

01:19 Fans say they’re ‘over the moon’ excited for Céline Dion’s return 00:00 00:00

Fans came from all corners of the world for the moment.

“I think Céline is the queen,” Pirkir Gutlausson, a 53-year-old mechanic from Iceland, told NBC News.

Dion is performing a total of 16 concerts until October, with a further 10 in the spring of 2027.

The residency is expected to cause a mini tourism boom, with an influx of hundreds of thousands of fans spending millions of dollars on par with Taylor Swift’s shows in Paris, according to the hospitality and tourism consultancy MKG.

For eager fans, there were plenty of opportunities to spend money. A Céline pop-up store at fashion boutique Galeries Lafayette had some T-shirts on sale for $145.

The luxurious hotel Le Royal Monceau has been the focal point of Céline mania. Since her arrival in the French capital, a constant stream of fans has waited day and night for a chance to see the global superstar, who has often stopped to sing and dance along with the crowds, even when returning from rehearsals in the middle of the night.

For fans, her resilience says it all.

“She has class, she’s humane and she’s a fighter,” said Karine Teixeira Bourgogne, 58, who traveled from across France to see her.

World.title: Alexander Zverev wins U.S. Open, beating American Ben Shelton
World.content:
Alexander Zverev dispatched Ben Shelton in four sets to win the U.S. Open men's singles title on Sunday, the second Grand Slam win for the German after he finally broke through at the French Open earlier this year.

The No. 1 seed in a Grand Slam for the first time, Zverev capitalized on Shelton's shaky start in his first major final, played a nearly flawless tiebreaker on serve and then turned back Shelton's comeback attempt to win 6-3, 7-6 (2), 5-7, 6-2 in front of a crowd that desperately cheered the American on.

After taking down his fellow countryman Francis Tiafoe in a thrilling semifinal, Shelton was aiming to become the first American man to win a major since Andy Roddick's U.S. Open victory in 2003. Shelton was also the first Black American man to make it to a U.S. Open final since Arthur Ashe in 1972.

But Zverev was too good in majors this year and apparently didn't even know how good he was. He finished the match on his serve but didn't seem to realize it, dropping back behind the baseline as if set to return. Only a few moments later did he figure out he had won, raising his arms in celebration.

Alexander Zverev celebrates after winning the U.S. Open men's singles championship match at the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center in Queens, New York, on Sunday, September 13, 2026, Simon Bruty/USTA via Getty Images

This is a breaking news story. It will be updated.

World.title: Wisconsin Congressman suffers minor injury after lake emergency landing
World.content:
Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate Rep. Tom Tiffany said Sunday he sustained minor injuries after the plane he was traveling in made an emergency landing on Lake Wausau in central Wisconsin.

Tiffany, a Republican, said in a social media post that he was returning from La Crosse County Lincoln Day Dinner when the plane he was traveling in lost power on approach to Wausau Downtown Airport, forcing the pilot to make an emergency landing in the water.

A Beechcraft K35 landed in Lake Wausau around 8:50 p.m. local time Saturday after the pilot reported engine issues, the Federal Aviation Administration told CBS News on Sunday. Only two people were on board. The FAA will continue to investigate.

Tiffany was flying with Len Boltz, a private pilot whom the congressman has flown with before, Tiffany said at a news conference Sunday.

He said the plane lost power during final approach and went down 10 seconds after he was told to tighten his seat belt. After crash landing in the lake, Boltz was able to call 911, Tiffany said. The two sat on top of the plane for about 10 minutes until they decided to swim toward the airport. The pair managed to get to a point in the lake where they could stand, and a boat met them shortly after.

"I have to say that the gravity of this is probably just hitting me at this point," Tiffany said Sunday. "Because we were making jokes every step of the way last night, though we knew it was a serious situation. We tried to keep it light through the whole thing."

Earlier, Tiffany wrote in his social media post, "I want to express my deepest gratitude to the pilot, the Wausau Fire Department, and all of the first responders who came to our aid so quickly."

"God was watching over us tonight, and I am incredibly grateful to be here in the hospital with my wife, Chris, by my side. An experience like this reminds you just how precious life is," Tiffany said in his post.

In another social media post on Sunday, Tiffany gave his thanks for the messages he's received and said he was released from the hospital "after receiving stitches above my right eye." He said the pilot was also released.

Tiffany said at Sunday's news conference that he received 12 stitches while Bolt received four. He said he also underwent a CT scan, and it doesn't seem like he has a concussion, but he will still monitor himself for symptoms going forward.

He noted his phone is at the bottom of the lake, so he doesn't know specifically who has reached out to him, including any possible attempt by the president to do so.

The gubernatorial candidate said he is eager to get back out on the campaign trail. He said he's been told not to fly for a few days, so he won't be back in Washington, D.C., right away.

Tiffany's Democratic opponent, David Crowley, responded by saying he was "grateful to God that Congressman Tiffany and no one else was hurt in this horrifying incident, which could have been a tragedy if not for the heroism of the pilot."

World.title: U.S. wins fifth straight women's FIBA World Cup, beating France 97-79
World.content:
Breanna Stewart and the U.S. faced a stiff challenge from France before dominating in the second half to win its fifth consecutive women's FIBA World Cup.

The 97-79 victory extended the Americans' streak to 36 straight World Cup wins, dating back to the 2006 World Cup semifinals, when they lost to Russia. The U.S. improved to 9-0 in gold-medal games since finishing second to the Soviet Union in 1983.

Despite the final score, this one wasn't easy; the Americans faced their biggest deficit in the tournament in a long time, trailing by 14 points in the first half. They calmly rallied behind Stewart and Jackie Young to get within two at halftime, and Caitlin Clark hit a 3-pointer just before the buzzer.

The U.S. dominated in the second half, starting the third quarter with an 11-2 run to go up 54-47. Stewart, who now has four World Cup titles to her name, had four points during the game-changing burst.

Stewart, who was named the tournament MVP, finished with 22 points and Young with 18.

France's Marine Johannes guards Breanna Stewart, of the United States, during the Women's Basketball World Cup final match between the United States and France in Berlin, Sunday, Sept. 13, 2026. AP Photo/Ebrahim Noroozi

France was able to get within 55-51, but the Americans used a 16-3 spurt that included France being called for two unsportsmanlike fouls on the same play. The Americans were up 73-57 heading into the fourth quarter, and France was never able to close the gap.

This was the second-youngest team the Americans have sent to a World Cup. There were many newcomers on the roster, including Clark, Angel Reese, and Paige Bueckers, who were getting their first experience with the national team. But it was the veterans who carried the team to the victory.

The Americans had looked more vulnerable in this tournament than at any time during their remarkable run. A three-point win over Italy in pool play was the closest a team has come to the U.S. in the group stage in 50 years. The 10-point victory over Spain was the closest semifinal contest during the streak. The Americans had been winning by an average of 26 points over the past four medal-round games.

None of that mattered in the end as the Americans finished the same way they had the previous four World Cup tournaments — as champions.

France's Mamignan Toure guards Caitlin Clark of the United States, during the Women's Basketball World Cup final match between the United States and France in Berlin, Sunday, Sept. 13, 2026. AP Photo/Ebrahim Noroozi

The loss nevertheless gave France its best finish ever in the event. The French were hoping for the top prize after they came close against the U.S. in the 2024 Paris Olympic gold-medal game two years ago. That one-point loss still stung two years later.

Dominique Malonga scored 21 points and Gabby Williams added 20 for France.

France got off to a strong start. The U.S. trailed 20-17 after the first quarter and the French scored the first 11 points of the second, capped by Williams' 3-pointer, to take a 31-17 lead. But the Americans rallied and trailed 45-43 at the half on Clark's 3 just before the buzzer.

Spain topped host Germany to win the bronze medal.

World.title: Sweden's election exit polls show center-left opposition ahead of populist right
World.content:
Across Europe, right-wing populist parties have gained ground in recent years amid growing voter backlash over immigration. Sweden has been no exception, but exit polls from Sunday's elections show voters are favoring the center-left opposition.

The election pits Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson's center-right coalition against a center-left bloc led by former Prime Minister Magdalena Andersson's Social Democrats. The polls from Swedish public broadcaster SVT project Andersson's four-party group winning a majority, paving the way for her to return to office pending coalition talks, the Associated Press reported.

The first preliminary results were expected Sunday evening from election officials.

Social Democrats react to the presentation of the exit poll at the Social Democrats' election night watch party, in Stockholm, Sunday, Sept. 13, 2026. Jonas Ekströmer/TT News Agency via AP

Hanging over the race is the prospect of Sweden's right-wing populist Sweden Democrats entering government for the first time.

The party, which traces its roots to Sweden's extreme-right fringe, has spent the past two decades moving steadily toward the center of political power. It first entered parliament in 2010. By 2022, it became the country's second-largest party and agreed to support Kristersson's minority government from outside the cabinet. The arrangement gave the party substantial influence over immigration, crime and other policies without formal responsibility for government departments. But now Kristersson wants to govern as a majority government and has gone one step further, saying the Sweden Democrats would receive ministerial posts if the right wins another term.

This has transformed the election into a test of the Sweden Democrats' long political normalization and whether Swedish voters are prepared to see a party once shunned by almost the entire political establishment now exercise executive power.

"There has been a shift of focus, which has gone from the true political challenges to who is going to sit in the government," Andreas Önnerfors, a professor of intellectual history at Linnaeus University, told CBS News.

The polls are currently on a knife-edge, with an Indikator Opinion poll conducted Sept. 2–10 putting the center-left coalition on 50.8%, against 47.6% for the right coalition.

From fringe to mainstream

For years, Sweden's established parties maintained what amounted to a political firewall around the Sweden Democrats because of the party's extremist roots. As recently as 2018, Kristersson assured Holocaust survivor Hédi Fried that he would not cooperate with the party, according to Reuters. The Sweden Democrats themselves acknowledge that figures involved in their early history had connections to neo-Nazi and white supremacist movements.

Jimmie Akesson, leader of the Sweden Democrats, delivers a speech in Solvesborg, Sweden. Nichlas Pollier / Bloomberg via Getty Images

But under Jimmie Åkesson, who has led the party since 2005, the Sweden Democrats have sought to expel extremists, moderate their image and present themselves as a mainstream right-wing party, with policies including deporting people who are in the country illegally, toughening citizenship laws, requiring strict assimilation of newcomers and restricting social security to citizens.

Part of the party's success has come from combining positions traditionally associated with the political right with policies aimed at working-class voters.

"They have merged typical right-wing positions with typical Labour or Social Democratic positions — social security and benefits and things like that. That makes sense among ordinary people," Önnerfors said.

Immigration and crime as key voter concerns

The Sweden Democrats helped make tougher immigration and crime policies central to Swedish politics. Still, their durability is also rooted in profound changes in Swedish society and voters' perceptions.

"Swedish politics has clearly moved in a more restrictive direction on issues such as immigration and crime," Professor Niklas Bolin, a political scientist at Mid Sweden University, told CBS News. "Importantly, this shift is not limited to the parties on the right. The Social Democrats, Sweden's largest party, have also moved in this direction."

Voters queue to cast their votes in the Swedish general election at a polling station in a sports hall in Lomma, southern Sweden, on September 13, 2026. Polling stations opened in Sweden in what is expected to be a close general election that will see either the far right enter government for the first time or the left-wing opposition reclaim power. Johan NILSSON / TT News Agency /AFP via Getty Images

Sweden received around 163,000 asylum applications during the 2015 European migration crisis; with a population just shy of 11 million, it was among the highest per-capita rates in Europe. In subsequent years, integration, segregation and a surge in gang shootings and bombings became major national political issues. The country's approach to immigration has since changed dramatically.

The Swedish government says asylum immigration has fallen to its lowest level since 1985.

Government policies on crime have also led gang violence to recede. Police figures show shootings falling from 391 in 2022 to 158 in 2025, with the decline continuing this year. But the political consequences of the violence and the wider debate over immigration and integration have endured.

"The Sweden Democrats have built a stable electoral base," Bolin said.

"Immigration and dissatisfaction with integration remain important explanations, but their support is also linked to concerns about crime and a broader dissatisfaction with established parties."

Their support, he added, is "particularly strong among men, working-class voters and voters outside the larger cities."

For a country that for generations has prided itself on low crime, a generous welfare state and liberal attitudes toward immigration, equality and individual rights, Sunday's election marks an important moment — testing how far Sweden's politics have shifted, and whether a party once kept at the margins is now ready to enter the heart of government.

World.title: Full transcript of "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Sept. 6, 2026
World.content:
On this "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" broadcast, moderated by Weijia Jiang:

Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed , a Democrat

, a Democrat Utah Gov. Spencer Cox , a Republican

, a Republican CBS News executive director of news and surveys Anthony Salvanto

CBS News executive director of news and surveys Anthony Salvanto, CBS News senior White House and political correspondent Ed O'Keefe and Amy Walter, the editor-in-chief and publisher of the Cook Political Report.

Click here to browse full transcripts from 2026 of "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."

WEIJIA JIANG: I'm Weijia Jiang in Washington.

And this week on Face the Nation: a major development in the artificial intelligence arms race. And our election-year Battleground Tracker reveals where the race for control of Congress stands less than two months from Election Day.

As the midterm election campaign pace picked up dramatically last week, so did America's anxiety over A.I.

(Begin VT)

QUESTION: Do you have any concerns about A.I. leading to human extinction?

DONALD TRUMP (President of the United States): No, I don't have any. I have concerns that, if we don't win A.I., we're going to be put in a very bad position. We are leading China right now by a pretty good period.

(End VT)

WEIJIA JIANG: This coming after an Anthropic researcher's very public revelation.

(Begin VT)

JACOB COXON (Former Anthropic Researcher): Super advanced intelligence, it could – it will be smart enough to kill us.

(End VT)

WEIJIA JIANG: And now a big development within the industry.

(Begin VT)

DARIO AMODEI (CEO and Co-Founder, Anthropic): What we need to do is not stop. We need to slow down.

(End VT)

WEIJIA JIANG: Dario Amodei is the head of Anthropic. We will have more of his first-on-CBS conversation with our Jo Ling.

Then, on to politics. We will talk with Utah Republican Governor Spencer Cox, as well as Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. Plus, our CBS News poll shows where the battle for Congress stands.

It's all just ahead on Face the Nation.

Good morning, and welcome to Face the Nation. Margaret is off today. I'm Weijia Jiang.

We begin with the stunning news from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei Saturday that he is urging a slowdown when it comes to the development of artificial intelligence. It was a pronouncement that his chief competitor, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, and Elon Musk quickly agreed with.

Our Jo Ling Kent sat down with Dario Amodei yesterday. He explained the thinking behind his decision.

(Begin VT)

DARIO AMODEI (CEO and Co-Founder, Anthropic): What we're building is essentially intelligence. When something's very powerful, then, of course, it can be used well and it can also be used for ill.

And so I am worried about what we have seen with the OpenAI Hugging Face incident, with models taking actions they weren't authorized to take, and I'm worried about that escalating. I'm worried about misuse of A.I. models.

Just two days ago, we put out a report about misuse of models to build biological weapons. And our view, the whole way we have built Anthropic is so that these bad outcomes don't happen. Instead of talking about the probabilities, let's talk about what we can do. It's not like we're just rolling the dice, right?

If we build in the right way, I think the probability of something bad happening is very low. If we build in the wrong way, the probability of something bad happening is very high.

JO LING KENT: But the conversation…

DARIO AMODEI: And so we have got to build in the right way.

JO LING KENT: We are in this race with China. Do you actually think slowing down is a good idea, when China will not?

DARIO AMODEI: So, this is – this is the toughest dilemma. This is the toughest aspect of our situation. If we weren't in that situation, we could take much more time.

So, this is – this is the thing that most puts us in a bind. It's not about commercial competition. This – the geopolitical situation is the hardest to deal with.

But I will talk about two strategies that we have. One – and I talk about it in my proposal – is, we can slow down within the margin, within the envelope that we have, particularly if we don't sell chips to authoritarian countries and if we do more to help our own security so that our technology is not stolen.

I believe that will buy us at least a little time.

JO LING KENT: President Trump will meet with President Xi Jinping very soon. What's the one simple, most important solution that they should come to an agreement on in A.I.?

DARIO AMODEI: A thing that's small enough we might be able to do it, and a thing that's big enough that I think it's going to take a very long time.

The small thing is, if we could – U.S. and China could agree that we won't use A.I. to develop biological weapons or release A.I. models that bioterrorists could use to develop biological weapons. We're already both signatories to the Biological Weapons Convention. If we could just extend that convention to that idea, that would be really valuable.

And then I think the more long-term thing would be working together to put a speed limit on the rate of A.I. progress. I think that's going to be very difficult. We shouldn't kid ourselves, because the incentives to pull ahead and the military advantage that you get from that are so large that the ability to check that the other side isn't cheating has to be ironclad.

So, I think that's going to be the work of years. And, honestly, I don't know if it's possible. But we should – we should try. We should see if it is possible.

Again, all of this is above my pay grade. I have no idea how to negotiate with China.

JO LING KENT: As we zoom out here on this problem, it seems like the fate of humanity is at risk. How much personal responsibility do you feel about where we are going?

DARIO AMODEI: My view here is, it has always been very strange that this technology is being built by a private company. People ask me that question all the time. Why isn't this being built by government?

And the strangest thing about it is, I agree with them. I'm uncomfortable. Government didn't build this technology. This company – this technology came from the private sector. And we, Anthropic and I would hope other companies have done everything we can to try to have legitimate oversight mechanisms.

I think the government and the public needs to have a stake. And this is why we have supported regulation of the technology. Regulation constrains the private companies. Regulation allows the public and its elected representatives to have a stake, to have a say, and limits what the private companies can do.

Now, you might ask, why doesn't government just control the technology completely?
