The forum brought together government officials, maritime administrations, international organizations, port operators, logistics companies and industry experts.

Discussions covered port infrastructure, maritime cooperation, digital transformation, navigation and shipping safety, and applying the single-window principle in the maritime sector.

Discussions on the Middle Corridor also highlighted the need for further infrastructure investment. Speaking at the 5th International Forum on Freight Transport in the Black and Caspian Regions 2026 in Baku, World Bank Senior Transport and Logistics Specialist Luis Blancas said a new comprehensive report on the Middle Corridor is scheduled for publication on Sept. 27, Trend reported.

The report covers all nine participating countries and identifies 16 critical investment priorities worth around US$25 billion. More than three-quarters of the required investment is already underway, Blancas said.

The report is expected to provide a broader assessment of infrastructure needs as cargo flows between Asia and Europe continue to grow.

World.title: “Injustice prevails under oligarch Ivanishvili” — video podcast “Protests in Georgia”
World.content:
For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. The results of the parliamentary elections held in autumn 2024 are still not recognised by part of Georgian society.

Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms.

For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti.

In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years.

To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

World.title: “Arresting a person in Georgia over their views on a 34-year-old war is a legal absurdity” – opinion
World.content:
Opinion on Giorgi Baramidze’s arrest

“Arresting someone over an opinion expressed in a historical programme about a 34-year-old war — especially when he has since apologised for the statement — is a legal absurdity,” said Tamta Mikeladze, director of the Social Justice Center, commenting on the arrest of Georgian opposition leader and former defence minister Giorgi Baramidze.

On 11 September, Giorgi Baramidze was arrested on charges of treason against the state, specifically sabotage. His arrest followed an interview on the programme “Birth of Georgia”, in which he said that at the beginning of the 1992–93 Georgian-Abkhaz war, the Georgian side had no prisoners because they were “shot”.

Tamta Mikeladze: “Arresting someone over an opinion expressed in a historical programme about a 34-year-old war — especially when he has since apologised for the statement — is a legal absurdity.

The prosecutor’s argument that the statement damaged Georgia’s international standing and image, offended the honour of war veterans and so on has no basis in criminal law. If specific individuals believed Baramidze had defamed them, they could have taken him to court in a civil case.

Claims that the statement could be used in international legal proceedings are also unfounded. There are no international legal proceedings concerning the war in Abkhazia, and Baramidze was not a decision-maker at the time. His words therefore could not carry the kind of weight that would affect any legal consequences.

Arresting someone for expressing an opinion – even if that opinion is unfounded, foolish, offensive or unacceptable – is therefore an unimaginable departure from the rule of law.”

Mikeladze also examines the alleged offence in detail and points to a mismatch between the charge and the statement, arguing that no remarks of this kind can legally constitute sabotage.

News in Georgia

World.title: One of Georgia’s opposition leaders, Giorgi Baramidze, detained on “treason and sabotage” charges
World.content:
Opposition figure Baramidze arrested in Georgia

Giorgi Baramidze, one of the leaders of the opposition United National Movement and Georgian former defence and interior minister, has been detained in Georgia.

Prosecutors searched his home before handcuffing him.

The detention stems from an interview Baramidze gave on the programme “Birth of Georgia”, in which he said that at the beginning of the 1992–93 Georgian-Abkhaz war, the Georgian side had no prisoners of war because they were “shot”.

On 7 August, the prosecutor’s office said it had opened an investigation into “treason against the state and sabotage” over the statement.

As of today, five former Georgian defence ministers are (!) in prison, while a sixth is facing criminal charges.

Giorgi Baramidze is now the seventh on the list.

What the prosecutor’s office says

Deputy Prosecutor General Amiran Guluashvili confirmed that Giorgi Baramidze was detained on charges of treason against the state, specifically sabotage. The charge carries a prison sentence of up to four years.

Giorgi Baramidze, one of the leaders of the opposition United National Movement and Georgian former defence and interior minister

The prosecutor’s office says its investigation found no evidence that prisoners of war were executed by Georgian armed forces or other participants in the conflict. It therefore described Baramidze’s claim as “baseless and fabricated” and said it was part of a targeted information campaign.

According to the prosecutor’s office, Baramidze’s statement could damage Georgia’s international image, the reputation of its defence forces and the dignity of those who took part in the war. It could also undermine efforts to reconcile with communities affected by the conflict and rebuild trust.

The prosecutor’s office says Baramidze’s remarks harmed Georgia’s peace and de-occupation policy and obstructed the work of state agencies, including the Office of the State Minister for Reconciliation and Civic Equality, which is working to restore trust and cooperation.

The prosecutor’s office will ask the court to remand Baramidze in custody. The investigation is ongoing.

What Giorgi Baramidze said

During the programme “Birth of Georgia”, Giorgi Baramidze recalled the exchange of prisoners during the Georgian-Abkhaz war and said: “We had no prisoners. Our side did not take prisoners — they were shot.”

Baramidze’s statement drew a strong reaction from government officials. He later explained several times what he had meant.

He said he was referring to the very beginning of the war, when the Georgian side still had no regular, organised army and some fighters, driven by grief after losing loved ones in the fighting, sometimes did not take enemy combatants prisoner.

“During the first period, this was the situation: people whose mothers, fathers or other loved ones had been killed were so consumed by anger that they did not take prisoners during fighting and killed them instead. They had been driven to despair. This is the bitter truth about the early stage of the war, which I know because I was personally involved in prisoner exchanges,” Baramidze explained.

He said the situation later changed, with the Georgian side beginning to take prisoners, making prisoner exchanges possible.

Baramidze also says he was personally involved in the process, which ultimately helped secure the return of around 200 Georgian prisoners.

News in Georgia

World.title: Live from Gyumri, Armenia, in photos and videos
World.content:
Gyumri, Armenia, photos and video

Gyumri is the second-largest city in Armenia after Yerevan. The video was filmed during a journey from Georgia to Armenia, and the story follows this route.

As soon as you cross the Georgian border and enter Armenia, the road becomes mountainous. The plains and forest-covered mountains gradually give way to rocky slopes.

The road runs across the Ashotzk Plateau along the Akhuryan River gorge and around the Shirak Range. This is where Gyumri lies, at an altitude of more than 1,500 metres above sea level.

The air is noticeably cooler here, which is why both tourists and residents of the capital come here in summer.

Locals are particularly proud of their drinking water. It comes from mountain springs and is exceptionally cold and delicious.

Small drinking fountains can be found throughout the city. Locals call them “pulpulak”. They attract attention partly because of their distinctive designs, with no two fountains looking quite alike.

They are usually built from local stone — tuff or basalt — and decorated with national ornaments, crosses and various symbols.

There is also a tradition of building pulpulaks in memory of deceased loved ones.

A defining feature of Gyumri is its black stone. Almost all the city’s old buildings are made from local volcanic tuff.

Drinking fountain in Gyumri, Armenia. JAMnews photo.

In the city centre lies Vardanants Square. It was named in memory of the battle between the Armenian army, led by commander Vardan Mamikonian, and the Persian army in 450–451.

Vardanants Square in Gyumri, Armenia. JAMnews photo.

Churches of Gyumri

On either side of the square stand two churches: the Church of the Holy Mother of God, also known as the Church of the “Seven Wounds”, and the Church of the Holy Saviour.

The Church of the Holy Mother of God holds a special place in Gyumri’s history. During the Soviet period, when most churches in the city were closed and converted into warehouses or museums, the “Seven Wounds” Church remained one of the few still operating. It became a centre that preserved church traditions and a symbol of believers’ resistance.

Symbolically, the church courtyard contains a brass cross riddled with bullet holes. It commemorates the clergy who continued their service and supported believers during Stalin’s anti-religious campaign. Dozens of members of the Shirak Diocese clergy were arrested and executed.

Today, the bullet holes in the cross are clearly visible even from a distance. The names of clergy members who died during those years are engraved on its lower section.

On 7 December 1988, an earthquake almost destroyed the city in just 30 seconds.

The entire northern part of Armenia was affected. More than 27,000 people died, and 750,000 were left homeless.

A huge fragment of stone broke off the Church of the Holy Saviour in Gyumri during the earthquake. They left it lying beside the church. According to local residents, it serves as a reminder of that terrible day.

A bronze memorial, “To the Innocent Victims, the Compassionate Hearts”, was built nearby. The inscription appears on the monument in three languages: Armenian, Russian and English.

It depicts figures emerging from the rubble and helping one another.

The scale of the destruction clearly showed the difference in quality between older buildings and structures from the Soviet period.

Low-rise buildings in Gyumri made from traditional black tuff. JAMnews photo.

One- and two-storey buildings dating from before the Soviet era proved more resilient, while high-rise buildings constructed in the 1970s and 1980s were completely destroyed.

The tragedy fundamentally changed the city’s future development strategy. Based on the findings of seismologists and architects, Gyumri banned the construction of high-rise residential buildings.

The city returned to its historic style: low-rise, sturdy buildings made from local black and orange tuff.

Tourists often explore the city in these horse-drawn carriages, which are popular in Gyumri. JAMnews photo.

Gyumri, Armenia, photos and video

World.title: Armenian citizenship to become harder and five times more expensive under Interior Ministry draft
World.content:
New requirements for obtaining Armenian citizenship

The procedure for obtaining Armenian citizenship could change. If parliament approves the draft, obtaining citizenship will become not only more difficult but also more expensive.

The Interior Ministry proposes increasing the state fee for obtaining Armenian citizenship fivefold and the fee for renouncing it tenfold. Applicants will have to pay 250,000 drams ($690) to obtain Armenian citizenship and 1.5 million drams ($4,143) to renounce it.

The ministry has already published its draft on the electronic platform where legal acts are made available for public discussion.

The authorities justify the proposed changes by the need to “rethink” the institution of citizenship:

“In recent years, the number of people without a sufficient factual connection to Armenia has increased. These are people who have never visited the country or lived there for a significant period, but obtained Armenian citizenship for practical benefits, including when planning trips.”

The package of amendments includes not only changes to the state fees but also procedural changes. The government expects the amendments to take effect on 1 January 2028.

Between 1 January 2021 and 31 August 2026, 110,219 people obtained Armenian citizenship. Over the past 15 years, 250,000 people have obtained Armenian citizenship. Most of the new citizens did not live in the country permanently.

Those who renounce Armenian citizenship will not be able to regain it for five years

Applications to obtain or renounce Armenian citizenship will be submitted electronically. If necessary, applicants will then be able to schedule an appointment and submit their documents in person.

Under the new procedure, applicants must have legally resided in Armenia for the past five years to qualify for citizenship. They must also have spent at least 915 days in the country during that period.

Ethnic Armenians will face less stringent requirements. They will need to have legally resided in Armenia for the past two years and spent at least 366 days in the country.

A special commission within the Interior Ministry will verify ethnic background. Applicants will have to provide the relevant documents and archival records. The commission may also request certificates from religious or community organisations.

“People who have previously renounced their citizenship may apply to restore it only after five years have passed. They must also have lived in Armenia for at least 366 days during the two years preceding their application,” the draft’s explanatory note says.

Under the current legislation, people who have renounced Armenian citizenship can restore it without observing a minimum waiting period.

A presidential decree granting citizenship will take effect within one year of the applicant signing the oath. From now on, applicants will be able to take the oath only on the territory of Armenia.

If the authorities deny citizenship on grounds related to threats to national security or public order, the president’s decision cannot be challenged or changed through administrative or judicial proceedings.

The project aims to strengthen the standing and stability of the institution of citizenship

The authors of the bill say they have identified numerous applications to restore citizenship shortly after applicants renounced it. They cite the example of a parent who renounces citizenship to terminate their sons’ Armenian citizenship, allowing them to avoid compulsory military service.

The same person may then seek to restore their citizenship and regain the relevant rights and privileges. The amendments would make this impossible.

The authors justify the five-year restriction by arguing that the restoration of citizenship must not become a “situational mechanism”:

“Citizenship is not merely a formal legal status, but a long-term legal and political bond between the state and the individual.”

According to the drafters, the five-year restriction will promote:

“the stability of the institution of citizenship;

preventing its use for opportunistic purposes;

viewing citizenship as a long-term bond with the state”.

They stress that restrictions on restoring citizenship also apply in the Scandinavian countries, as well as in Germany, France and the United Kingdom.

Specialised commission to verify Armenian ancestry

The draft says that the system for making decisions on citizenship matters will also change. In particular, the interagency commission that reviews applications for the granting or termination of citizenship will be abolished.

The Interior Ministry considers that the commission’s work provides little practical benefit. It has almost never reviewed negative decisions or changed the administrative body’s preliminary position.

A specialised commission will be established in its place. Its task will be to verify applicants’ ethnicity, including their Armenian ancestry.

Until now, the authorities have based the verification of ethnicity solely on the availability of certain documents.

However, the Interior Ministry has concluded that applicants’ documents do not always provide a reliable basis for confirming Armenian ancestry. There have been cases in which people submitted forged or altered documents to take advantage of the simplified citizenship procedure available to ethnic Armenians.

According to the ministry, more than 70 such cases were identified between 2023 and 2026. The number of such incidents has also tended to increase each year.

“There were five such cases in 2023, 21 in 2024, 26 in 2025, and 19 in the first half of 2026 alone,” the Interior Ministry reports.

New requirements for obtaining Armenian citizenship

World.title: EPRC: Wildberries expansion poses significant risks for Georgia
World.content:
According to the Economic Policy Research Center (EPRC), the expansion of the Russian online platform Wildberries in Georgia poses significant risks for the country.

The centre makes this assessment in a new report examining the threats that Wildberries-related activities could pose to Georgian brands represented on the platform, consumers, Georgian banks and Georgia’s economic and financial system as a whole.

Wildberries is an online marketplace often described as “Russia’s Amazon”.

According to EPRC, at least eight Wildberries warehouses were put out of operation by Ukrainian strikes in late August 2026, while more than 20 facilities were damaged. During the same period, part of the company’s financial ecosystem, Wildberries Bank, was placed under international sanctions.

The centre says that, while Wildberries’ warehouse infrastructure in Russia became a target for Ukrainian drones and the company’s banking arm was placed on a sanctions list, Wildberries used Georgia and other neighbouring countries to expand its trading network and logistics capabilities.

EPRC predicts that, as a result, Georgia could become part of a regional infrastructure helping a company linked to the Kremlin and sanctioned Russian businesses reduce losses caused by the war and sanctions.

The report notes that Wildberries’ official infrastructure in Georgia includes warehouses, sorting centres and collection points. According to the company’s instructions, updated on 4 June 2026, Georgian sellers can choose a warehouse or sorting centre and review the conditions for accepting products, logistics rates, sorting times and delivery times to consumers.

According to EPRC, this indicates that the company’s activities in Georgia are no longer limited to collection points. Local infrastructure is also being used to receive, sort and subsequently deliver products. However, open sources do not currently confirm the existence of a large logistics centre in Georgia. A similar situation exists in Azerbaijan.

According to the report, information spread in September 2025 that local businesses had been given the opportunity to sell their products directly through the Wildberries platform.

EPRC also publishes what it believes is an incomplete list of Georgian brands available on the platform. The centre explains that finding a complete list is difficult because Wildberries does not allow users to search for brands by country of origin.

At this stage, the list of Georgian products and brands on the platform is believed to include Borjomi, Nabeghlavi, Natakhtari, Zedazeni, Gurieli, Kula, Badagoni, Chateau Mukhrani, Askaneli, Sarajishvili, MACH & MACH, ANOUKI and Aleksandre Akhalkatsishvili.

EPRC stresses that Wildberries operates as a marketplace. The presence of a particular product on the platform does not automatically mean that the manufacturer or an official brand representative is selling it directly. The product may be listed either by the manufacturer or by an independent reseller.

According to the centre, if an independent retailer sells the product, the brand may restrict those sales by protecting its intellectual property or using contractual mechanisms.

In EPRC’s assessment, Wildberries’ expansion in Georgia is no longer solely a matter of developing online trade. The centre identifies several major risks.

In particular, the report says Wildberries is linked to Russia’s trading and financial system, and its ties to the Kremlin have also been confirmed. The company’s financial arm, Wildberries Bank, has been placed under UK and EU sanctions. According to EPRC, the sanctions are linked to the bank’s role in financially supporting the military and the Russian authorities’ aggressive interests.

The centre also says the Wildberries platform is used to purchase goods needed by the Russian military, including military equipment and dual-use goods. According to EPRC, independent journalistic investigations have also confirmed this.

Against this backdrop, the report’s authors question the effectiveness of controls over the trade and export of such products in Georgia. In their assessment, this increases the risk that sanctioned goods or dual-use items could enter or be re-exported through the country.

EPRC pays particular attention to the development of Wildberries’ logistics capabilities in Georgia. The centre believes that, after a significant part of the company’s warehouse network in Russia was damaged, infrastructure outside Russia has become even more important to Wildberries. Georgia could therefore become part of the company’s regional diversification network.

The report also describes the growing integration of Georgian businesses into the Wildberries system. Products from Georgian brands are already sold on the platform, and Georgian entrepreneurs can join it as direct sellers. EPRC believes this creates both reputational and potential financial risks for companies in the future.

According to the centre, Georgia’s financial sector is also at risk. Wildberries Bank came under UK and EU sanctions in 2026, while 5% of the bank is also owned by the sanctioned Russian bank VTB.

EPRC says that the fact that customers in Georgia pay for purchases on Wildberries using Georgian bank cards means that the local banking sector must comply with the sanctions regime and carry out additional transaction checks. According to the centre, after sanctions were imposed on Wildberries Bank, the National Bank of Georgia shifted responsibility to individual financial institutions, explaining that each bank must assess the risks of violating or circumventing sanctions independently.

In EPRC’s assessment, given these circumstances, the development in Georgia of infrastructure linked to a sanctioned financial institution, a business close to the Kremlin and a platform used to supply the Russian military cannot simply be viewed as foreign investment or the expansion of retail trade.

The centre suggests that if Wildberries continues to expand in Georgia without state oversight or proper customs and financial monitoring, and Georgian companies and banks deepen their cooperation with the platform, the country could become part of an economic and logistics network that helps Russian businesses continue operating amid war and international sanctions.

EPRC believes that such a process could have long-term economic and reputational consequences for Georgia.

EPRC on the risks posed by Wildberries in Georgia

World.title: Georgian Legion commander on former prosecutor general: ‘He is following directives from Russian intelligence services’
World.content:
According to a statement by Mamuka Mamulashvili, commander of the pro-Ukrainian Georgian Legion, former Georgian prosecutor general Otar Partskhaladze, who recently took command of a unit fighting on Russia’s side, is following directives from Russian intelligence services. Mamulashvili also said Partskhaladze’s value as a military figure was zero.

The Georgian Legion is a volunteer formation established in 2014 after Russia invaded eastern Ukraine. In 2016, the Georgian Legion officially joined Ukraine’s 25th Motorised Infantry Battalion. It is now subordinate to the Main Directorate of Intelligence of Ukraine’s Defence Ministry. The unit includes Georgian volunteers as well as fighters of other nationalities. It currently has around 2,000 members. In 2023, Russia’s Interior Ministry added Georgian Legion commander Mamuka Mamulashvili to its wanted list.

According to Mamulashvili, Otar Partskhaladze will try to draw ethnic Georgians living in Russia into his adventure — the war against Ukraine. However, his chances of success are doubtful, as very few Georgians fighting on Russia’s side are seen on the front line, and most of them have already been killed.

Former Georgian prosecutor general Otar Romanov-Partskhaladze, who is fighting on Russia’s side, told Russian pro-Kremlin media that members of the Georgian Legion are “war criminals” and will face prosecution under Russian law. Earlier, on 7 September, it became known that Partskhaladze would lead the international “St George” unit, which was created to take part in the war against Ukraine.

Mamuka Mamulashvili: “Partskhaladze will get a response. He will realise that he made a serious mistake by launching a campaign against the Georgian Legion.

No unit, not even Ukrainian ones, has faced the kind of pressure the Georgian Legion has endured. We are one of the oldest units, even compared with Ukrainian volunteer formations. Russia does not like the fact that so many Georgians are fighting on Ukraine’s side. That is why Russia has been fighting us for more than 12 years, both informationally and physically.

Since they failed to destroy the Georgian Legion physically, they have now tried to create a counterweight by forming another Georgian unit that supposedly will fight on Russia’s side. In reality, this is an attempt to discredit Georgia and bring it under the same sanctions that Russia faces. To do this, they are using people with Georgian surnames who live in Russia and who make all sorts of absurd claims that the Georgian Legion should be tried under Russian law.

In 2022, Russia designated the Georgian Legion as a terrorist organisation. This is hardly surprising, as the Georgian Legion has inflicted enormous damage on the Russian Federation. We can see that their disinformation machine has become much more active. Attempts to kill us physically and attacks have also increased. I have personally been attacked seven times and have survived three attempts to poison me.

Partskhaladze is following directives from Russian intelligence services because his own value as a military figure is zero. I doubt that this man knows which end of a weapon fires. Most likely, he was ordered to finance and create another battalion. He will then try to draw people with Georgian surnames who live in Russia into this adventure. I do not know how successful he will be, because over these 12 years I have encountered very few Georgians on the front line — and those I did encounter were already dead.

The battalion will most likely consist of Russians, with a few Georgian-speaking people who will claim that the unit is mainly made up of Georgians.”

Commander of the Georgian Legion on former prosecutor general

World.title: Mzia Amaglobeli: ‘All it takes to avoid asking the regime for pardon is self-respect’
World.content:
“I don’t need advice to avoid apologising to an aggressor or asking the regime for a pardon. A sense of self-respect is enough,” political prisoner Mzia Amaglobeli writes in response to a statement by Shalva Papuashvili, speaker of the parliament of Georgia. At a briefing on 9 September, Papuashvili called prisoners of conscience “prisoners of Brussels’ shamelessness”.

The publication Batumelebi published Amaglobeli’s letter.

Mzia Amaglobeli: “The briefing in parliament was a display of shamelessness and nothing else. The regime has no morals. They do not even want to take responsibility for the unjust verdict that, in the name of Georgia, sent us to prison and branded us dangerous criminals.

They point the finger at Brussels and European diplomats. Shame on them. I don’t need advice to avoid apologising to an aggressor or asking the regime for a pardon. A sense of self-respect is enough.

If two years in prison is not humiliating enough, it will not be difficult for you to come up with something else if you want to keep me behind bars.

Power and state institutions are in your hands.

As for me, I will wait for international justice. I will wait for the day when the European Court of Human Rights examines the legality of the charges against me and the sentence imposed on me for slapping someone.

And you wait too, Mr Papuashvili. The European Court will examine the fairness and legitimacy of the repressive laws you have adopted, as well as their compliance with the Constitution and democratic processes.”

What Shalva Papuashvili said

On 9 September, commenting on the situation of political prisoners and prisoners of conscience, Shalva Papuashvili said they were “prisoners of Brussels’ shamelessness”. Papuashvili also spoke specifically about convicted journalist Mzia Amaglobeli, claiming that the court had given her the lightest possible sentence.

“Under Georgia’s Criminal Procedure Code, a lesser sentence is possible only through a plea agreement. That is what both the law and practice provide. A plea agreement was offered to her. It required only one thing: for Mzia Amaglobeli to acknowledge that what she had done was a crime and that her conduct had been wrong.

Mzia Amaglobeli is a prisoner of the shamelessness of those ambassadors who sat in court, looked her in the eye and effectively told her: ‘Do not plead guilty. Stay in prison.’ It is also the fault of those who awarded her completely unjustified prizes, including the European Parliament, thereby encouraging her not to admit that attacking a police officer is a crime,” Papuashvili said.

Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the well-known publications Batumelebi and Netgazeti, is the first female journalist in Georgia to become a prisoner of conscience.

Authorities arrested her in January 2025 in the city of Batumi during a protest after she slapped the head of the local police, Irakli Dgebuadze. The incident followed a confrontation between protesters and police, which the officers had provoked.

On 6 August 2025, Batumi City Court sentenced Mzia Amaglobeli to two years in prison. The court rejected her lawyer’s request to change her pre-trial measure.

Mzia Amaglobeli responds to the speaker of parliament

World.title: Standard Chartered arranges almost $115M loan for Uzbekistan’s Asakabank
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 14. Standard Chartered has arranged a 770 million yuan (about $114.8 million) syndicated loan for Uzbekistan’s Asakabank, supporting clients importing goods from China and facilitating growing trade and investment flows between Uzbekistan and China.

This was reflected in the press release by Standard Chartered.

The transaction marks Asakabank’s first yuan-denominated syndicated loan and is Standard Chartered’s third transaction with the Uzbekistan-based bank. Standard Chartered acted as the Sole Mandated Lead Arranger, with the proceeds to be used by Asakabank to finance clients involved in imports of Chinese goods.

The deal was announced in London on September 11 and comes as the yuan plays a growing role in Uzbekistan-China trade and cross-border financing. The transaction is also part of a broader cooperation between the two banks focused on yuan-denominated business and opportunities along the China-Central Asia trade corridor.

"Trade ties between Uzbekistan and China continue to strengthen, driving growing demand for RMB-denominated financing solutions," said Amin Semmari, CFO of Asakabank. "This transaction reflects the strong commitment of both Asakabank and Standard Chartered to supporting these flows and facilitating cross-border business."

As part of the expanded cooperation, Standard Chartered and Asakabank recently signed a memorandum of understanding at the 11th Belt and Road Summit in Hong Kong, held September 9-10. The agreement covers cooperation in yuan-related business and trade-corridor opportunities and complements Asakabank’s plans to open a yuan account with Standard Chartered in Hong Kong.

Lucy Rahal, executive director for Public Sector Coverage at Standard Chartered, said the transaction reflects the "growing role of RMB in facilitating trade and investment flows between Uzbekistan and China." She added that demand for yuan-based solutions is increasing alongside commercial links between China and Central Asia.

Trend’s calculations show that the 770 million yuan facility is equivalent to roughly $108 million at current exchange rates. More importantly, the financing is specifically linked to imports from China, making it a direct mechanism for supporting bilateral trade rather than general-purpose bank funding.

In Trend’s assessment, the transaction highlights the growing use of the yuan in Uzbekistan’s external economic relations. For Uzbek banks and companies trading with China, yuan-denominated financing can reduce the need to convert between multiple currencies and provide a closer match between financing and underlying trade flows.

Furthermore, Trend’s analysis shows that the deal also has significance beyond Asakabank’s immediate financing needs. The planned yuan account in Hong Kong and the new MoU could create a broader financial channel connecting Uzbek companies with Chinese suppliers and investors. As China remains one of Uzbekistan’s largest trading partners, the expansion of RMB financing infrastructure could support deeper bilateral trade while gradually diversifying the currencies used in Uzbekistan’s international transactions.

World.title: China becomes Georgia's top FDI source in Q2 2026
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 14. China became the largest source of foreign direct investment in Georgia in the second quarter of 2026, accounting for the largest share among investor countries.

"China reaching USD 219.5 million in Q2 2026 (46.8%) was the major foreign direct investor country," National Statistics Office of Georgia (Geostat) said. The United Kingdom ranked second with $123.5 million, or 26.3%, followed by the United Arab Emirates with $47.7 million, or 10.2%.

Trend's calculations show that Chinese investment in Georgia reached $219.5 million in the second quarter of 2026, compared with $16.4 million in the first quarter of the year. On a year-on-year basis, Chinese investment flows changed from a net outflow of $21.6 million in the second quarter of 2025 to a net inflow in the same period of 2026.

The difference between the two periods amounted to approximately $241.1 million, according to Trend calculations.

Trend's calculations also reveal that China's net investment in Georgia amounted to $8.2 million for full-year 2024 and included a net outflow of $44.3 million in 2025. The second quarter of 2026 therefore represented the highest quarterly level of Chinese investment recorded in Geostat's available data series starting from 2024.

China accounted for 46.8% of Georgia's total FDI inflows in the second quarter, ahead of the United Kingdom and the United Arab Emirates. The figures highlight changes in the geographic composition of foreign investment flows during the period.

For reference, Geostat's investor-country breakdown reflects the immediate source of investment flows and does not necessarily indicate the ultimate beneficial ownership of the underlying capital.

World.title: Türkiye’s producer inflation tops consumer prices in August 2026
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 14. Türkiye's producer price growth in August 2026 was estimated to have exceeded consumer price inflation during the month.

The estimate is derived from TURKSTAT's report on real investment returns, cross-referenced with the agency's separately published Consumer Price Index (CPI) data. The calculations suggest that domestic producer prices increased by approximately 2.55-2.6% month-on-month in August, compared with officially reported CPI inflation of 1.84%.

"Gold (ingot) yielded the highest monthly real profit rate," TURKSTAT said in the report, noting that the same financial instruments showed different real return figures depending on whether returns were adjusted using the domestic producer price index (D-PPI) or CPI. For example, gold's monthly real return was 7.17% based on D-PPI and 7.93% based on CPI, while deposit interest generated 0.33% by D-PPI and 1.05% by CPI.

Since each instrument's nominal return in lira terms remains unchanged regardless of the inflation measure applied, Trend's calculations use the difference between the two real-return figures to estimate the implied monthly D-PPI inflation rate. Using gold, deposit interest, the U.S. dollar and the euro as four separate reference points, and TÜİK's officially reported CPI monthly inflation rate of 1.84% for August, the calculations indicate an implied D-PPI increase of approximately 2.55-2.6% during the month.

Trend's calculations indicate that the estimated D-PPI rate was around 0.7-0.8 percentage points above CPI inflation for August.

The calculations also show that, if a similar difference between producer and consumer prices continued over a full year, the implied annual D-PPI rate would be approximately 9-10 percentage points above Türkiye's annual CPI inflation rate of 31.51% recorded in August. However, a single month's comparison does not necessarily represent a longer-term trend.

For reference, TÜİK (TURKSTAT) publishes official Domestic Producer Price Index figures separately from CPI data. The calculation above represents an independent Trend estimate based on TÜİK's investment returns report and should not be considered an official D-PPI figure.

World.title: Crows to report skipper's 'disgusting' targeting by troll to police
World.content:
The Adelaide Crows have condemned the "disgusting and disturbing" trolling of captain Jordan Dawson, saying the incident would be reported to SA Police.

Dawson was the target of a social media message containing a self-harm reference, following his side's defeat in Saturday night's semi-final against Brisbane.

The club said fellow player Callum Ah Chee was also subjected to abuse, understood to be racist in nature, and that the matter would be raised with the league.

"We will provide Jordan and Cal with the appropriate support, as is the case when any of our people are subjected to online attacks and abuse," Crows CEO Tim Silvers said in a statement.

"We will also be reporting these latest incidents to SA Police and the AFL's integrity unit.

" Unfortunately, this disgusting and disturbing behaviour is becoming more common. "

If you or anyone you know needs help: Lifeline on 13 11 14

Suicide Call Back Service on 1300 659 467

Beyond Blue on 1300 224 636

Headspace on 1800 650 890

ReachOut at au.reachout.com

Dawson shared a picture of the message he received on his Instagram account.

At the recent All-Australian awards, Dawson, who was named vice-captain, used his speech to speak about mental health — something especially important to him in the wake of his brother's death earlier this year.

"The mental health space is something new to me, but something I want to learn more about," he said in August.

"I want everyone to know who is struggling with their mental health that you are definitely loved and that the world is a better place with you in it. You are enough. We all love you, you have friends and family around you."

The heartfelt speech won Dawson plaudits from the mental health sector.

In the wake of the weekend's trolling incidents, the club's CEO urged an end to such abuse throughout society.

"It's simply not good enough and it has to stop," Silvers said.

"There's no place for it."

World.title: Working holiday visa pause leaves farms short as harvest season looms
World.content:
Farmers are worried there won't be enough workers to pack fruit and harvest crops after recent changes to visa processing.

The federal government has paused working holiday visa applications coming from 24 of 29 countries, amid a slowdown in processing skilled visa applications.

These two quiet changes, made to curb net overseas migration, have raised fears in the agricultural sector.

Operating heavy machinery is a key part of grain and crop harvest across Australia. (ABC Mid West and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Victorian contractor Matt Bourke had planned to hire 30 staff members ahead of the grain harvest in just a few weeks, with many coming from overseas on both visas.

"Not one working holiday visa has been approved yet," Mr Bourke said.

"There are probably 60 or 70 per cent who have worked with me in the past. I've never had this issue before."

Working holiday visas

The National Farmers Federation estimates that overseas workers make up about half of Australia's peak harvest casual workforce.

Agricultural workers predominantly use two types of visas to apply for seasonal harvest jobs: the work and holiday visa for backpackers, and the skilled visa for skilled workers like heavy machinery operators.

The Australian government's Department of Home Affairs website shows application cap indicators for the Working Holiday Maker (WHM) program. (Image: ABC News)

In a statement, a Department of Home Affairs spokesperson said the number of working holiday-makers (WHMs) in Australia was at a historically high level.

As a result, "applications may take longer than usual and may be finalised outside the published processing time frames."

As of June 30, 2025, there were 206,187 working holiday-makers in Australia.

But despite the high figures, farmers across the country say they're struggling to recruit pickers.

In the Northern Territory, Berry Creek mango packing manager Phillipa Johnson said she was still looking for workers just a few weeks out from harvest.

Because it's a short two-to three-month season, many of her workers come from overseas on a working holiday visa.

Farm workers from overseas are crucial during the harvest season. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"We're getting some applications from overseas, but their visas haven't been approved," Ms Johnson said.

" We're going to have to go back to the drawing board. "

Skilled workers needed

In July, the Department of Home Affairs issued a new ministerial direction prioritising skilled visa processing for defence and law enforcement workers, followed by construction, healthcare, teaching, and people already in Australia.

While many farmers use working holiday visa applicants on their farm for a seasonal workforce, other farmers need specific skills they can't find in Australia.

Mr Bourke said professionally trained skilled workers had been vital to his operation over the harvest period.

"The guys we're bringing into the country are currently running those machines at home, in their own country, on their own farms or on farms around them," he said.

" They are here for good reason because the availability of this labour is not here in Australia. "

Earlier this year, Tasmanian dairy farmer Michele Lawrence gave evidence to the parliamentary inquiry into the value of skilled migration in Australia.

Meander Valley dairy farmer, Michele Lawrence. (Supplied: Michele Lawrence)

The chair of People and Communities Policy Advisory at Australian Dairy Farmers spoke about the essential role overseas workers on both visas play in sustaining dairy production and food security.

"We need these people; the working holiday-makers will stay on our farm for as long as they can on their visas," she said.

Ms Lawrence employs several working holiday makers on her Meander Valley property, and said she's still waiting for an ag science engineer to arrive from Argentina.

"Within that we've got a skill set of science degrees, nursing degrees and electrical trades," she said.

"They're really strategic people on our farm."

No clarity on delays

A Department of Home Affairs spokesperson said it was taking a range of measures to put pressure on overseas migration, better manage demand for the WHM program, and support a fairer allocation of visas.

"These actions will be rolled out progressively to ensure the long-term sustainability of the WHM program while continuing to support the tourism economy and workforce needs, particularly in regional Australia," they said.

"Visa applicants are advised not to arrange travel to Australia until they have been notified in writing of the grant of their visa."

World.title: Australia's 'incognito' nuclear reactor marks 20 years of innovation
World.content:
Behind the dense bushland and barbed wire that surround the Open Pool Australian Lightwater (OPAL) nuclear reactor is a human story that affects every Australian.

The reactor, located at the Australian Nuclear Science and Technology Organisation (ANSTO) site on the outskirts of Sydney, is the only one in the country and is used every day to produce nuclear medicine and to do experiments.

ANSTO CEO Shaun Jenkinson once had a stranger thank him personally for prolonging the life of the man's father.

"There have been tens of millions of doses of nuclear medicine that have been produced here," he said.

"In nuclear medicine, what they're doing is diagnosing, staging and treating diseases like cancer.

"Our clinicians require isotopes to do that, and those isotopes are made at ANSTO."

Shaun Jenkinson says it is rare for a nuclear reactor to also process the finished nuclear medicine product on site. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

He said he likes to remember that the complex nuclear science developed at ANSTO becomes an essential medicine product that helps families.

"There's probably about five or six reactors globally that are able to do the radiation like we do here, but in addition to the radiation, we also do the processing on site and then from there we send the finished goods to the hospital," he said.

"There's probably only one other place globally that does all three of those components in one place, so ANSTO is almost unique."

Silicon ingots are treated in the nuclear reactor and sent back to companies to produce electronic products. (Supplied: ANSTO)

Creating electronics that cannot afford to fail

The OPAL reactor marks 20 years in operation this year.

Alongside producing nuclear medicine, the reactor also treats silicon that ends up in high-powered objects like fast trains, electric vehicles, air conditioning systems, hospital equipment and power grids.

Nuclear silicon treatment at ANSTO provides a deeper, more comprehensive result, making it ideal for high-voltage power systems like electric trains and power grids.

ANSTO services more than half the global market for this higher-grade irradiated silicon.

OPAL is a 20-megawatt reactor that uses low-enriched uranium-235 fuel. (Supplied: ANSTO)

"We do this highly reliable product that affects people's lives every day, but you probably never know it's there," Mr Jenkinson said.

"But Lucas Heights and ANSTO capture 60 per cent of the global market."

Pure cylinders of silicon are lowered into the OPAL reactor and irradiated to convert some of the silicon atoms to phosphorus.

"Those silicon crystals are then processed, and they end up in devices that affect our everyday life," Mr Jenkinson said.

"All the sort of equipment that you need to operate when you need it — it must be reliable."

Thousands of school students and members of the public tour the ANSTO facilities every year. (Supplied: ANSTO)

Nuclear research to help train tracks and phone batteries

Next door to the OPAL reactor sits the Australian Centre for Neutron Scattering.

Neutrons are sent from the nuclear reactor next door and used to study materials and liquids that other methods cannot study.

"We've been able to look at the crystal structure and how it changes in the charge and discharge of batteries," senior instrument scientist Kirrily Rule said.

"The results that came out of ANSTO showed that once a rechargeable battery was charged beyond around 90%, the crystal structure changed significantly and caused a lot of strain, and this is one of the reasons why battery materials lose their lifetime.

Kirrily Rule works in the research section of OPAL at the Australian Centre for Neutron Scattering. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

" So I guess one of the outcomes of this work is don't overcharge your phone or leave it on charge overnight. "

Professor Rule said they worked in partnership with companies developing new battery technology, as well as government organisations like Sydney Trains.

"We have an engineering beam line we use for industrial purposes," she said.

"We have a relationship with Sydney Trains, and we look at how their rails change their structure or positions, particularly if we have a cold frost or hot day.

"We bring parts of Sydney's rail here, have a look at them and advise better ways to maintain the rail network so people can get to work in the morning."

OPAL reactor operator Nathan Markovski calls himself an ANSTO "lifer" after starting there as an apprentice. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

Making a 'violent form of physics' elegant

Nathan Markovski started as an apprentice fitter machinist at ANSTO in 2012 and is now one of the OPAL reactor's operators.

He said people did not realise the significance of the science happening on site.

"It works under the radar, and you almost feel quite stealthy in your job because a lot of people don't know where the nuclear medicine comes from, so it's quite incognito working that way," he said.

"We're the only place in Australia that sustains nuclear fission and it's a violent form of physics but we've got it down to a subtle, elegant system.

"People drive past and see the bushes and don't think much of it, but there's a lot going on here physics-wise that's really quite amazing."

World.title: Alexander Zverev wins US Open without realising it
World.content:
Alexander Zverev has won his second grand slam title of 2026, beating American Ben Shelton in four sets to claim the US Open in New York.

Zverev, who won his first major crown at this year's French Open, wrapped up the 6-3, 7-6(7/2), 5-7, 6-2 victory over Shelton in three hours and 33 minutes but he did not even realise he had won in the moment.

After banging down another unreturnable serve at 40-15 in the eighth game of the fourth and final set, the German simply turned to prepare to return, before he realised what had happened when he looked up at the big screen.

When it eventually clicked for the 29-year-old, he said "I've won?" with a smile, rushing to the net to commiserate with first-time finalist Shelton before the celebrations began.

"We went 30 years without winning a grand slam title and now we've won two in the span of three months," Zverev said.

Zverev said he would "bet all [his] money" that 23-year-old Shelton would lift the trophy one day, but it was not to be this day.

Both teams have strong family connections in their coaches' box, with Shelton coached by father Bryan, and his mother and sister also among his supporters in the stands.

Ben Shelton had the crowd on his side at his first grand slam final. (Getty Images: Simon Bruty/USTA)

"It's exactly what my family is and that's why I'm so happy to see you guys in these kinds of finals," Zverev said.

As he was looking around Shelton's supporters, Zverev spied US football star Trinity Rodman, Shelton's girlfriend who rushed from her Washington Spirit's 3-0 loss to Boston in DC to see the end of the match.

Zverev described her as Shelton's "lucky charm", to which she replied: "Clearly not."

The newly minted world number two also took time to thank former Australian Open director Craig Tiley after his first US Open as United States Tennis Association boss.

"He decided to move to New York, which we as players were not very happy about because he made the Australian Open the best tournament in the world," he said.

"But from now on I think the US Open will probably be the best tournament in the world since you're here. Thank you for moving here, thank you for being here, [but] move back to Australia for like three months and come back at the end of January, that would be great."

World.title: Australia's most expensive bull could earn $1m from semen sales
World.content:
You might expect a prize bull to be in a lush paddock surrounded by cows, but Australia's most expensive bull will be spreading his seed another way.

Angus bull Millah Murrah Wyatt W50 sold for a record beef price of $420,000 earlier this month and work now begins to see him bring in more than $1 million for his new owners.

That will be through semen sales, with interest flowing from cattle producers across Australia and the world.

"Wyatt certainly created a few headlines, and he's certainly had us in a spin for the last week," Fletch Kelly, the man tasked with selling the semen straws, said.

Mr Kelly is the beef product manager with ABS Australia, an artificial insemination (AI) company that manages the marketing of genetic products, like bull semen, around the world.

" He's a phenomenal bull, he offers the industry so much. "

Fletch Kelly says thousands of cows could be carrying Millah Murrah Wyatt's calves each year once his semen hits the market. (Supplied: ABS Australia)

Mr Kelly described Wyatt as "the ultimate all-rounder", who would "appeal to a pretty wide range of the market".

He assesses a bull through what he calls the "golden triangle" of bloodline, the traits it is likely to pass on to its calves and its physical build.

"Some bulls can make well over $1 million in semen sales in their lifetime.

"Millah Murrah Paratrooper is a bull that we have that's been really popular for the last six or seven years, and his return has been certainly in the seven figures so there's no reason why a bull like Wyatt can't get into that territory, provided he collects well."

How is it all collected?

Wyatt will head to Total Livestock Genetics at Camperdown in Victoria, where the semen will be collected, tested and stored.

Mr Kelly said the facility staff were well-trained in collecting the product.

"The semen is collected having the bull literally jump, so the bull mounts a teaser and then they collect semen from there.

"From that point, it goes through a very stringent process of quality control."

The straws are stored in liquid nitrogen until needed. (Supplied: ABS Australia)

If Wyatt remains "healthy, happy and relaxed", Mr Kelly said he could produce enough straws for thousands of cows to carry his offspring each year.

But it will be some time before Wyatt is in the paddock, covering cows the old-fashioned way.

"We'll need to leave him in collection to collect as many straws as we possibly can of semen, and to build up that inventory.

" Once we have a big inventory, we can then send the bull out in three or four years' time back to one of the purchasers' properties where he can naturally serve cows. "

Strong returns for owners, but genetic gains for entire beef industry

Despite Wyatt's eye-watering price tag, Mr Kelly says "the beauty of AI" is that anyone can now tap into his genetics.

"Whether it's in the commercial space or in the seed stock space … if they deem that the bull is a good fit for their herd, they can purchase semen and through artificial insemination, they can get those genetics," he said.

For a fee, of course.

The semen is expected to initially sell for about $300 per dose, with indicative volume pricing of $300 per dose for 20 units, and $250 for 50 units.

Fletch Kelly says the whole industry will benefit from the bull's genetics being widely available. (Supplied)

It will need to be tested and meet licensing requirements before being exported overseas, but Mr Kelly says there have already been significant inquiries in Australia and abroad for the record-breaking bull.

" So, fingers crossed he produces some good straws soon and we can share the love and get him out there into the domestic market soon. "

He said a bull of this calibre being globally available, "certainly puts us on the map".

"Not that Australia needs any introduction on the world stage.

"Across all breeds, not just Angus, but Herefords, Charolais, wagyu as well, Australia is really seen as a genetic powerhouse across the world.

" The more genetic gain we can make as a nation across our whole beef herd is really important to continue to lift the meat standards, which Australia has been so well known for so long. "

World.title: Fugitive property developer Jean Nassif to front NSW ICAC from Lebanon
World.content:
Fugitive property developer Jean Nassif is expected to front the NSW corruption watchdog this afternoon, after cancelling an earlier scheduled appearance on medical grounds.

Mr Nassif had initially declined to assist the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC), but was added to the schedule earlier this month to appear via video link from Lebanon.

The hearing was postponed when Mr Nassif provided a medical certificate excusing him from giving evidence in the inquiry.

As per Monday's witness list, he is expected to appear later today.

NSW Police issued an international arrest warrant for Mr Nassif in June 2023. (ABC News)

It comes as ICAC examines whether political donations linked to Mr Nassif were used to build influence within the NSW Liberal Party and advance his development interests.

Under NSW law, property developers and anyone donating on their behalf are prohibited from making political donations.

The key figures in ICAC investigation Eight weeks of public hearings by the ICAC that could change the NSW Liberal Party forever begin on Monday.

Mr Nassif has not returned to Australia since fleeing to Lebanon in December 2022, the month a previous parliamentary inquiry began.

NSW Police issued an international arrest warrant for Mr Nassif over alleged fraud offences in June 2023.

His construction and property development company, Toplace, then collapsed into administration the following month, owing creditors a reported $2 billion and leaving thousands of apartment owners facing repairs to properties affected by serious defects.

In a letter tabled at a parliamentary inquiry in 2023, Mr Nassif described allegations against him as "not credible".

World.title: Whyalla's imminent blast furnace call could hit hundreds of jobs
World.content:
An announcement is expected as soon as today that will potentially impact hundreds of jobs at the Whyalla steelworks, the ABC understands.

The site's aging blast furnace has been offline since April, but the ABC understands that a decision on its future is imminent.

There is the potential for administrators KordaMentha, along with the state government, to tell workers at the blast furnace to stop trying to bring it back online.

That would potentially result in the loss of hundreds of jobs at the blast furnace, as well as contract jobs and indirect jobs.

The steelworks has been in administration for 19 months, but the current situation is not expected to impact the sale process.

Speaking publicly on Sunday, SA Premier Peter Malinauskas indicated the blast furnace was approaching a crunch point.

"The blast furnace's days have always been numbered, and it's looking as though that that number is becoming increasingly small, to say the least," he said.

"The blast furnace is in an exceptionally precarious position and that problem has only been intensifying.

"This is a challenge we always knew was coming and … I think that's becoming increasingly well-known in Whyalla and to those that are working on the project."

The Whyalla steelworks says it is the only Australian manufacturer of steel long products. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

Two bidders, Jindal Steel and M Resources, remain in the running to buy the steelworks, but BlueScope Steel retains its right of last offer.

Mr Malinauskas said a sale was still likely in the next three-and-a-half months.

"We intend to finalise the sale and the transaction by the end of this year. We're on track to do that. We're now sitting in September so hopefully we're not too far away from announcing who that new owner is," he said.

"What that will set up is a massive injection of capital into Whyalla to set it up for a new long-term future."

The state government, unions and steelworks administrator KordaMentha have all been preparing for a scenario where the furnace permanently shuts before the steelworks transitions to a direct-reduced iron plant and electric arc furnace.

"The big picture here, of course, is the transaction that will see a new owner come in and put new technology and capital into the steelworks, and in that regard we remain very optimistic about the long-term future of Whyalla," the premier said.

The remaining two bidders were announced in May.

Jindal Steel is an Indian company and M Resources is an Australian-owned enterprise.

World.title: Citizen scientist drone pilots to monitor coastal erosion
World.content:
As regional communities try to comprehend the challenge they face from coastal erosion, researchers are recruiting citizen scientists to fly drones and measure changes.

The District Council of Robe has called for expressions of interest for a project working with Flinders University, with low-cost drones and training to be supplied to participants.

Flinders University associate professor Graziela Miot da Silva is a coastal geomorphologist and oceanographer.

She said the work was a new initiative of the National Collaborative Research Infrastructure Strategy (NCRIS) aimed at increasing the observation of coastal erosion around Australia.

"We're trying to get community members involved so we can cover more coastline, more area, and also a greater number of storm events," she said.

"We are asking people to go once a month during the two years, and also keep an eye on storm events.

"Then they just go back to the beach after the storm events to measure the change."

Nearly 10m of cliffs near the Robe lighthouse collapsed in July 2025. (Supplied: District Council of Robe/Chris Matthews Photography)

An ever-changing coastline

District Council of Robe CEO Nat Traeger said there was strong community interest in understanding how erosion is progressing.

"Our coastline is vulnerable, it's eroding fast," she said.

"We need as much data and help as we can get to help inform future grants and adaptation pathways."

Nat Traeger says the community is concerned about erosion. (ABC South East SA: Josh Brine)

Ms Traeger said while the council had a drone and did its own imagery, a wider and more consistent project to monitor the coast was useful.

"To have the opportunity to have a scheduled, structured process that includes community volunteers will bolster our resources," she said.

"We had a cliff collapse last year, and the obelisk is a strong point of interest.

"Fox and Hoopers [beaches] have properties near them, and particularly at Hoopers we do have properties at risk there."

Graziela Miot da Silva says the data will help guide decision-makers. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

While members of the public would gather the information, experts would analyse it and calculate the changes to the shoreline and sand volume.

"That kind of information we're hoping can inform councils and coastal managers on the best strategies to manage the coast," Dr Miot da Silva said.

"In some locations, the best strategy could be sand replenishment. Other strategies could be retreat or adapt.

"With that kind of baseline information, we're hoping to give the decision-makers the information they need to make the best decisions for their councils."

She said anyone interested could be involved, and that the research team would inform participants when storm events were forecast.

Robe's iconic obelisk is among the parts of the town at risk. (ABC South East SA: Josh Brine)

Banding together for nature

Local woman Tina van Nispen was among those keen to be involved with the project.

She said as a nature lover she had noticed how erosion had impacted the movement of sand over the years.

"You can only hope we can protect and love the environment that we're in so we can all flourish together," she said.

Tina van Nispen is among those interested in piloting a drone. (Supplied: Tina van Nispen)

Having never used a drone before, Ms van Nispen said she was keen to see from above how erosion was shaping the coastline.

"I've walked a lot of the beaches, but that's the only way I notice it," she said.

"That's why I've jumped at this chance."

She hoped the visual data from the drones could also be used to monitor things like seagrass movement.

"There are so many applications with a drone," she said.

"We could just be scratching the surface."

Researchers have used drones to monitor erosion in various parts of the country. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

Scope for expansion

Dr Miot da Silva said other parts of the South Australian coastline would also be monitored.

"If there's any other councils interested in the project, we are happy to hear from everybody," she said.

"We chose Robe and a few other councils that already have some coastal data in place and other projects that we have already been doing with them, but it's not exclusive."

Erosion at Robe is occurring faster than previously anticipated. (Supplied: Patrick Hesp)

If the pilot project is successful, Dr Miot da Silva said it could be rolled out more widely.

"In Victoria they have already done a study similar to what we are trying to apply to Robe, which is using citizen science to give us information about storm impacts and coastal erosion," she said.

"We're trying to apply this model that has already been tested and been successful to sites in South Australia.

" If we see the same sort of success they had in Victoria, we're hoping to then expand to other sites as well. "

World.title: Zverev no longer ‘third guy’ of men’s tennis after winning US Open final to claim second slam title
World.content:
SportTennisUS Open Zverev no longer ‘third guy’ of men’s tennis after winning US Open final to claim second slam title Marc McGowan September 14, 2026 — 8:39am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Tennis’ so-called “third guy” has taken a big step towards creating a modern Big Three with his maiden US Open title, before paying tribute to his mother’s support after being diagnosed with type-one diabetes as a child. Alexander Zverev started the year known, and at-times derided, as the best player never to win a grand slam trophy, but ends it as the only man to capture two majors in 2026 after triumphing in New York. Alexander Zverev won his second grand slam singles title at the US Open. AP Photo/Adam Hunger The giant German, contesting his third consecutive slam final, also ensured the United States’ major title drought would extend into a 24th year while taking down ballistic-serving American Ben Shelton 6-3, 7-6 (7-2), 5-7, 6-2 on Monday (AEST). Zverev’s brother Mischa and father Alexander snr are part of his team, but he paid special thanks to his mother – ex-player Irina – for her role in him achieving his tennis dreams.



“We went 30 years without winning a grand slam title, and now we won two in a span of three months,” Zverev said. “I think God has seen how hard we worked, how much we suffered, how much pain we went through, and I think 2026 is the outcome of all the years that happened before. So, thank you guys. You guys are absolutely amazing, and I couldn’t be here without you. Loading “I want to thank one more person who’s never actually watching my matches, but is the most important person in my tennis life, and in my life in general. “When your four-year-old son gets diagnosed with diabetes, and doctors in the office tell you that life and sports will be very limited for that child, it takes a very strong mother to walk out of those offices and to say, ‘My son will be whatever he wants to be. If he wants to be a tennis player, he’ll be a tennis player. If he wants to do something else, he’ll do something else, but this illness will not define us’.



“My mother is the most important and strongest person I know. It takes an unbelievably strong woman to do what she did.” The four-set victory adds to Zverev’s Roland-Garros breakthrough in June that shed his bridesmaid status and means he matches US Open women’s champion Elena Rybakina with two grand slam championships this year. Ben Shelton’s career-best major run ended in a US Open final defeat. Getty Images This result looked unrealistic as he laboured through consecutive five-setters across almost nine-and-a-half hours, but he dropped just one more set in his last five matches. Zverev started his career pitting wits with tennis titans Novak Djokovic, Roger Federer and Rafael Nadal before Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz arrived to torture him once more – with Djokovic still hanging around, too.



Sinner and Alcaraz missed three majors between them because of injury this season, which paved the way for Zverev’s career year, but at least one of them contested both of the grand slam titles he won. Related Article US Open Why this week could bring an end to the great American tennis chase Italy’s world No.1 Sinner suffered a befuddling second-round loss from two sets and 5-1 up in Paris, while Alcaraz’s first tournament since April after recovering from a wrist setback ended in the US Open quarter-finals to Shelton. Shelton was trying to be the first American since Andy Roddick in 2003 to win a major, but he played catch up from the moment he crashed a second serve into the net in the opening game to gift Zverev an instant break. He had never beaten Alcaraz before this fortnight and winning his maiden grand slam final depended on him upsetting Zverev – the top seed in Sinner’s absence – for the first time in their sixth meeting.



However, Zverev has made a habit of chewing up and spitting out left-handers, winning 44 of his past 45 clashes with southpaws entering his latest battle with Shelton, who won an all-American clash with Frances Tiafoe to advance to the last day of the event. No longer burdened by the gaping hole in his otherwise bulging resume, Zverev presented an even tougher challenge to Shelton on this stage despite emphatically having the crowd on his side. Zverev was mostly outstanding, except for a dip late in the third set. AP Photo/Adam Hunger Shelton settled after his erroneous opening, but could not penetrate his rival’s own service game, which became a trend. Zverev won more than 90 per cent of points on his first serve, which the 198-centimetre German traditionally lands more than any player on the planet – and it was more of the same in the final. Serving to stay in the opening set, Shelton repeated his mistake from the first game of the match when he double-faulted into the net on break point to go down a set.



The second set was a closer affair, giving the American more opportunities to electrify the home fans, which included everyone from Roddick and Jimmy Connors to Hollywood actors Brad Pitt, Amy Schumer, Rami Malek, Pierce Brosnan, Chris Pine and Brazilian football superstar Ronaldo. Shelton pricked his ear several times to urge the crowd to rally behind him, but they needed little prompting to do so. Pierce Brosnan (right) was among the celebrities in the crowd. AP Photo/Kirsty Wigglesworth He double-faulted to go down another break point in the third game of the second set, but bellowed “Yes!” as Zverev’s subsequent backhand return thudded into the net. Shelton stretched Zverev to deuce at 3-3, but the world No.2 kept coming up with the answers to that point.



They traded blows until a tiebreak was required. Zverev produced an outstanding 10 minutes to blow Shelton away, starting with a spectacular down-the-line forehand pass winner on his way to a 5-0 lead that comfortably converted to a two-set lead. Shelton was up against it from that deficit, but Zverev began showing signs of frailty as the third set progressed. Zverev is a two-time grand slam champion. Getty Images The German followed two loose points from 30-0 in the sixth game by narrowly missing an inside-out forehand where he didn’t need to be so perfect as he finally offered Shelton a break point. Zverev dispatched that one with a thunderous backhand, but imploded at 5-6. He shanked a forehand wide to fall in a 0-40 hole, then put a volley shockingly wide two points later to drop the third set.



Shelton never lost his swagger throughout the entire contest, theatrically responding to Zverev’s dip with raised eyebrows before again pricking his ear to energise the crowd. Related Article US Open The best rivalry in women’s tennis: Celebs in the stands as new world No.1 thwarts Sabalenka His momentum did not last long. Shelton immediately found himself in trouble on serve in the fourth set, staving off one break point before tugging a backhand crosscourt pass wide to hand Zverev the advantage. Trying to break Zverev is one of the sport’s greatest challenges, particularly with the finish line in sight.



The door was slightly ajar at 30-all as Zverev served for a 3-1 lead, then received a time violation, but he again held firm to clear that hurdle then broke Shelton again for 5-2 to as good as seal the win. Zverev served the match out with ease, but did not realise for several moments he had clinched the title before breaking into a huge smile and later embracing his team then Shelton’s father and coach Bryan.
