World.title: Australia exposed to growing risk from deepening China-Russia-North Korea alliance
World.content:
Exclusive WorldEuropeRussia-Ukraine war Australia exposed to growing risk from deepening China-Russia-North Korea alliance September 14, 2026 — 8:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australia is exposed to a deepening military alliance between Russia, China and North Korea as the three partners work together in the war on Ukraine, prompting experts to warn of the risks to security in Asia. Former CIA director David Petraeus warned that China was proving its capacity to design new weaponry and manufacture it in large volumes for Russia, heightening concerns for all Western nations. Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin tour an exhibition in Beijing in May. Alexander Kazakov/Pool Sputnik Kremlin via AP Political leaders and experts also pointed to the Kremlin’s reliance on North Korea as a rising threat to Asia, given that the rogue state is supplying Russia with scores of missiles in an expanding weapons trade.



General Petraeus, who served 37 years in the US Army, told this masthead that China was innovating rapidly to supply Russia and apply lessons from the war in Ukraine. “We should be very concerned that China is learning assiduously from what Russia and Ukraine are doing,” he said on the sidelines of a security conference in Kyiv. David Petraeus was America's most high-profile general for much of the past 20 years. AP “It’s providing the bulk of the components for the Russian military-industrial complex, and it is a leader in the world in robotic systems and drones and so forth. “And it has an ability to do something that is hugely important in this war, which is not just to innovate but to scale the production of those weapons.”



Related Article Russia-Ukraine war The new terror stalking Kyiv day and night Petraeus, an influential voice in defence investment as chairman of the KKR Global Institute, forecast a total shift in military doctrine due to the changing nature of war in Ukraine and argued that China was a key force in the conflict. As the “manufacturing capital” of the world, he said, China was gaining expertise in the mass production of drones and other weapons. “We should obviously be very keenly aware of that,” he said. “We should be very keenly aware of what is being developed here on this battlefield because it is the future of war, and it’s changing quite rapidly. “And that should lead us, all Western countries, to develop a new concept of war that can drive, urgently, revolutionary institutional change.”



One of the most influential investors in new drones, former Google chairman Eric Schmidt, said he saw the impact of Russia’s partnership with North Korea during a previous visit to the Ukrainian capital. “The North Koreans are giving the Russians the KN-25, which is a major ballistic missile – it’s an enormous size and does enormous damage,” he told this masthead. North Korean leader Kim Jong-un inspects a Hwasong-17 intercontinental ballistic missile. AP “I was here when it was shot at Kyiv. I know it to be true. That’s very, very worrisome. So the connection between China and North Korea and Russia is a great concern.” One of Schmidt’s companies, Perennial Autonomy, develops the Merops interceptor drones used by regiments across Ukraine and sold at low cost, in a sign of his support for the country.



Related Article Russia-Ukraine war Four years on, Ukraine is under more pressure than ever. So is Russia The defence and investment chiefs were at the Yalta European Strategies Conference in Kyiv in recent days, where most discussions focused on the threat to Europe posed by Russian President Vladimir Putin. Rising risks to Asia region The risks for the Indo-Pacific, however, are rising as Russia relies on China and North Korea. Petraeus estimated that Russia would build 10 million drones this year, while Ukraine was seeking to increase its production from 8 to 10 million.



North Korea has supplied an estimated 10,000 troops to Russia, as well as large volumes of artillery ammunition and more than 100 missiles. Former Swedish prime minister Carl Bildt said the concern should not only be about what Russia received, particularly in Asia. ‘It may seem like Ukraine’s a long way away from Australia, but the North Koreans don’t think so’ Emily Thornberry, chair of UK Foreign Affairs Committee “The worrying thing is, of course, that the Russians are delivering things back,” he told this masthead. Bildt noted speculation that North Korea wanted to build a nuclear submarine and needed Russian help to develop the propulsion systems.



Dame Emily Thornberry, the chair of the foreign affairs committee in the UK parliament, said Asia would see the impact of the ties between Russia and its partners. “It may seem like Ukraine’s a long way away from Australia, but the North Koreans don’t think so, right? They’re sending troops in to fight for the Russians,” the Labour MP said on the sidelines of the conference. A North Korean government image shows soldiers assembled with short-range, nuclear capable missiles. AP “I mean, it’s extraordinary, what’s going on – the idea that there’s an Asian country that’s just sending their troops through. China doesn’t seem to be doing anything about it. “China’s closeness to Russia is really interesting, and I think that Russia is essentially, in order to get the help, becoming a vassal state of China.



“And that, I think, does have an impact on geopolitics and will have an impact on Australia. “So you can’t close your eyes and look the other way and think that’s a long way away because everything is connected with everything else these days.” A Polish soldier activates a Merops in 2025. Omar Marques/Getty Images Concerns about the Kremlin’s partners in East Asia are yet to result in any consensus on the best international response, despite attempts to impose sanctions on Russia to stymie vital supplies. A draft US law proposed by Republican senator Lindsey Graham, who died in early July, would toughen sanctions on Russia and give the American president the power to impose sanctions on nations that trade with it – including China.



Related Article Opinion

North Korea diplomacy The Chinese president has arrived in North Korea. The world is watching Peter Hartcher Political and international editor Some Democrat and Republican politicians are seeking to force the bill through Congress in a debate that could begin later this month. Even if the bill passes, it would be up to the president to decide whether to apply 100 per cent tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil and gas, such as China and India. President Donald Trump aired his frustration with Ukraine on Sunday (early on Monday AEST) in a complaint about its attacks on Russian oil refineries. “Mr Zelensky has to do one thing: he has to ‌stop ⁠knocking out diesel fuel in Russia,” Trump said during a visit to Ireland. “We spoke ​to Mr ⁠Zelensky about it. There are plenty of other targets. Don’t hit diesel fuel. That’s hurting the ​world.”



American journalist and author Anne Applebaum responded on X: “How about calling on Putin to stop killing Ukrainian civilians.” While Western nations could try to impose sanctions on China, Professor Carlo Masala of the Bundeswehr University Munich said the cost might be too high. Loading “The minute we do it, they will retaliate, which will harm our economies,” he said. “So that’s the reason why they’re shying away, and that’s the point why, at the end of the day, you know, the Russians will be supplied with whatever they need in order to assemble their weapons.” Masala, the author of a recent book, If Russia Wins, said the pressure was on Europe to increase defence production to support Ukraine and prevent a Russian victory.



“The only thing is to basically outproduce China, to create the industrial base for a much stronger support for Ukraine,” he told this masthead. Related Article War Are we in World War III, and just don’t know it? China, however, appears to feel little competition from other nations in its production of military drones and other weapons. “I think this war suits China just fine,” Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski told the YES conference. “China is getting a vassal not just on the cheap, [but] making money in the process – taking over the Russian market for everything.



“If I were a Russian nationalist I would be horrified that Russia will become a very, very junior partner to China.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: ‘Whoever wins with AI wins’: Trump hits back at tech chiefs’ calls to slow down
World.content:
Updated BusinessCompaniesAI ‘Whoever wins with AI wins’: Trump hits back at tech chiefs’ calls to slow down Darlene Superville and Didi Tang Updated September 14, 2026 — 7:20am ,first published 10:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

President Donald Trump played down the need for his administration to check the development of artificial intelligence, saying he worried about ceding America’s edge over China in a global competition and that winning would help address the risks from the advancing technology. While acknowledging the need for some regulation, Trump provided no specifics about potential rules and attributed warnings about the technology moving too quickly and with little oversight to “negative forces” he did not identify, though industry pioneers have raised such concerns. “Whoever wins with AI, wins”: US President Donald Trump. Getty Images “We can put guardrails, we can do this and that, but I think you have a lot of negative forces that are bringing it up that ... shouldn’t be bringing it up, and they’re bringing up things that won’t happen,” Trump told reporters during a weekend trip to Ireland. “But whoever wins with AI, wins.” Asked by a reporter if the industry should slow down or be regulated, Trump said – after watching a golfer tee off in the Irish Open at his resort in Doonbeg – that the United States is leading China in the development of AI and “frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins.”



Related Article Opinion

AI The economic puzzle behind AI giants’ doomsday warnings Clancy Yeates Deputy business editor Chinese President Xi Jinping is due at the White House later in September to meet with Trump, and AI is likely to be among the items they discuss. The Republican president spoke a day after Dario Amodei, CEO of the artificial intelligence company Anthropic, said the industry should put the brakes on its fast-moving development to give safety measures time to catch up. Other tech leaders, including Elon Musk and Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, publicly agreed with Amodei. Amodei issued a lengthy blog post on Saturday, saying his company would implement new safety steps, such as third-party evaluators, while calling on the industry to support a broader downshift. OpenAI chief Sam Altman quickly pledged to adopt Amodei’s suggestion of “independent evaluators with employee-like access”, while Elon Musk, who runs xAI Corp, wrote, “Dario is right”.



While all three leaders have over the years warned of the risks of AI, an actual co-ordinated slowdown has little precedent in a cutthroat industry that has historically cranked out one product after another in the name of boosting user engagement, grabbing market share and striving for sales gains. But the anxiety about severe AI risks has begun to enter the mainstream, driven in part by last week’s high-profile resignation of an Anthropic researcher over existential fears that his company was acting irresponsibly. It’s unclear how far the leading AI companies – which are fierce rivals themselves and also face stiff competition from Chinese firms – will go in imposing new limits or safety checks. Dario Amodei said the tech industry “must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models”. Bloomberg Amodei cited two main factors for his new caution: AI’s ability to improve itself and the recent incident involving OpenAI and Hugging Face, where a swarm of AI agents collaborated to breach a third-party website.



“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” he wrote in a blog post on Saturday. “Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain.” Related Article Analysis

AI ‘We must be stopped’: Why Australia needs to listen to the experts on AI Throughout the AI boom, executives at the leading AI labs have warned about potential existential risks – claims that have sometimes been dismissed as attempts to market the capabilities of their products and position themselves as the best stewards for the technology. Amodei himself has previously said there’s a 25 per cent chance things go “really, really badly”. Anthropic has long positioned itself as being focused on developing AI more responsibly and safely to mitigate the technology’s potential dangers and maximise the societal benefits. The company took pains earlier this year to limit the release of its Mythos model after determining it posed unique cybersecurity threats. Anthropic has also previously said the world needs a system to collectively decide when to slow work on the technology.



At the same time, Anthropic has remained locked in a fierce competition with long-time rival OpenAI to build increasingly sophisticated models that can automate more complex and valuable tasks for business customers. The two firms have both filed confidential paperwork to go public, with Anthropic expected to make its Wall Street debut as soon as this year. Related Article AI The 27-year-old who warned that AI could ‘kill us all’ faces intense scrutiny OpenAI’s Altman said this year would be an “ill-advised moment” to go public, telling Fortune in an interview published on Saturday that a listing would not take place until 2027. “I think it is unacceptable to be taking, like, a 10 per cent chance of killing everybody by the end of the decade,” he added. Growing alarm Earlier this week, Altman said his company was considering slowing down the development of cutting-edge AI, preferably in conjunction with the broader industry.



The company’s top scientist, Jakub Pachocki, had posted a warning about the dangers of AI, saying that he believes companies should be “coordinating to slow down future development as needed”. On Tuesday, Jacob Coxon, an AI researcher, quit his job and accused both of his former employers – Anthropic and OpenAI – of “gambling with our lives” by racing toward superintelligent AI. Coxon said in a social media post that the people building AI believe it could “kill us all by the end of the decade”. In response, Evan Hubinger, a current Anthropic employee, said he and others at the company do worry about this scenario. “I personally think it is >10 per cent within the next decade,” he wrote on X. Back in July, more than 1000 staffers across top AI firms signed a petition calling on the US government to support a mechanism that would help “deliberately pace” AI development to prevent the technology from advancing too fast. AI models are proving increasingly adept at carrying out their own hacks, with Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta Platforms all disclosing in recent months that their models had escaped testing environments, accessed the open internet and breached real-world victims during testing.



Amodei, in his post, wrote that a co-ordinated strategy would allow AI industry leaders in the US to complete needed safety work without sacrificing any competitive advantage. He said that this would require some antitrust exemptions in the US to allow companies to co-ordinate in specific areas, as well as co-operation with China. Related Article AI ‘Could kill us all’: Anthropic insiders say AI has more than 10% chance of ending humanity – soon “If we greatly restrain our AI capabilities in the belief that China will do the same, and then China defects, AI could be so powerful that such a defection could lead to their geopolitical dominance,” he wrote. One Nation NSW leader Mike Newman says Pauline Hanson is unlikely to apologise for her criticism of Anthony Albanese’s mother for living in social housing, labelling the emergence of the months-old comments as a “gotcha moment”.

Asked whether he would be evoking politicians’ family members in political debate, Newman said he wouldn’t adopt Hanson’s style of inflammatory rhetoric, saying: “I’m not going to be talking about any of that”.

Barnaby Joyce, One Nation NSW leader Mike Newman and Pauline Hanson in late August. James Brickwood

After Hanson criticised Albanese’s mother, Maryanne Ellery, for living in social housing for decades, Newman said he didn’t believe the Queensland senator’s comments were “directly aimed at her.”

However, Newman claimed the Prime Minister’s media team had been sitting on Hanson’s criticism since she made them on Karl Stefanovic’s podcast in January, waiting for the opportune moment to release the content.

“The whole point here is that now that the polls are really going the wrong way, that they really want to … get One Nation on yet another sort of, you know, gotcha moment,” Newman told 2GB’s Ben Fordham on Monday morning.

Newman, asked whether Hanson would be apologising, said: “That’ll be up to Pauline. I wouldn’t imagine so.”

World.title: Bodies recovered as rescuers search for more than 100 missing from capsized Indonesian ferry
World.content:
WorldAsiaIndonesia Bodies recovered as rescuers search for more than 100 missing from capsized Indonesian ferry Iman Satria and Niniek Karmini Updated September 14, 2026 — 6:28am ,first published 4:18pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Jakarta: The search is continuing for at least 129 people missing after a ferry overturned in bad weather in Indonesia’s Java Sea on Sunday. At least 108 people were rescued, and the bodies of six passengers were recovered as the search operation expanded around the vessel’s last known position. Images from Indonesian search-and-rescue teams showed the vessel completely capsized. BASARNAS via AP The ferry, with more than 240 people on board, was travelling from Surabaya in East Java to Banjarmasin in South Kalimantan province, on Borneo Island, officials said. The captain had reported rough seas with waves up to 3 metres before issuing a distress call, saying the ship was listing, said I Putu Sudayana, who heads the Banjarmasin Search and Rescue Office. Authorities later received information indicating the vessel had overturned.



The ship was encountering heavy seas when it got into difficulties. BASARNAS via AP The rescue agency in Banjarmasin said it received a report two hours after contact was lost with the Virgo Transport 8 about 2am Sunday. A rescue ship was headed to the vessel’s last known position, the agency said, and by Sunday afternoon authorities were deploying teams supported by a dozen vessels, including four navy ships, and two helicopters. Bodies recovered Initial information indicated the vessel’s last known position was in the Java Sea, about 148 kilometres from Banjarmasin. The ship’s manifest said it was carrying 243 people – 213 passengers and 30 crew members – although it is common in Indonesia for the number of passengers to differ from the manifest. The vessel was also transporting 89 vehicles.



Sudayana, who is co-ordinating the search, said search teams, assisted by nearby tugboats and other passing vessels, had rescued 107 people and recovered six bodies by Sunday afternoon. The 119-metre Virgo Transport 8 ferry was built in Japan in 1987 and operated there until last year, when it was sold to the current Indonesian operator, PT Virgo Karya Shipping. Transportation Minister Dudy Purwagandhi said aerial searches showed the ferry was floating upside down and had not sunk. Rescuers were concentrating search efforts around the overturned vessel, he told reporters. Videos released by the National Search and Rescue Agency on Sunday showed an overturned ferry floating in choppy waters during a helicopter search operation.



Separate footage captured exhausted survivors disembarking from a rescue ship at a port in Banjarmasin, while injured victims were carried on stretchers before being taken by ambulances to nearby hospitals. Distraught relatives wait for news Hundreds of relatives gathered at a command centre in Banjarmasin’s Trisakti port, awaiting word on family members believed to be aboard the ferry. Many anxiously checked passenger manifests and rescue lists as authorities continued searching for survivors. Relatives of passengers look on as a National Search and Rescue Agency (Basarnas) officer writes updates on a whiteboard, amid ongoing rescue operations on the stricken Virgo Transport 8 ferry. AFP “I was shocked when I saw my uncle’s name on the passenger list,” said a woman who goes by a single name, Bunga. “But I felt relieved after officials told me he had been rescued.”



Indonesia has more than 17,000 islands where ferries are a common mode of travel. Disasters occur regularly, with weak safety enforcement often blamed. AP Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Zverev no longer ‘third guy’ of men’s tennis after winning US Open final to claim second slam title
World.content:
SportTennisUS Open Zverev no longer ‘third guy’ of men’s tennis after winning US Open final to claim second slam title Marc McGowan September 14, 2026 — 8:39am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Tennis’ so-called “third guy” has taken a big step towards creating a modern Big Three with his maiden US Open title, before paying tribute to his mother’s support after being diagnosed with type-one diabetes as a child. Alexander Zverev started the year known, and at-times derided, as the best player never to win a grand slam trophy, but ends it as the only man to capture two majors in 2026 after triumphing in New York. Alexander Zverev won his second grand slam singles title at the US Open. AP Photo/Adam Hunger The giant German, contesting his third consecutive slam final, also ensured the United States’ major title drought would extend into a 24th year while taking down ballistic-serving American Ben Shelton 6-3, 7-6 (7-2), 5-7, 6-2 on Monday (AEST). Zverev’s brother Mischa and father Alexander snr are part of his team, but he paid special thanks to his mother – ex-player Irina – for her role in him achieving his tennis dreams.



“We went 30 years without winning a grand slam title, and now we won two in a span of three months,” Zverev said. “I think God has seen how hard we worked, how much we suffered, how much pain we went through, and I think 2026 is the outcome of all the years that happened before. So, thank you guys. You guys are absolutely amazing, and I couldn’t be here without you. Loading “I want to thank one more person who’s never actually watching my matches, but is the most important person in my tennis life, and in my life in general. “When your four-year-old son gets diagnosed with diabetes, and doctors in the office tell you that life and sports will be very limited for that child, it takes a very strong mother to walk out of those offices and to say, ‘My son will be whatever he wants to be. If he wants to be a tennis player, he’ll be a tennis player. If he wants to do something else, he’ll do something else, but this illness will not define us’.



“My mother is the most important and strongest person I know. It takes an unbelievably strong woman to do what she did.” The four-set victory adds to Zverev’s Roland-Garros breakthrough in June that shed his bridesmaid status and means he matches US Open women’s champion Elena Rybakina with two grand slam championships this year. Ben Shelton’s career-best major run ended in a US Open final defeat. Getty Images This result looked unrealistic as he laboured through consecutive five-setters across almost nine-and-a-half hours, but he dropped just one more set in his last five matches. Zverev started his career pitting wits with tennis titans Novak Djokovic, Roger Federer and Rafael Nadal before Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz arrived to torture him once more – with Djokovic still hanging around, too.



Sinner and Alcaraz missed three majors between them because of injury this season, which paved the way for Zverev’s career year, but at least one of them contested both of the grand slam titles he won. Related Article US Open Why this week could bring an end to the great American tennis chase Italy’s world No.1 Sinner suffered a befuddling second-round loss from two sets and 5-1 up in Paris, while Alcaraz’s first tournament since April after recovering from a wrist setback ended in the US Open quarter-finals to Shelton. Shelton was trying to be the first American since Andy Roddick in 2003 to win a major, but he played catch up from the moment he crashed a second serve into the net in the opening game to gift Zverev an instant break. He had never beaten Alcaraz before this fortnight and winning his maiden grand slam final depended on him upsetting Zverev – the top seed in Sinner’s absence – for the first time in their sixth meeting.



However, Zverev has made a habit of chewing up and spitting out left-handers, winning 44 of his past 45 clashes with southpaws entering his latest battle with Shelton, who won an all-American clash with Frances Tiafoe to advance to the last day of the event. No longer burdened by the gaping hole in his otherwise bulging resume, Zverev presented an even tougher challenge to Shelton on this stage despite emphatically having the crowd on his side. Zverev was mostly outstanding, except for a dip late in the third set. AP Photo/Adam Hunger Shelton settled after his erroneous opening, but could not penetrate his rival’s own service game, which became a trend. Zverev won more than 90 per cent of points on his first serve, which the 198-centimetre German traditionally lands more than any player on the planet – and it was more of the same in the final. Serving to stay in the opening set, Shelton repeated his mistake from the first game of the match when he double-faulted into the net on break point to go down a set.



The second set was a closer affair, giving the American more opportunities to electrify the home fans, which included everyone from Roddick and Jimmy Connors to Hollywood actors Brad Pitt, Amy Schumer, Rami Malek, Pierce Brosnan, Chris Pine and Brazilian football superstar Ronaldo. Shelton pricked his ear several times to urge the crowd to rally behind him, but they needed little prompting to do so. Pierce Brosnan (right) was among the celebrities in the crowd. AP Photo/Kirsty Wigglesworth He double-faulted to go down another break point in the third game of the second set, but bellowed “Yes!” as Zverev’s subsequent backhand return thudded into the net. Shelton stretched Zverev to deuce at 3-3, but the world No.2 kept coming up with the answers to that point.



They traded blows until a tiebreak was required. Zverev produced an outstanding 10 minutes to blow Shelton away, starting with a spectacular down-the-line forehand pass winner on his way to a 5-0 lead that comfortably converted to a two-set lead. Shelton was up against it from that deficit, but Zverev began showing signs of frailty as the third set progressed. Zverev is a two-time grand slam champion. Getty Images The German followed two loose points from 30-0 in the sixth game by narrowly missing an inside-out forehand where he didn’t need to be so perfect as he finally offered Shelton a break point. Zverev dispatched that one with a thunderous backhand, but imploded at 5-6. He shanked a forehand wide to fall in a 0-40 hole, then put a volley shockingly wide two points later to drop the third set.



Shelton never lost his swagger throughout the entire contest, theatrically responding to Zverev’s dip with raised eyebrows before again pricking his ear to energise the crowd. Related Article US Open The best rivalry in women’s tennis: Celebs in the stands as new world No.1 thwarts Sabalenka His momentum did not last long. Shelton immediately found himself in trouble on serve in the fourth set, staving off one break point before tugging a backhand crosscourt pass wide to hand Zverev the advantage. Trying to break Zverev is one of the sport’s greatest challenges, particularly with the finish line in sight.



The door was slightly ajar at 30-all as Zverev served for a 3-1 lead, then received a time violation, but he again held firm to clear that hurdle then broke Shelton again for 5-2 to as good as seal the win. Zverev served the match out with ease, but did not realise for several moments he had clinched the title before breaking into a huge smile and later embracing his team then Shelton’s father and coach Bryan. World.title: Australia exposed to growing risk from deepening China-Russia-North Korea alliance
World.content:
Exclusive WorldEuropeRussia-Ukraine war Australia exposed to growing risk from deepening China-Russia-North Korea alliance September 14, 2026 — 8:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australia is exposed to a deepening military alliance between Russia, China and North Korea as the three partners work together in the war on Ukraine, prompting experts to warn of the risks to security in Asia. Former CIA director David Petraeus warned that China was proving its capacity to design new weaponry and manufacture it in large volumes for Russia, heightening concerns for all Western nations. Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin tour an exhibition in Beijing in May. Alexander Kazakov/Pool Sputnik Kremlin via AP Political leaders and experts also pointed to the Kremlin’s reliance on North Korea as a rising threat to Asia, given that the rogue state is supplying Russia with scores of missiles in an expanding weapons trade.



General Petraeus, who served 37 years in the US Army, told this masthead that China was innovating rapidly to supply Russia and apply lessons from the war in Ukraine. “We should be very concerned that China is learning assiduously from what Russia and Ukraine are doing,” he said on the sidelines of a security conference in Kyiv. David Petraeus was America's most high-profile general for much of the past 20 years. AP “It’s providing the bulk of the components for the Russian military-industrial complex, and it is a leader in the world in robotic systems and drones and so forth. “And it has an ability to do something that is hugely important in this war, which is not just to innovate but to scale the production of those weapons.”



Related Article Russia-Ukraine war The new terror stalking Kyiv day and night Petraeus, an influential voice in defence investment as chairman of the KKR Global Institute, forecast a total shift in military doctrine due to the changing nature of war in Ukraine and argued that China was a key force in the conflict. As the “manufacturing capital” of the world, he said, China was gaining expertise in the mass production of drones and other weapons. “We should obviously be very keenly aware of that,” he said. “We should be very keenly aware of what is being developed here on this battlefield because it is the future of war, and it’s changing quite rapidly. “And that should lead us, all Western countries, to develop a new concept of war that can drive, urgently, revolutionary institutional change.”



One of the most influential investors in new drones, former Google chairman Eric Schmidt, said he saw the impact of Russia’s partnership with North Korea during a previous visit to the Ukrainian capital. “The North Koreans are giving the Russians the KN-25, which is a major ballistic missile – it’s an enormous size and does enormous damage,” he told this masthead. North Korean leader Kim Jong-un inspects a Hwasong-17 intercontinental ballistic missile. AP “I was here when it was shot at Kyiv. I know it to be true. That’s very, very worrisome. So the connection between China and North Korea and Russia is a great concern.” One of Schmidt’s companies, Perennial Autonomy, develops the Merops interceptor drones used by regiments across Ukraine and sold at low cost, in a sign of his support for the country.



Related Article Russia-Ukraine war Four years on, Ukraine is under more pressure than ever. So is Russia The defence and investment chiefs were at the Yalta European Strategies Conference in Kyiv in recent days, where most discussions focused on the threat to Europe posed by Russian President Vladimir Putin. Rising risks to Asia region The risks for the Indo-Pacific, however, are rising as Russia relies on China and North Korea. Petraeus estimated that Russia would build 10 million drones this year, while Ukraine was seeking to increase its production from 8 to 10 million.



North Korea has supplied an estimated 10,000 troops to Russia, as well as large volumes of artillery ammunition and more than 100 missiles. Former Swedish prime minister Carl Bildt said the concern should not only be about what Russia received, particularly in Asia. ‘It may seem like Ukraine’s a long way away from Australia, but the North Koreans don’t think so’ Emily Thornberry, chair of UK Foreign Affairs Committee “The worrying thing is, of course, that the Russians are delivering things back,” he told this masthead. Bildt noted speculation that North Korea wanted to build a nuclear submarine and needed Russian help to develop the propulsion systems.



Dame Emily Thornberry, the chair of the foreign affairs committee in the UK parliament, said Asia would see the impact of the ties between Russia and its partners. “It may seem like Ukraine’s a long way away from Australia, but the North Koreans don’t think so, right? They’re sending troops in to fight for the Russians,” the Labour MP said on the sidelines of the conference. A North Korean government image shows soldiers assembled with short-range, nuclear capable missiles. AP “I mean, it’s extraordinary, what’s going on – the idea that there’s an Asian country that’s just sending their troops through. China doesn’t seem to be doing anything about it. “China’s closeness to Russia is really interesting, and I think that Russia is essentially, in order to get the help, becoming a vassal state of China.



“And that, I think, does have an impact on geopolitics and will have an impact on Australia. “So you can’t close your eyes and look the other way and think that’s a long way away because everything is connected with everything else these days.” A Polish soldier activates a Merops in 2025. Omar Marques/Getty Images Concerns about the Kremlin’s partners in East Asia are yet to result in any consensus on the best international response, despite attempts to impose sanctions on Russia to stymie vital supplies. A draft US law proposed by Republican senator Lindsey Graham, who died in early July, would toughen sanctions on Russia and give the American president the power to impose sanctions on nations that trade with it – including China.



Related Article Opinion

North Korea diplomacy The Chinese president has arrived in North Korea. The world is watching Peter Hartcher Political and international editor Some Democrat and Republican politicians are seeking to force the bill through Congress in a debate that could begin later this month. Even if the bill passes, it would be up to the president to decide whether to apply 100 per cent tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil and gas, such as China and India. President Donald Trump aired his frustration with Ukraine on Sunday (early on Monday AEST) in a complaint about its attacks on Russian oil refineries. “Mr Zelensky has to do one thing: he has to ‌stop ⁠knocking out diesel fuel in Russia,” Trump said during a visit to Ireland. “We spoke ​to Mr ⁠Zelensky about it. There are plenty of other targets. Don’t hit diesel fuel. That’s hurting the ​world.”



American journalist and author Anne Applebaum responded on X: “How about calling on Putin to stop killing Ukrainian civilians.” While Western nations could try to impose sanctions on China, Professor Carlo Masala of the Bundeswehr University Munich said the cost might be too high. Loading “The minute we do it, they will retaliate, which will harm our economies,” he said. “So that’s the reason why they’re shying away, and that’s the point why, at the end of the day, you know, the Russians will be supplied with whatever they need in order to assemble their weapons.” Masala, the author of a recent book, If Russia Wins, said the pressure was on Europe to increase defence production to support Ukraine and prevent a Russian victory.



“The only thing is to basically outproduce China, to create the industrial base for a much stronger support for Ukraine,” he told this masthead. Related Article War Are we in World War III, and just don’t know it? China, however, appears to feel little competition from other nations in its production of military drones and other weapons. “I think this war suits China just fine,” Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski told the YES conference. “China is getting a vassal not just on the cheap, [but] making money in the process – taking over the Russian market for everything.



“If I were a Russian nationalist I would be horrified that Russia will become a very, very junior partner to China.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

One Nation NSW leader Mike Newman says Pauline Hanson is unlikely to apologise for her criticism of Anthony Albanese’s mother for living in social housing, labelling the emergence of the months-old comments as a “gotcha moment”.

Asked whether he would be evoking politicians’ family members in political debate, Newman said he wouldn’t adopt Hanson’s style of inflammatory rhetoric, saying: “I’m not going to be talking about any of that”.

Barnaby Joyce, One Nation NSW leader Mike Newman and Pauline Hanson in late August. James Brickwood

After Hanson criticised Albanese’s mother, Maryanne Ellery, for living in social housing for decades, Newman said he didn’t believe the Queensland senator’s comments were “directly aimed at her.”

However, Newman claimed the Prime Minister’s media team had been sitting on Hanson’s criticism since she made them on Karl Stefanovic’s podcast in January, waiting for the opportune moment to release the content.

“The whole point here is that now that the polls are really going the wrong way, that they really want to … get One Nation on yet another sort of, you know, gotcha moment,” Newman told 2GB’s Ben Fordham on Monday morning.

Newman, asked whether Hanson would be apologising, said: “That’ll be up to Pauline. I wouldn’t imagine so.”

World.title: Bodies recovered as rescuers search for more than 100 missing from capsized Indonesian ferry
World.content:
WorldAsiaIndonesia Bodies recovered as rescuers search for more than 100 missing from capsized Indonesian ferry Iman Satria and Niniek Karmini Updated September 14, 2026 — 6:28am ,first published 4:18pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Jakarta: The search is continuing for at least 129 people missing after a ferry overturned in bad weather in Indonesia’s Java Sea on Sunday. At least 108 people were rescued, and the bodies of six passengers were recovered as the search operation expanded around the vessel’s last known position. Images from Indonesian search-and-rescue teams showed the vessel completely capsized. BASARNAS via AP The ferry, with more than 240 people on board, was travelling from Surabaya in East Java to Banjarmasin in South Kalimantan province, on Borneo Island, officials said. The captain had reported rough seas with waves up to 3 metres before issuing a distress call, saying the ship was listing, said I Putu Sudayana, who heads the Banjarmasin Search and Rescue Office. Authorities later received information indicating the vessel had overturned.



The ship was encountering heavy seas when it got into difficulties. BASARNAS via AP The rescue agency in Banjarmasin said it received a report two hours after contact was lost with the Virgo Transport 8 about 2am Sunday. A rescue ship was headed to the vessel’s last known position, the agency said, and by Sunday afternoon authorities were deploying teams supported by a dozen vessels, including four navy ships, and two helicopters. Bodies recovered Initial information indicated the vessel’s last known position was in the Java Sea, about 148 kilometres from Banjarmasin. The ship’s manifest said it was carrying 243 people – 213 passengers and 30 crew members – although it is common in Indonesia for the number of passengers to differ from the manifest. The vessel was also transporting 89 vehicles.



Sudayana, who is co-ordinating the search, said search teams, assisted by nearby tugboats and other passing vessels, had rescued 107 people and recovered six bodies by Sunday afternoon. The 119-metre Virgo Transport 8 ferry was built in Japan in 1987 and operated there until last year, when it was sold to the current Indonesian operator, PT Virgo Karya Shipping. Transportation Minister Dudy Purwagandhi said aerial searches showed the ferry was floating upside down and had not sunk. Rescuers were concentrating search efforts around the overturned vessel, he told reporters. Videos released by the National Search and Rescue Agency on Sunday showed an overturned ferry floating in choppy waters during a helicopter search operation.



Separate footage captured exhausted survivors disembarking from a rescue ship at a port in Banjarmasin, while injured victims were carried on stretchers before being taken by ambulances to nearby hospitals. Distraught relatives wait for news Hundreds of relatives gathered at a command centre in Banjarmasin’s Trisakti port, awaiting word on family members believed to be aboard the ferry. Many anxiously checked passenger manifests and rescue lists as authorities continued searching for survivors. Relatives of passengers look on as a National Search and Rescue Agency (Basarnas) officer writes updates on a whiteboard, amid ongoing rescue operations on the stricken Virgo Transport 8 ferry. AFP “I was shocked when I saw my uncle’s name on the passenger list,” said a woman who goes by a single name, Bunga. “But I felt relieved after officials told me he had been rescued.”



Indonesia has more than 17,000 islands where ferries are a common mode of travel. Disasters occur regularly, with weak safety enforcement often blamed. AP Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Here Now: China’s booming coffee scene is challenging Kiwi ideas about the perfect brew
World.content:
New Zealanders are serious about their coffee. But while most of the coffee consumed here comes from traditional producing nations such as Brazil and Colombia, another coffee-growing region is quietly attracting attention: China's Yunnan province.

Coffee grows in a band around the globe known as the "green belt", which spans the region between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn. China's southwestern province of Yunnan sits on the northern edge of that zone and has spent the past two decades building a reputation as a producer of Arabica coffee.

Kelly Qu, co-owner of MQ Coffee in Auckland, told RNZ's Here Now that a visit to a coffee farm in Yunnan changed the way she thought about coffee.

Qu first encountered the region'scoffee industry while travelling through Yunnan, where she learned how coffee is picked, processed and roasted at origin.

"The average coffee consumer doesn't always think about where coffee comes from. They just think about the final product," she said.

Coffee beans grown in Yunnan MQ Coffee

MQ Coffee's head of education Hubs Tong said investment, research and strong domestic demand had transformed China's coffee sector.

"At first, it was not of very good quality Arabica," he said. "But with more and more resource being poured into it ... the procedures being taken at the region to produce higher quality coffee has been expanding and growing."

While coffee production has grown rapidly in China, the country's coffee culture has evolved differently from New Zealand's.

Tong said coffee was still relatively new in China, gaining mainstream popularity after the arrival of Starbucks. Since then, a generation of growers, roasters, café owners and specialty coffee enthusiasts has emerged.

One of the biggest differences is how coffee is consumed.

In China, specialty coffee drinkers often preferred brewed or filter coffee rather than espresso, Tong said.

Filter coffee produces a lighter, less intense drink that highlights delicate flavours such as citrus, floral and honey notes. Tong believes that preference aligns closely with China's long tea-drinking tradition, as filter coffee is "a more tea-like beverage".

Most coffee grown in Yunnan is consumed within China, but Qu said New Zealand consumers were starting to see it appear in some specialty roasteries.

Tong described Yunnan coffee as having plenty of sweetness, body and complexity.

Kelly Qu Supplied

Qu adds, "It holds up well in the milk beverage", which could make it a good fit for New Zealand's enduring love affair with flat whites.

Despite growing interest in filter coffee, Tong said New Zealand's mature café culture could make consumers slower to embrace new trends.

"Our coffee culture [has] had its heyday," he said. "Our consumer market is now finding it hard to take on newer ideas and research that's being done in coffee."

Still, he believes tastes are changing.

The New Zealand Specialty Coffee Association recently revived its brewers competition after a long hiatus, reflecting growing interest in pour-over and filter coffee.

If we continue to see consumer demand shift, that gap may start to narrow. And for New Zealand coffee lovers, the next great cup could come from an origin they least expect.

World.title: Person taken to hospital following 'water incident' at Manawatū beach
World.content:
A person is in hospital following an emergency callout to a lower North Island beach.

Hato Hone St John said it was notified of a "water incident" at Tangimoana Beach in Manawatū at 8.14am on Monday.

A spokesperson said two ambulances, an operations manager, and one rapid response vehicle attended.

"One patient has been transported to Palmerston North Hospital in a moderate condition."

In a statement, police said they were at the scene of the incident which involved a capsized boat.

"Police were first made aware of the incident at 8.35am.

"Emergency services are on scene and more information will be provided when available."

Fire and Emergency confirmed crews were also on site.

World.title: Westpac warns El Niño impact on the primary sector could slow GDP growth
World.content:
Westpac economists warn of El Nino risks to NZ economy Morning Report Download MP3 7m

Westpac Bank is warning developing El Niño conditions could impact badly on pasture-based agriculture, particularly dairy, sheep and beef.

El Niño increases the risk of drought in many parts of New Zealand - especially in eastern regions and the upper North Island - which can reduce pasture growth, lower production, lift costs and disrupt processing patterns across the season.

Senior Westpac economist Michael Gordon said previous drought impacts suggested it could potentially slow GDP growth by as much as one percentage point in a "worst-case scenario".

"There is still no certainty around how this big climate pattern translates into localised weather patterns in New Zealand, but certainly there are heightened risks there."

He said while the impacts were mostly concentrated to the primary industries it could have flow-on effects for other industries like transport and food processing.

For consumers, Gordon said there was a risk it could raise the price of some imported food products.

"It's perhaps more a question of what happens to prices of a lot of the foods that we import.

"Because this is an event that is affecting many parts of the world - it can affect crops in Australia and in Indonesia - it's difficult to trace all the effects of that but it generally means some upwards pressure on prices.

"And it can be things like quite subtle events like vegetable oil prices going up. There's a little bit of that in everything."

He said while more livestock flowing through to processors during drought will push meat prices down, the following year it would likely see prices up as herds rebuild.

One advantage is that in dairy and meat, much of the production occurs before drought becomes a major issue, which naturally limits the impact.

Gordon said New Zealand's farmers were fairly resilient, have already adapted many systems and had had an early warning about this event.

World.title: New apple variety grown in New Zealand makes world debut in Vietnam
World.content:
Grower T&G has launched its newest premium apple variety, the Joli, in Vietnam, ramping up its push into the lucrative Asian export market.

T&G Apples managing director Shane Kingston said the new variety - a large red apple that is sweet, juicy and perfect for families - was designed specifically for sharing.

"For the first time, shoppers will be able to buy premium Joli apples and experience a brand we know has strong global potential, with the makings of the next billion-dollar apple in our portfolio," he said.

"Joli builds on T&G's proven ability to take outstanding New Zealand-bred apple varieties to the world."

Kingston said a new apple like the Joli represented over a decade of breeding, testing and growing before it could be brought to market.

"When it succeeds, the value is felt well beyond the orchard - by growers, regional communities, customers and the national economy."

He said T&G's other premium apple variert, the Envy, had shown how New Zealand innovation can create value in global markets - having this year surpassed $1 billion in global sales.

While overall global apple consumption is growing modestly, the premium apple category is expanding, driven by consumers willing to pay more for brands they trust to consistently deliver a superior eating experience.

Between 2025 and 2030, the global premium apple category is expected to grow from US$13 billion (NZ$22.3b) to US$19b (NZ$32.7b), representing a compound annual growth rate of almost 8 percent.

Kingston said the company had big plans for Joli and it aimed to significantly increase production in New Zealand by 2030.

He said, to achieve that, T&G was encouraging growers in regions such as Marlborough to consider diversifying into planting Joli apples.

World.title: Warriors warning on tickets for Knights clash: 'Get out of the road, you scalpers, no room for you'
World.content:
Warriors boss Cameron George is urging ticket scalpers to stay away and let genuine fans enjoy this weekend's last home game of the season.

Saturday night's loss to the Dolphins means the Warriors now face a must-win game against Newcastle to keep their hopes of a maiden NRL Premiership alive.

Last week many fans missed out on tickets for the Mount Smart game and were then left fuming as tickets appeared online just minutes later at vastly inflated prices.

One listing offered four tickets in the Eastern Stand for a buy-now price of $1200.

Working in the club and fans favour this week is that the game will be played at the 55,000 capacity Eden Park which holds roughly double the number of fans as Mount Smart.

Warriors boss discusses weekend loss, plans for next game Morning Report Download MP3 5m

Club CEO Geroge was critical of those who were making money from the resale of tickets.

"They've just got to pull their heads in those people, let the genuine people buy the tickets and come to the game and enjoy it with their family," George told Morning Report.

"I was really disappointed to see it last week and I just hope they pull their heads in this week and get out of our road and let the families and the genuine people pay for the tickets at the right price.

"If I was to ever catch anyone doing it, I'd be barring them from every Warriors game for the rest of their life."

Crowd attendance number - Warriors v Dolphins - NRL Finals Week 1. 2026. Brett Phibbs / www.photosport.nz

Reselling of legitimate tickets is allowed in New Zealand as long as the seller has the tickets in their possession.

However George had a message for those hoping to make a financial gain.

"Just get out of our road, you scalpers. No room for you. Let us have the right people buy the tickets."

Warriors CEO Cameron George PHOTOSPORT

George is expecting Sunday's game against the Knights to sell out for a game he describes as an international for his side.

"It's us versus Australia. So the more people we get there, the better New Zealand will be.

"There are 17 teams in this comp and we're the only one from here so it's us against them. This is our New Zealand grand final in the NRL and it's pretty special."

Warriors club members can buy tickets from midday Monday with general public tickets going on sale Tuesday.

World.title: Bougainville president condemns 'terroristic acts of violence' at Panguna Mine
World.content:
The president of the Autonomous Bougaville Government (ABG) has condemned the arson attack on a foreign mining company's equipment at the Panguna mine site.

Armed men are alleged to have entered the site and set fire to heavy haul trucks and other equipment belonging to Indian company Lloyds Metals and Energy Limited.

President Ishmael Toroama said he strongly condemned the actions of those who assaulted personnel and destroyed equipment at the Lloyds Metals camp.

He said his government and the people of the autonomous Papua New Guinea region will not be intimidated by people seeking to undermine efforts to redevelop the Panguna Mine.

Toroama said while the majority of Bougainvilleans look forward to this development, certain elements have chosen to undermine it.

"The actions of these individuals are selfish and serve only their own greedy intent," Toroama said in a statement late Sunday.

"They do not have the best interests of our government or our people at heart. This type of behaviour has no place in Bougainville and will not be tolerated."

More on Bougainville:

Lloyds was selected by the ABG almost a year ago as one of the developers involved in assessing the future rehabilitation and possible reopening of the copper and gold mine.

Regarding the attack on Lloyds personnel and equipment, Toroama said those responsible for this incident will face the full force of the law through the Bougainville Police Service.

"A coordinated community effort is also underway to apprehend the suspects and prevent any further incidents of this nature."

The president said the incident will only strengthen the resolve of those behind the effort "to enforce the government's mandate to reopen the Panguna Mine."

"Let me be very clear: this government is of the people and by the people.

World.title: Petone Beach's leopard seal found dead, being tested for bird flu
World.content:
A leopard seal which hundreds of spectators visited has died, a Hutt City councillor says.

The female leopard seal was spotted two weeks ago lounging on Petone Beach, with some concerns members of the public were harassing the animal.

Councillor Brady Dyer said the seal died on Sunday night, and will be removed by the Department of Conservation (DOC) on Monday.

Conservationists echoed the news on social media, saying they suspected the seal looked unwell.

A leopard seal on Petone Beach garners keen public interest, 6 September, 2026

DOC acting operations manager Olivia Keane said the female rāpoka / leopard seal was found dead in the Hutt River on Saturday afternoon.

Keane said the Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) had been informed and would be testing for H5 bird flu.

World.title: Student dies after binge drinking, choking on vomit
World.content:
The death of a 20-year-old University of Otago student after choking on his own vomit at his birthday party is a woeful illustration of the country's youth drinking culture, a coroner says.

In findings released on Monday, Associate Coroner Emma van Son said it was critical that young people understood the serious dangers of binge drinking and hoped lessons could be learned from the young man's tragic death in 2023.

The first-year student, whose name has been suppressed, went to the party with friends at about 6.40pm, where he drank a significant amount of alcohol and was later found passed out and "pretty much unresponsive" in the kitchen.

He started vomiting, so other partygoers carried him to one of the bedrooms and put him to bed where he continued to throw up, although it was unclear if anyone stayed with him.

Witnesses suggested that it was unusual for him to "get that drunk".

The coroner said a witness described a "big group of people" clearing vomit from the man's throat before emergency services were called at 11.25pm and he was carried into the hallway.

Partygoers did CPR, which was continued by paramedics, but the man could not be revived.

The report said the man died from asphyxia due to the aspiration of gastric contents while intoxicated.

The student's blood alcohol level was 319 milligrams of alcohol per 100 millilitres of blood. The legal blood alcohol limit for drivers from 20 years-old is 50 milligrams per 100 millilitres.

Van Son said the young man's death was the tragic consequence of excessive alcohol consumption.

"His death was senseless and is a woeful illustration of the prevalent youth drinking culture in New Zealand. Sadly, [his] death is not an isolated incident," she said.

"Alcohol is a central nervous system depressant that exerts its effects in a manner similar to that of general anaesthetics. The toxicologist advised that where alcohol is concerned there is a 'fine line' between anaesthesia and death. If a person becomes unconscious as a result of heavy alcohol consumption, there is always a risk that the person could die."

Van Son said she hoped that greater public awareness of the risks of binge drinking could reduce the chance of other deaths happening in similar circumstances.

"At very high levels alcohol can cause a person to become unconscious. As a result, that person has less control of breathing and is in danger of their airway becoming blocked, particularly if they vomit and aspirate on their gastric contents," she said.

"It is critical that young drinkers, particularly, appreciate the seriousness of the dangers of binge drinking and know what to do if someone becomes unresponsive after drinking."

While people's first instinct might be to let someone who has passed out drunk "sleep it off", things could quickly go from bad to worse when someone drank enough to lose consciousness, the associate coroner said.

She said knowing the signs of acute alcohol intoxication, including confusion, vomiting, seizures, blue-looking or pale skin, being uncoordinated and stumbling, passing out and being unable to be woken, and slow or irregular breathing, could save someone's life.

Van Son said the safest first aid treatment for a person who fell unconscious because of the effects of alcohol was to call for an ambulance and let properly trained medical professionals assess them.

St John and Health New Zealand advised people to treat alcohol poisoning as an emergency.

Van Son extended her deepest condolences to the young man's family, friends and loved ones for their very sad loss.

A University of Otago spokesperson said it welcomed and endorsed the associate coroner's recommendations and comments.

"The safety and wellbeing of our students remain our top priorities and we will continue to communicate regularly with students about responsible consumption of alcohol," they said.

"As well as proactive communications, the university has a range of services available dedicated to supporting students' safety, health and wellbeing, including clinicians with specialist drug and alcohol harm expertise."

World.title: Hull bounces back for surprise second, 'perfect race' not enough for Myers
World.content:
Cam Myers and Jess Hull have both delivered superb performances on the track to give Australia an impressive final day of the inaugural Ultimate Athletics Championship in Budapest.

Myers ran what he felt was a "perfect" race as he again finished runner-up to Commonwealth Games mile champion Josh Kerr in the 1,500 metres, while Hull was second in the 5,000m as they both picked up $US75,000 ($105,000) for their efforts.

"Sometimes you run a perfect race and it's still not enough," Myers wrote on Instagram.

Ultimately, the Australian challenge ended without a victory in the sport's new, lucrative three-day global event.

Olyslagers shocked by pay packet Australia's Nicola Olyslagers finishes second in the high jump at the new Ultimate Championship competition.

There was a disappointing start to the night when 21-year-old Torrie Lewis withdrew from the 200m with injury, a day after the country's fastest man, Lachlan Kennedy, failed to make the men's 100m final by 0.05 of a second.

Hull, as she does so often, immediately lifted the mood, though.

After fading to ninth in Saturday's 1,500m final, she was an outsider in the longer event with her best time among the slowest in the field, but with the race run at a steady pace, both she and Commonwealth champ Rose Davies settled into the pack.

Runaway winner Likina Amebaw injected some serious speed to open a 30m lead with two laps to go, but Hull turned on her afterburners to find a way through on the inside and snatch a brilliant second behind the Ethiopian star in a massive lifetime best of 14 minutes and 32.39 seconds.

"That's much more reflective of the athlete I am," Hull said.

"I don't have an answer for the 1,500m last night. I was just quick to say, 'Forget about it and move on.' I've been able to do that a few times in a 5K now — bounce back — so I'm really proud of that. I've had a great year."

The men's 1,500m was one of the deepest fields of the competition — even without Norwegian great Jakob Ingebrigtsen, who withdrew after winning the 5,000m — as mile world record holder Kerr, Olympic champion Cole Hocker and last year's surprise world champion Isaac Nader all lined up.

Cameron Myers (left) had to settle for second behind Josh Kerr (right) again. (Getty Images: Martin Rickett/PA Images)

But 20-year-old Myers was more than qualified to operate in such company after winning the Diamond League final in Brussels a week ago.

Annoyed at how he raced when losing to Kerr over the mile in the Commonwealth Games, he ran a much smarter race in Hungary, extricating himself from the inside at the bell to move second and give himself clear track to try to reel in Kerr.

The Briton did not falter, clocking 3:29.35 and leaving Myers to settle for second in 3:29.68.

Loading Instagram content

"It's bittersweet," Myers said.

"I thought at 200m to go that I was going to give it a proper crack. I felt like I wasn't working too hard.

"At 100m I thought I still had a good chance and then I came to 50 to go and I was like, 'Wow, that's what a world record holder looks like.'

Myers wins Diamond League Final Cameron Myers has beaten a star-studded field at the Diamond League Final in Brussels.

"So, he was just too strong today, but I think I ran a perfect race."

Myers said he had an "awesome season" and made a real step up after years of collecting age-group records and titles.

"This is me becoming the athlete I wanted to be," he said.

The event closed in front of another capacity 20,000 crowd with two excellent 200m finals where American duo Kenny Bednarek and Melissa Jefferson-Wooden — whose 21.47-second run made her the third-fastest ever over the distance — completed 100/200m doubles to earn $US300,000 ($419,000) each.

World.title: Opetaia's KO fuels duel between 'two baddest dudes'
World.content:
Jai Opetaia and David Benavidez have taken the matchmaking into their own hands after the Australian stopped Noel Mikaelian for the first time in the German-Armenian's 32-fight career to pave the way for the Las Vegas blockbuster.

The cruiserweight improved to 31-0 on Sunday (AEST), picking apart the WBC champion before landing a short right hook in the ninth round that stunned Mikaelian at T-Mobile Arena.

He followed up with three more punches to send Mikaelian onto the ropes and trigger a standing count he had no chance of beating.

It was the first time Mikaelian had been stopped, after three tight losses and 28 wins previously.

American star Benavidez was ringside and Opetaia called him onto the canvas, where the two-belt cruiserweight champion, who has won world titles in two other divisions, agreed to fight the Australian on May 5 in Vegas next year.

"I'm still here, still undefeated and like I said — who's next?" Opetaia, who had his IBF title stripped when debuting for new promoter Zuffa Boxing earlier this year, asked before inviting the WBA and WBO champion into the ring.

"I respect him. He's done a lot for the sport and what better fight to make. Respectfully, let's get it on."

Benavidez is set to defend his belts in December but was keen to clear up any conjecture around his interest in fighting Opetaia, who was immediately sent to hospital for scans as a precaution following the fight.

"Let's do it right here, Cinco de Mayo (May 5) next year," Benavidez said, before the pair shook hands.

"I like this man. He looks like he likes war. I am the same way, so we're going to give the fans a hell of a fight."

Opetaia, sporting a swollen left eye from a first-round head clash, could not hide his delight.

"He's said it now, he's not taking it back," the Australian said.

Zuffa boss Dana White, who runs UFC, is no fan of post-fight match-making in either sport but admitted the prospect of the pair facing off next year was irresistible.

"There was a lot of wheeling and dealing going on in this arena tonight," he said.

Mikaelian entered the clash with the WBC belt but it's unlikely that will be taken by Opetaia, given the organisation's unwillingness to sanction the Zuffa bout.

Benavidez could hold it by the time they meet though, with his December fight potentially including that prize if opponent and number one WBC contender Michal Cieslak is awarded full status.

Opetaia remains in a court battle, with the IBF attempting to claim back his belt, while the WBA are currently the sole member of boxing's four major bodies willing to work with Zuffa.

But with both boxers keen and the boxing world fixated on a match-up, White thinks the politics will be irrelevant.

"We've gotten into a better place with the sanctioning organisations so we'll see how that plays out," he said.

"But we all know these are the two baddest dudes in the world in that weight class. So belts, no belts, whatever."

AAP
